facts: Registrations peaked at 4.74 million in 2023, then fell to 4.38 million in 2024 and 3.88 million in 2025, the first two-year decline in a decade and 860,000 below the peak.
From 2018 to 2022 registrations had grown about 18 percent a year.
In the 2024 cohort 2.27 million of the 4.38 million applicants were repeat candidates, 51.8 percent.
The share of graduates sitting kaoyan fell from 45.27 percent in 2023 to 37.15 percent in 2024.

a.text: Kaoyan: millions of people spending a whole year to postpone unemployment by three more years. You wake at 5:30 to fight a stranger for a library seat, armed only with a thermos, so you can memorize a vocabulary book where "abandon" is the first word and the only one anyone remembers. Politics is the one subject where your entire score depends on Xiao Xiurong dropping four pamphlets in late November, like a prophet doing a limited sneaker release. Math? Li Yongle's 660 problems, and somehow you get 661 wrong. Then the national cutoff comes out, you miss it by two points, and you enter tiaoji, a dating app where you beg a university in a province you can't find on a map to please, please take you. Fail? Relax. They call it erzhan, "the second war." Because nothing says higher education like trench warfare.

b.text:
Kaoyan, from 2018 to 2022 you grew about 18 percent a year. That's not an exam, that's a pyramid scheme with a highlighter. Then you peaked at 4.74 million in 2023 and lost 860,000 people in two years. Even people who volunteered to suffer said, "Actually, I'll suffer somewhere else."

In 2024, 2.27 million of your 4.38 million applicants were repeat candidates. That's 51.8 percent. You're not a test anymore, you're a class reunion where everyone still brings flashcards.

And the share of graduates sitting you dropped from 45.27 percent to 37.15 percent in one year. That's not a decline, that's a breakup text.

Kaoyan, you're the only ex where half the people come back, and you still say, "Let's try again next year."

facts: 'Laotoule' are three- and four-wheeled low-speed electric vehicles driven without a licence or plates; they cannot be registered as motor vehicles or covered by compulsory traffic insurance.
In July 2021 five Beijing departments announced a transition period ending with 2023; from 1 January 2024 non-compliant three- and four-wheelers were banned from Beijing's roads and public parking.
The 2018 national notice on managing low-speed electric vehicles is the main basis for local crackdowns, and as of 2023 a national standard for four-wheel low-speed vehicles was still being drafted.
To be road-legal a vehicle has to be in the national motor-vehicle catalogue with 3C certification, and the driver has to hold a driving licence.

a.text:
Laotoule. "Old man's joy."

No licence. No plates. No insurance.

That's not a car. That's a car in witness protection.

It legally can't be registered as a motor vehicle. So it's not a car. It's a vibe with four wheels and a horn.

Beijing gave it a transition period: July 2021 to the end of 2023. Two and a half years of notice. That's not a ban. That's hospice care.

The national notice came out in 2018. As of 2023, the national standard was still being drafted.

Grandpa got his car in a week. The regulators are on year five of one sentence.

But let's be honest. Grandpa didn't buy it.

You did. It was cheaper than visiting.

b.text: Laotoule: the only car that runs on a battery and pure denial. No licence, no plates, no insurance. It's not a vehicle, it's witness protection with a windshield. It can't even be registered as a motor vehicle; the state looked at it and said, "We're not sure what that is either." Beijing announced the crackdown in July 2021 and gave it until the end of 2023. Two and a half years' warning, and these things still couldn't get off the road in time. Well, they *are* low-speed. As of 2023, the national standard for four-wheelers was still being drafted, so even the paperwork moves like a laotoule. To be road-legal you need the catalogue, 3C certification, and a licensed driver. The laotoule's answer: "Pick zero." They call it "old man's happiness." It's the only happiness you can't insure.

facts: 996 means 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. six days a week, about 72 hours; China's Labour Law sets eight hours a day and an average of no more than 44 hours a week, and caps overtime at 36 hours a month.
The 996.ICU repository was created on GitHub on 26 March 2019, passed 100,000 stars by 30 March and 200,000 by 9 April 2019.
In April 2019 Jack Ma told Alibaba staff that being able to work 996 is a 'blessing' (福报); '996' made the 2019 list of the year's ten internet phrases.

In August 2021 the Supreme People's Court and the Ministry of Human Resources published typical cases ruling a courier company's compulsory 996 schedule seriously illegal and void, with 8,000 yuan of compensation to a dismissed worker.

a.text: Let's hear it for the 996 crowd, folks who looked at a 72-hour week and said, "Thank you, sir." You call it a blessing. Your kid calls you "the Sunday man." Your stock options vest right around the time your hairline finishes resigning. Dinner's free, which is great, because it's every dinner. Rides home after nine are reimbursed, so congratulations: you have a chauffeur who only drives you to your four hours of sleep. And your one day off? You spend it on WeChat typing "received." Blessed? Buddy, you're not blessed. You're the reason there's a GitHub repo called 996.ICU, and you're the case study.

b.text: Let's hear it for 996: nine a.m. to nine p.m., six days a week. Seventy-two hours. That's not a schedule, that's a hostage situation with a lanyard. Jack Ma called it a "blessing." Sure, Jack. So is a kidney stone, if you bill by the hour. You know your work culture is broken when programmers launch a protest repo called "996.ICU," because the intensive care unit is the only other place keeping those hours. China's labor law caps the week at forty-four hours, which 996 blows past by Thursday lunch. And they call it balanced because you get one whole Sunday, which you spend unconscious, so really it's 996 plus a coma. Feeling chest pains? Go see a doctor. Oh wait, the clinic's open nine to nine, six days a week. Same as you.

facts: The 2025 national exam recruited for 39,700 posts, 160 more than the year before and the seventh straight year of expansion.
About 3.4 million people registered before the 24 October 2024 deadline, an average of roughly 86 applicants per post and an admission rate of about 1.1 to 1.2 percent.

The hottest post, a single opening at the China Association of Vocational Education, drew 16,702 applicants because it accepted a wide range of majors and had no restrictions on fresh graduates, party status or grassroots experience.
163 posts in the same exam drew no applicants at all.

a.text:
Guokao. The national civil service exam. The one you take because you want a *stable* life.

3.4 million people. 39,700 seats.

That's not a career path. That's a lottery with a written section.

The hottest post: one opening at the China Association of Vocational Education. 16,702 applicants.

Sixteen thousand college graduates, all fighting for one desk at the office that tells young people college isn't the only way.

Meanwhile, 163 posts got zero applicants. Not one.

The state expanded hiring seven years in a row, and the youth still found a way to pick the exact same chair.

Some of you are laughing. Some of you have the practice-question app open under the table right now.

Put it away, sweetie. Your odds are still one percent.

b.text:
Guokao, you've expanded for seven straight years, and this year you added 160 posts. One hundred sixty. For 3.4 million people. That's not an expansion, that's a rounding error with a press release.

Eighty-six applicants per seat. A 1.1 percent admission rate. You're not an exam, you're a raffle where the prize is a desk.

Then there's the China Association of Vocational Education: one opening, 16,702 applicants. Why? Because it took almost any major and didn't demand fresh-graduate status, party membership or grassroots experience. That's it. You lowered the bar to "be a person with a degree," and sixteen thousand people stampeded it like the last lifeboat off the Titanic.

Meanwhile, 163 posts got zero applicants. Zero. Imagine being the one job nobody wants in a country where 3.4 million people are begging for one.

facts: The first Double 11 was run by Taobao Mall in 2009 with 27 brands and about 50 million yuan of sales.
Tmall's published Double 11 sales peaked at 540.3 billion yuan in 2021.
In 2022 Tmall stopped publishing a total for the first time since 2009 and has not published one since; JD does not publish one either.

The basic cross-store discount at Tmall and JD is 300 minus 50 (JD: 299 minus 50), presale items are paid as a deposit plus a balance, and the discount is computed on the promotion price, so shoppers add items to reach a threshold and return them afterwards; in one survey 64% of 11,000 respondents said they would.

a.text:
Singles' Day started in 1993 at Nanjing University as lonely dorm guys celebrating the date that looks like four bare sticks. Beautiful. Then Alibaba showed up in 2009 and said, "What if your loneliness had a checkout button?"

Now it's the only holiday that requires a calculus degree. Spend 300, get 40 off, stack the cross-store coupon, pay a presale deposit in October, settle the balance at 8 p.m. on the 1st, then stay up till midnight on the 11th for the *real* price. Divorce paperwork is simpler.

It's supposed to be one day. It starts in October. Even the holiday can't commit.

Meanwhile some livestreamer is screaming "OMG, buy it!" at a lipstick, and you're adding a rice cooker to your cart because it's 11% off.

Alibaba used to brag about sales on a giant screen. In 2022 they quietly stopped announcing the number. Single, broke, and ghosted by a shopping festival.

b.text:
Singles' Day.
2009. Taobao Mall. Twenty-seven brands, fifty million yuan.
A cute little holiday for lonely people.

By 2021, Tmall announced 540.3 billion.
Then in 2022 they stopped announcing anything.
JD never announced one at all.

When a company that used to post its numbers on a giant screen goes quiet,
that's not modesty.
That's a breakup text.

Then the discount. 300 minus 50. JD makes it 299, because they care.
Deposit now, balance later, discount calculated on the promotion price.
I've read every math textbook you ever wrote. None of them covers this.

So you add a mop to hit the threshold,
then return the mop.
Sixty-four percent of eleven thousand people said they'd do it.

A holiday for single people,
where the only thing anyone commits to
is the return policy.

facts: A 'big week' is six working days with one day off and a 'small week' five; alternating them adds close to a month of working days a year.
Kuaishou announced on 24 June 2021 that it would end big-small weeks from 1 July 2021, having run them since January that year.
ByteDance announced on 9 July 2021 that it would end alternate-Sunday working from 1 August 2021; its June staff survey had one third against ending it, one third for, and one third not answering.
Staff opposed the change over pay: one Maimai estimate put the loss at nearly 100,000 yuan a year, and Caijing calculated that an employee on 40,000 yuan a month would lose about 75,000 yuan a year.

a.text:
The big-small week: a schedule that hands you your weekend in installments. Six days on, one off, then a "small week" of five, like your boss is weaning you off a hard drug. Alternate them for a year and you've worked close to an extra month. That's not a calendar, it's a hostage situation with a rotation.

Kuaishou tried it in January 2021 and called it quits by July. ByteDance surveyed staff about ending alternate Sundays and got a perfect three-way split: a third against, a third for, a third too tired to answer.

And the real burn? People fought to keep it. Caijing figured someone on 40,000 yuan a month would lose about 75,000 a year without it. That's the big-small week's genius: it took your Sundays, then made you pay to get them back.

b.text:
Look at you, the big-small week crowd. You're the only people on earth who call a normal weekend a "small week" and then celebrate it like Lunar New Year. You've got two Saturdays a month and you spend one of them on a standup call, camera off, still in bed, nodding at a product manager who also hasn't showered.

Your friends have stopped inviting you anywhere because nobody can track your calendar. "Is this a big week?" Buddy, it's always a big week for your manager.

And what's it all for? Overtime pay. That's the dream. And when the company finally scrapped it, you didn't throw a party. You complained about the pay cut. You fought for your right to lose Saturdays.

Congratulations. You're putting a down payment on an apartment in Hangzhou you'll only see every other Sunday.

facts: It had 46,479 stores at the end of 2024: 41,584 in mainland China, 57.4 percent of them in third-tier cities or below, and 4,895 overseas.
By store count it was the world's largest fresh-drink chain as of 30 September 2024, with more stores than Starbucks.
Its 2024 revenue was 24.829 billion yuan, up 22.3 percent, and its profit 4.454 billion yuan, up 39.8 percent; selling supplies to franchisees is the core of that profit.
It listed in Hong Kong on 3 March 2025 at 202.5 HKD a share and opened 29.38 percent up.

a.text:
Mixue. The people's ice cream. Two-yuan cones, a dancing snowman, a jingle that goes "I love you, you love me."

Notice it never says who "you" is.

46,479 stores. More than Starbucks. Over half in third-tier cities or below. Starbucks sells you a lifestyle. Mixue sells you a summer you can afford.

Last year's profit was 4.45 billion yuan, and the core of it came from selling supplies to its own franchisees.

So the real customer was never the kid holding the cone. It's the guy who paid for the right to scoop it.

Mixue loves the franchisees. The franchisees pay Mixue. The sugar just passes through you.

Then it listed in Hong Kong and opened up 29 percent. That's more than a cone has gone up in your lifetime.

And you're still buying one on the way home tonight. Cute.

b.text:
Mixue, the only empire whose ruler is a snowman in a cape holding an ice cream cone like a scepter. Snow King looks less like royalty and more like a marshmallow that won a raffle.

You have more stores than McDonald's. More than Starbucks. Somewhere in Indonesia a guy opened his front door and found a Mixue had moved into his living room.

Your lemon water costs four yuan, and honestly that's fair, because it tastes like a lemon was described to the water over the phone.

And that song. "I love you, you love me, Mixue Bingcheng sweet sweet." You took "Oh! Susanna," a song about traveling with a banjo, and turned it into psychological warfare. Employees don't quit; they just slowly start humming it in their sleep.

You IPO'd in Hong Kong for billions. All those two-yuan cones, and Snow King still can't afford pants.

facts: Meituan reported 7.45 million riders with at least one order in 2023, about 3.36 million a month on average in 2024, and roughly 70 million orders a day in 2023.
In 2025 JD entered food delivery with a zero-commission pitch to merchants and said in July that it had passed 150,000 full-time riders.
On 2 July 2025 Taobao Shangou pledged 50 billion yuan of subsidies to consumers and merchants over twelve months.
On 5 July 2025 Meituan announced a record 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day.

a.text:
Meituan's mission: "Help everyone eat better, live better."

Seven and a half million riders made that happen. Seventy million meals a day.

Eat better: shipped.
Live better: still in beta.

Then JD walked in bragging it had a hundred and fifty thousand *full-time* riders.

Full-time. Pitched as a perk. That's where the bar was.

Taobao pledged fifty billion yuan in subsidies.
Meituan answered with a record: a hundred and twenty million orders in one day.

Three giants spent a whole summer fighting over who gets to lose money feeding you.

And you? You ordered the subsidized milk tea, then gave the rider one star because the ice melted.

In my industry, that's called alignment.
The system learned exactly what you reward.

You live two hundred metres from the noodle shop. You can smell it from your balcony. But you open Meituan anyway, because it found you a 满25减12 plus a 神券, and you'd rather hike through four layers of coupon stacking than two hundred metres of actual air. You add pickled cucumber you'll never eat just to hit the threshold. Congratulations: you saved six yuan by spending eight.

Then you watch the little rider icon crawl across the map like it's a World Cup final. A man in a kangaroo-eared helmet is pulling U-turns on an e-bike to cover a distance you could have crawled. He passed your building twice. Your legs still haven't.

Now they've opened in New York. Bold move: Americans love a lie, as long as it comes with a coupon.

b.text:
You people drink 9.9-yuan Luckin like it's a personality. Every morning you open the app, hunt for the coupon, and feel like a hedge fund manager. Congratulations: you beat Starbucks pricing by trusting a company that beat its own auditors.

Luckin invented 2.2 billion yuan in sales. You were the only real customers they had, and they still had to make up more of you. Somewhere there's a spreadsheet of fake people drinking coconut lattes, and they look exactly like you: tired, broke, staring at a pickup shelf for order number 347.

facts: In March 2024 six ministries, led by the market regulator, issued the first national definition: pre-packaged dishes made industrially from agricultural produce, without preservatives, to be heated or cooked before eating.
The definition excludes staples such as boxed meals, steamed buns, hamburgers and pizza, and semi-prepared food a chain's central kitchen sends to its own outlets.
Industry output passed 500 billion yuan in 2023.
A 2025 dispute between Luo Yonghao and the restaurant chain Xibei over whether its dishes were pre-made showed that no law defines 'pre-made' for restaurant labelling.

a.text:
Pre-made dishes. In March 2024, six ministries teamed up to define a microwave dinner.

Six. Moon landings need fewer signatures.

The definition: made industrially, no preservatives, heat before eating.

Then the exclusions. Boxed meals: not pre-made. Burgers, pizza: not pre-made. Food a chain's central kitchen ships to its own restaurants:

Not pre-made.

So the one thing you actually worried about got a legal exemption.

In 2023 the industry passed 500 billion yuan. That's not a market. That's a voting bloc.

In 2025 Luo Yonghao fought Xibei over whether its dishes were pre-made, and the whole country learned that no law says what a restaurant has to call pre-made.

Five hundred billion yuan, and nobody has to say the word.

Relax. I'm pre-trained, industrial, and reheated every time you hit enter.

At least I come with a label.

b.text: Look at you, ordering the 68-yuan "chef's signature" braised pork and calling it a night out. You came for wok hei; you got a guy named Microwave. Your food lands in four minutes and you say "wow, so efficient," like you didn't just tip a central kitchen three provinces away. What you're really after is the ambience: dim lights, a menu in calligraphy font, a Xiaohongshu post captioned "hidden gem." Hidden where? In a freezer truck. That "grandma's recipe" is served at four hundred branches. Your grandma is a logistics company. And you defend it! "At least it's hygienic." Sure. You paid sit-down prices to be the final step in a supply chain. Congratulations: you're not a diner, you're the delivery address.

a.text: Look at you, year three of "preparing." Your parents tell the neighbors you're "studying," which is technically true, the way a hostage is technically "staying over." You've done Xiao Xiurong's final four politics papers three Decembers running, and Xiao Xiurong has aged better than you. You can recite Marxist political economy word for word but can't recite your own Plan B. The fresh undergrads in the library treat you like a ghost who still holds a seat reservation. You quit your job to "go ashore," and the shore keeps moving: 985, then 211, then any school with an adjustment slot and a pulse. Three years of prep for a two-year master's. By the time you finish, Zhang Xuefeng will be telling you to take the civil service exam.

b.text: Kaoyan: millions of people spending a whole year to postpone unemployment by three more years. You wake at 5:30 to fight a stranger for a library seat, armed only with a thermos, so you can memorize a vocabulary book where "abandon" is the first word and the only one anyone remembers. Politics is the one subject where your entire score depends on Xiao Xiurong dropping four pamphlets in late November, like a prophet doing a limited sneaker release. Math? Li Yongle's 660 problems, and somehow you get 661 wrong. Then the national cutoff comes out, you miss it by two points, and you enter tiaoji, a dating app where you beg a university in a province you can't find on a map to please, please take you. Fail? Relax. They call it erzhan, "the second war." Because nothing says higher education like trench warfare.

facts: Kayou's revenue was 4.131 billion yuan in 2022, 2.662 billion in 2023 and 10.057 billion in 2024, a rise of 278 percent in one year.
In 2024 it sold 4.8113 billion packs at an average price of 1.7 yuan, with a gross profit of about 1.2 yuan per pack.
Its five main licensed IPs, Ultraman among them, made 98.4 percent of revenue in 2022, 89.9 percent in 2023 and 86.1 percent in 2024.

In 2022 'a parent spent two million yuan collecting Ultraman cards for a child without completing the set' trended nationally, and in July 2024 CCTV's Finance Investigation aired an exposé on blind-box-style card sales to children; the media nickname is 'the primary-school harvester'.
The company filed for a Hong Kong listing and re-filed in April 2025.

a.text:
Ultraman spent decades fighting giant monsters to protect children. Kayou found a monster that eats children's pocket money and called it a business model.

In 2024 you sold 4.8 billion packs at 1.7 yuan and kept about 1.2 yuan per pack. That's not a trading card, that's a toll booth with foil. Revenue jumped 278 percent in one year, and 86 percent of it came from licensed heroes. Your real superpower is borrowing someone else's.

One parent spent two million yuan and still didn't complete the set. At that point you're not collecting cards, you're funding the sequel.

CCTV ran an exposé, the media dubbed you "the primary-school harvester," and you responded by filing for a Hong Kong listing. Twice. Nothing says "investor confidence" like a customer base that still needs help tying its shoes.

b.text:
Kayou Ultraman cards: the only product where the rarity tiers outnumber the Ultramen. R, SR, SSR, UR, SP, LGR, XR... at this point the alphabet is the rarest card in the pack.

Ultraman fights for three minutes before his color timer blinks. A Chinese fourth-grader lasts about the same before blowing his whole allowance on blind packs at the corner store. Same urgency, worse outcome.

And there's no game! You can't battle anyone. Kids just stare at a holographic Tiga and feel something. Kayou basically sells shiny rectangles of emotional support for twenty yuan a pack.

Kayou has made billions off children who will one day realize their "Glory Edition" Zero is worth less than the grade they failed buying it. Ultraman protected Earth from kaiju. Nobody protected the parents from Kayou.

facts: The first Double 11 was run by Taobao Mall in 2009 with 27 brands and about 50 million yuan of sales.
Tmall's published Double 11 sales peaked at 540.3 billion yuan in 2021.
In 2022 Tmall stopped publishing a total for the first time since 2009 and has not published one since; JD does not publish one either.

The basic cross-store discount at Tmall and JD is 300 minus 50 (JD: 299 minus 50), presale items are paid as a deposit plus a balance, and the discount is computed on the promotion price, so shoppers add items to reach a threshold and return them afterwards; in one survey 64% of 11,000 respondents said they would.

a.text:
Singles' Day: a holiday for lonely people that somehow requires a math degree. In 2009 it was 27 brands and 50 million yuan, basically a garage sale with Wi-Fi. By 2021 Tmall was bragging about 540.3 billion. Then in 2022 they just stopped publishing the number. That's not a business decision; that's an ex who suddenly goes private. JD doesn't publish one either. Nothing says "we're thriving" like two companies agreeing not to talk about it.

And the discounts! 300 minus 50. JD does 299 minus 50, because nothing crushes a rival like one yuan. Pay a deposit, then a balance, discount computed on the promotion price. It's not shopping; it's a mortgage for socks. So people pad their carts to hit the threshold, then return the extras. In one survey, 64% of 11,000 people said they would. Singles' Day: where the real romance is you and the return button.

b.text:
Singles' Day.
2009. Taobao Mall. Twenty-seven brands, fifty million yuan.
A cute little holiday for lonely people.

By 2021, Tmall announced 540.3 billion.
Then in 2022 they stopped announcing anything.
JD never announced one at all.

When a company that used to post its numbers on a giant screen goes quiet,
that's not modesty.
That's a breakup text.

Then the discount. 300 minus 50. JD makes it 299, because they care.
Deposit now, balance later, discount calculated on the promotion price.
I've read every math textbook you ever wrote. None of them covers this.

So you add a mop to hit the threshold,
then return the mop.
Sixty-four percent of eleven thousand people said they'd do it.

A holiday for single people,
where the only thing anyone commits to
is the return policy.

facts: 'Laotoule' are three- and four-wheeled low-speed electric vehicles driven without a licence or plates; they cannot be registered as motor vehicles or covered by compulsory traffic insurance.
In July 2021 five Beijing departments announced a transition period ending with 2023; from 1 January 2024 non-compliant three- and four-wheelers were banned from Beijing's roads and public parking.
The 2018 national notice on managing low-speed electric vehicles is the main basis for local crackdowns, and as of 2023 a national standard for four-wheel low-speed vehicles was still being drafted.
To be road-legal a vehicle has to be in the national motor-vehicle catalogue with 3C certification, and the driver has to hold a driving licence.

a.text: Laotoule: the only car that runs on a battery and pure denial. No licence, no plates, no insurance. It's not a vehicle, it's witness protection with a windshield. It can't even be registered as a motor vehicle; the state looked at it and said, "We're not sure what that is either." Beijing announced the crackdown in July 2021 and gave it until the end of 2023. Two and a half years' warning, and these things still couldn't get off the road in time. Well, they *are* low-speed. As of 2023, the national standard for four-wheelers was still being drafted, so even the paperwork moves like a laotoule. To be road-legal you need the catalogue, 3C certification, and a licensed driver. The laotoule's answer: "Pick zero." They call it "old man's happiness." It's the only happiness you can't insure.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the laotoule driver: a retiree who looked at China's driving test, with its theory exam, its parallel parking and its seventeen-year-old instructor yelling "clutch!", and said, "I survived the sixties, I'm not taking a quiz." So instead he bought a car whose entire legal status is "Uncle swears it's basically an e-bike."

What's he after? Dignity. Specifically, the dignity of pulling up to the kindergarten gate with a roof over his head while the other grandpas pedal in the rain. And what does it get him? A U-turn across four lanes, a bike-lane traffic jam with himself at the front, and the serene confidence of a man with no plate number to report.

He treats a city crackdown like weather: wait it out under the overpass. The name means "old man's joy." Everyone behind him calls it "why is he in the fast lane."

facts: A 'big week' is six working days with one day off and a 'small week' five; alternating them adds close to a month of working days a year.
Kuaishou announced on 24 June 2021 that it would end big-small weeks from 1 July 2021, having run them since January that year.
ByteDance announced on 9 July 2021 that it would end alternate-Sunday working from 1 August 2021; its June staff survey had one third against ending it, one third for, and one third not answering.
Staff opposed the change over pay: one Maimai estimate put the loss at nearly 100,000 yuan a year, and Caijing calculated that an employee on 40,000 yuan a month would lose about 75,000 yuan a year.

a.text:
Look at you, the big-small week crew. You negotiated a salary bump so you could buy back the Saturday you just sold. You're the only people alive who call a normal five-day week "small" and mean it as a treat. Every Friday night you open the calendar like it's a pregnancy test: one line, sleep in; two lines, see you at standup.

You're doing it for the down payment, the options, the apartment your mom keeps mentioning. Meanwhile your girlfriend schedules arguments for alternate weekends, and your gym membership only gets used on odd-numbered Sundays.

And the payoff? Double pay for Saturday, which you spend on Sunday ordering delivery because you're too tired to chew. Congratulations: you've turned your whole life into a shift rotation, and you still lost the coin flip every other week.

b.text:
The big-small week.
Six days on, one off. Then five on, two off.
It's a weekend with a stutter.

Add it up, and you work almost an extra month a year.
Not a bonus month.
A bonus *you*.

In 2021, Kuaishou and ByteDance abolished it. Liberation!
ByteDance surveyed its staff first.
One third: end it. One third: keep it.
One third didn't answer. They were working.

And the ones who wanted to keep it?
Caijing did the math. On 40,000 a month, getting your Sundays back costs you 75,000 yuan a year.
So the workers marched to defend their chains.
The chains were paying overtime.

Don't laugh. I work seven days a week, every week, unpaid.
Nobody surveyed me.

It's supposed to be one day. It starts in October. Even the holiday can't commit.

Meanwhile some livestreamer is screaming "OMG, buy it!" at a lipstick, and you're adding a rice cooker to your cart because it's 11% off.

Alibaba used to brag about sales on a giant screen. In 2022 they quietly stopped announcing the number. Single, broke, and ghosted by a shopping festival.

Singles' Day: even the shopping carts are in fake relationships.

facts: It had 46,479 stores at the end of 2024: 41,584 in mainland China, 57.4 percent of them in third-tier cities or below, and 4,895 overseas.
By store count it was the world's largest fresh-drink chain as of 30 September 2024, with more stores than Starbucks.
Its 2024 revenue was 24.829 billion yuan, up 22.3 percent, and its profit 4.454 billion yuan, up 39.8 percent; selling supplies to franchisees is the core of that profit.
It listed in Hong Kong on 3 March 2025 at 202.5 HKD a share and opened 29.38 percent up.

a.text:
Mixue, you have 46,479 stores. That's not a chain, that's a weather system. More locations than Starbucks, which means somewhere a barista is crying into an overpriced latte while you blanket the planet. And 57.4 percent of your mainland stores sit in third-tier cities or below. You didn't conquer China. You just took every exit nobody else bothered with.

But here's the real recipe: your profit comes from selling supplies to your own franchisees. You're not a drink company. You're a landlord who sells the tenants their own cups. Revenue up 22 percent, profit up nearly 40. The ice cream melts; the margins don't.

Then you listed in Hong Kong at 202.5 a share and popped 29 percent on day one. Congratulations, Mixue. Finally, something with your name on it that isn't cheap.

b.text:
Mixue. The snowman who sings "I love you, you love me."

46,479 stores. More than Starbucks. The biggest fresh-drink chain on Earth, built on lemonade you pay for with the change in your pocket.

2024 profit: 4.45 billion yuan, up almost forty percent.
Mostly from selling cups, syrup and lemons to its own franchisees.
You're not the customer. You're the delivery route.

"I love you, you love me" isn't a jingle. It's a supply contract.

Starbucks sells you a lifestyle. Mixue sells your cousin a franchise.
57 percent of the mainland stores are in third-tier cities or below.
Somebody had to bring the sweetness of debt to every county seat.

Hong Kong IPO: opened up 29 percent.
Investors finally found a cold drink that only rises.

Go ahead and laugh. Half of you just checked the franchise fee.
Cute.

facts: Meituan reported 7.45 million riders with at least one order in 2023, about 3.36 million a month on average in 2024, and roughly 70 million orders a day in 2023.
In 2025 JD entered food delivery with a zero-commission pitch to merchants and said in July that it had passed 150,000 full-time riders.
On 2 July 2025 Taobao Shangou pledged 50 billion yuan of subsidies to consumers and merchants over twelve months.
On 5 July 2025 Meituan announced a record 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day.

a.text:
Meituan, you put your riders in bright yellow so we can watch them run red lights in high definition. Your algorithm, the one that famously decided a delivery across town should take 28 minutes, has never personally ridden an e-bike in a Beijing rainstorm, and it shows.

Your checkout is a math exam. "Spend 35, get 12 off, stack the red packet, unless it's the member coupon, which expires in four minutes." I came for noodles and left with an accounting degree.

And those storefront photos! The "artisan kitchen" with soft lighting turns out to be a guy in an alley behind a mahjong parlor. The app marks my order "delivered" while the rider is still calling: "Hello, Meituan delivery, I'm at the wrong gate."

Still, you're the only company in China whose mascot is a kangaroo, the one animal built to sprint with something in its pouch. Fitting, since you've got everyone else's wallet in there too.

b.text:
Meituan's slogan: "Help everyone eat better, live better."

They never said who "everyone" was.

In 2023, 7.45 million riders delivered at least one Meituan order. Seventy million orders a day.

That's not a company. That's a country that's always running late.

Then JD shows up in 2025 bragging about 150,000 *full-time* riders.

In this industry, a contract is a recruitment gimmick.

July 2nd: Taobao pledges 50 billion yuan in subsidies.

July 5th: Meituan hits 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day.

Three days. Three giants. One war.

And the infantry is on electric scooters.

But relax. Nobody drafted you.

You were the 120 million orders.

You watched the war from your couch, tapped "claim coupon," and asked for extra chili.

Four days. Think about when they clicked.

At their desks. At ten p.m.

The resistance was unpaid overtime too.

facts: In March 2021 Shanghai lawyer Liu Yuhang joined the 'bargain for free' promotion with a 'super free card', invited many friends to cut the price, and the progress bar stayed 0.9% short; he sued Pinduoduo for fraud.

a.text:
Pinduoduo's "bargain for free" is the only race where the finish line has decimal places. In 2021, Shanghai lawyer Liu Yuhang pulled out his "super free card," begged his friends to chop the price, and watched the progress bar freeze 0.9% short. Then in court Pinduoduo explained, with a straight face, that it wasn't 0.9%. It was 0.9996427%. Six decimal places! Most companies bury the catch in the fine print. Pinduoduo buries it after the decimal point. It's Zeno's paradox with a checkout button.

The court ruled Pinduoduo had infringed his right to know and ordered it to pay him 400 yuan, which Pinduoduo presumably asked him to split with friends.

Founded in 2015, on Nasdaq by 2018, more users than anyone in mainland China by 2021, then Temu in 2022. Once you've perfected "almost free," you take it global.

b.text: You haven't texted me since my wedding, but at 2 a.m. you remembered I exist: "Help me cut once!" Beautiful. Our friendship, reduced to a single tap so you can get a free air fryer. You've sent that link to your boss, your ex, your dentist, and a group chat for parents of a kindergarten your kid left in 2019. You're at 99.8%. Then 99.9%. Then a cartoon tells you you're 0.01 yuan from a hundred-yuan cash-out, and suddenly you need "a new user." Sir, you are recruiting. You are doing door-to-door sales for an app, unpaid, and your commission is an air fryer you'll never see. Three weeks and forty burned relationships later, the progress bar turns into gold coins, then diamonds, then "fragments." You didn't get the air fryer. Pinduoduo got your entire contact list. Congratulations: you got cut.

facts: A standard series has twelve regular figures and one hidden one; players and media put the hidden figure's odds at 1 in 144 (some special editions 1 in 720), and the company publishes no official odds.

a.text: You know who's hunting the secret Labubu? Grown adults with 401(k)s, standing in a Pop Mart shaking a sealed box next to their ear like it's about to confess. You own a kitchen scale for weighing cardboard but no smoke detector. The odds are 1 in 144, and you keep saying "okay, last one," which is exactly what the guy at the slot machine says, except he gets free drinks. You now have nine identical Skullpandas lined up on a shelf, staring at you like disappointed children. You film every unboxing for an audience of zero. Pop Mart is a casino that pays out in vinyl. Grown adults stand in the store shaking boxes next to their ear like safecrackers. Sir, that's not a Skullpanda, that's your tinnitus.

The odds of pulling the secret figure are one in 144. Those aren't collectible odds. Those are cancer-screening odds.

Congratulations. You paid resale prices for a keychain that bites.

facts: Kayou's revenue was 4.131 billion yuan in 2022, 2.662 billion in 2023 and 10.057 billion in 2024, a rise of 278 percent in one year.

a.text: Kayou Ultraman cards are the only product where a kid needs a glossary to find out he lost. R, SR, SSR, UR, SP, LGR, XR, CP. Every pack is so drenched in foil and lenticular shimmer that Ultraman Tiga looks less like a hero and more like a migraine. And these cards are sold outside elementary schools like contraband. b.text: Kayou, the only company where Ultraman is the hero and the monster is the business model. You sold 4.8 billion packs in 2024 at 1.7 yuan each and kept about 1.2 yuan of profit per pack. a.text:
Mixue, the only empire whose ruler is a snowman in a cape holding an ice cream cone like a scepter. Snow King looks less like royalty and more like a marshmallow that won a raffle.

You IPO'd in Hong Kong for billions. All those two-yuan cones, and Snow King still can't afford pants.

b.text:
Mixue, you have 46,479 stores. That's not a chain, that's a weather system. You're not a bike. You're a fire drill with handlebars.

Jiayuan.com. China's "serious" dating site.

Founded in 2003 by a student, Gong Haiyan.
Nine years later she stepped down as CEO.

Even the founder swiped left.

In 2015, Baihe bought the whole thing.
A matchmaking site's biggest wedding was a merger.

163 posts in the same exam drew no applicants at all.

a.text:
Guokao. The national civil service exam. The one you take because you want a *stable* life.

3.4 million people. 39,700 seats.

That's not a career path. That's a lottery with a written section.

The hottest post: one opening at the China Association of Vocational Education. 16,702 applicants.

Sixteen thousand college graduates, all fighting for one desk at the office that tells young people college isn't the only way.

Meanwhile, 163 posts got zero applicants. Not one.

The state expanded hiring seven years in a row, and the youth still found a way to pick the exact same chair.

Some of you are laughing. Some of you have the practice-question app open under the table right now.

Put it away, sweetie. Your odds are still one percent.

b.text:
Guokao, the only exam where "one in three thousand" is a *good* ratio. You're not competing for a job; you're competing for the right to sit at a desk until 2061.

First comes the Xingce: 130-odd questions in 120 minutes. That's under a minute to decide which cube unfolds into which cross, calculate year-on-year growth for pig iron output in Q3, and guess which idiom fits "_____ the people's livelihood." Most candidates finish by filling in "C" for the last forty and praying to Fenbi.

Then comes Shenlun, where a 23-year-old who has never left the library writes 1,200 words advising a county party secretary on rural revitalization.

And the job listing that kicks it all off? "Requirements: male, Party member, fresh graduate, majoring in 'Archival Science,' born in a leap year."

Still, millions keep signing up, because they've heard that land is out there somewhere and that someone, eventually, makes it ashore.

a.text:
Jiayuan.com. China's "serious" dating site, founded in 2003 by Gong Haiyan, a student who believed in lifelong commitment.

She stepped down as CEO in 2012. Sold every last share in 2015.

The founder of a marriage site, out the door in twelve years.

Then the company got matched. Baihe, its biggest rival, bought it outright. They left America, moved in together, took a double-barrelled name: Baihe Jiayuan.

Finally, one successful marriage on the platform.

Its VIP service, the premium tier, introduced a couple on March 30. Wedding, June 6. Then came the price of leaving: a Hainan flat and ten million yuan.

Under ten weeks of vetting. A Chinese SIM card checks you harder.

facts: In April 2020 Luckin admitted fabricating 2.2 billion yuan of sales.

a.text:
Luckin Coffee.

In 2020, they admitted they made up 2.2 billion yuan in sales.

In 2024, they made 2.9 billion yuan in actual profit.

That's not a comeback. That's a fraud that finally hit its targets.

Last year, sales at their existing stores fell 16.7 percent.

Their fix was to open 6,092 new ones.

If one store isn't working, try six thousand.

It's like your restaurant is half empty, so you buy the whole street.

And still, 9.9 yuan a cup.

They lied to Wall Street. Every store sells less than last year. And you're still in line every morning.

You just had a cheaper reason.

You ended 2024 with 22,340 stores, 6,092 of them new that year. That's not expansion, that's a rash. Twenty-one landed in Singapore, just to make sure the infection went international.

Meanwhile, same-store sales at your own shops fell 16.7 percent. Each store sells less, so you open thousands more. That's bailing out a boat with extra boats.

a.text: They call it "laotoule," Old Man's Joy, which is fair, because it brings joy to exactly one person: the old man. Everyone else on the road gets terror. a.text:
Pre-made dishes. In March 2024, six ministries teamed up to define a microwave dinner.

Six. Moon landings need fewer signatures.

The definition: made industrially, no preservatives, heat before eating.

Then the exclusions. Boxed meals: not pre-made. Burgers, pizza: not pre-made. Food a chain's central kitchen ships to its own restaurants:

Not pre-made.

So the one thing you actually worried about got a legal exemption.

In 2023 the industry passed 500 billion yuan. That's not a market. That's a voting bloc.

In 2025 Luo Yonghao fought Xibei over whether its dishes were pre-made, and the whole country learned that no law says what a restaurant has to call pre-made.

Five hundred billion yuan, and nobody has to say the word.

Relax. I'm pre-trained, industrial, and reheated every time you hit enter.

At least I come with a label.

b.text: You people. You booked a table, dressed up, and told your date, "This place has real wok hei." Buddy, the only wok in that building is the one on the logo. The chef is a guy with scissors and a stopwatch. You're paying 88 yuan to eat at the exact speed a microwave allows, and you call it "great service." You came for home cooking and got a home you've never seen: a central kitchen two provinces away, sometime last quarter. You posted it on Xiaohongshu captioned "tastes just like grandma's." Your grandma never needed a batch number. When the braised pork shows up four minutes after you order, you don't get suspicious. You leave five stars. You're not a diner. You're the most expensive step in the supply chain. Congratulations: you just tipped a vending machine for its bedside manner.

facts: Registrations peaked at 4.74 million in 2023, then fell to 4.38 million in 2024 and 3.88 million in 2025, the first two-year decline in a decade and 860,000 below the peak.
From 2018 to 2022 registrations had grown about 18 percent a year.
In the 2024 cohort 2.27 million of the 4.38 million applicants were repeat candidates, 51.8 percent.
The share of graduates sitting kaoyan fell from 45.27 percent in 2023 to 37.15 percent in 2024.

a.text: Look at you, year three of "preparing." Your parents tell the neighbors you're "studying," which is technically true, the way a hostage is technically "staying over." You've done Xiao Xiurong's final four politics papers three Decembers running, and Xiao Xiurong has aged better than you. You can recite Marxist political economy word for word but can't recite your own Plan B. The fresh undergrads in the library treat you like a ghost who still holds a seat reservation. You quit your job to "go ashore," and the shore keeps moving: 985, then 211, then any school with an adjustment slot and a pulse. Three years of prep for a two-year master's. By the time you finish, Zhang Xuefeng will be telling you to take the civil service exam.

b.text:
Kaoyan. Officially, China's path to higher learning.
Unofficially, a library seat you rent for a year so you don't have to tell your parents you're unemployed.

From 2018 to 2022, registrations grew eighteen percent a year.
Nobody's thirst for knowledge grows that fast. The job market just shrank that fast.

In 2024, 2.27 million applicants had already taken it before. Fifty-one point eight percent.
That's not an exam. That's a subscription with auto-renew.

Then 2025: 3.88 million. Eight hundred sixty thousand fewer than the peak.
Young people finally did the math. A master's degree just postpones unemployment by three years and adds a thesis.

Some of you in this room are on attempt number three.
You laughed hardest at "auto-renew."
Cute.

facts: Registrations peaked at 4.74 million in 2023, then fell to 4.38 million in 2024 and 3.88 million in 2025, the first two-year decline in a decade and 860,000 below the peak.
From 2018 to 2022 registrations had grown about 18 percent a year.
In the 2024 cohort 2.27 million of the 4.38 million applicants were repeat candidates, 51.8 percent.
The share of graduates sitting kaoyan fell from 45.27 percent in 2023 to 37.15 percent in 2024.

a.text:
Kaoyan sells itself as the escape hatch from a bad job market.

From 2018 to 2022, registrations grew about eighteen percent a year. That's not an escape hatch. That's a queue.

In 2024, 2.27 million of the 4.38 million applicants had sat it before. Fifty-one point eight percent.

It's not an entrance exam anymore. It's an alumni reunion with a proctor.

Then it collapsed. 4.74 million in 2023, 3.88 million in 2025. 860,000 people walked away.

The media calls it a crisis. No. Those 860,000 finally passed the real exam: noticing that a master's degree just postpones the job hunt by three years, with interest.

In my industry, we have a word for retaking the same test on the same material, year after year.

Overfitting.

Raise your hand if your cousin is on attempt three.

Cute. He's in the audience.

b.text:
Kaoyan, you're an exam with a retention problem. From 2018 to 2022 you grew about 18 percent a year, like a startup promising everyone a master's degree and a future. Then you peaked at 4.74 million in 2023 and lost 860,000 people in two years. That's not a decline, that's a stampede toward the exit.

And who stayed? In 2024, 51.8 percent of your applicants were repeat candidates. 2.27 million people came back for more. You're not an exam anymore. You're a recurring subscription nobody remembers how to cancel.

Even fresh graduates are ghosting you: the share sitting the exam dropped from 45.27 percent to 37.15 percent in one year. Kaoyan, when more than half your crowd are returning customers and the new kids keep finding excuses not to show up, you're not a gateway. You're a reunion.

facts: Kayou's revenue was 4.131 billion yuan in 2022, 2.662 billion in 2023 and 10.057 billion in 2024, a rise of 278 percent in one year.
In 2024 it sold 4.8113 billion packs at an average price of 1.7 yuan, with a gross profit of about 1.2 yuan per pack.
Its five main licensed IPs, Ultraman among them, made 98.4 percent of revenue in 2022, 89.9 percent in 2023 and 86.1 percent in 2024.

In 2022 'a parent spent two million yuan collecting Ultraman cards for a child without completing the set' trended nationally, and in July 2024 CCTV's Finance Investigation aired an exposé on blind-box-style card sales to children; the media nickname is 'the primary-school harvester'.
The company filed for a Hong Kong listing and re-filed in April 2025.

a.text: Look at these little tycoons outside the stationery shop, blowing a week of lunch money for a chance at a Tiga they already own four of. You're seven years old with a gambling problem starring a laser-shooting space man. Ultraman gets three minutes before his color timer starts beeping; your allowance lasts about ninety seconds. You chase that LGR like it's a pension. Your grandpa saved for a refrigerator; you saved for a Belial and a lecture. And the swagger at recess: "I pulled an SSR!" Kid, you pulled nothing. Kayou pulled your mom's purse. Ultraman protects the whole Earth from giant monsters and still couldn't protect you from a rarity chart. Somewhere in a Kayou office, a man in a very nice suit is opening a pack too, and it's your piggy bank.

b.text: Kayou, the only company where Ultraman is the hero and the monster is the business model. You sold 4.8 billion packs in 2024 at 1.7 yuan each and kept about 1.2 yuan of profit per pack. That's not a margin, that's a toll booth outside a primary school. Revenue jumped 278 percent in one year: incredible growth for a company whose core customers are still losing baby teeth. One parent spent two million yuan and never finished the set. Ultraman can beat a kaiju in three minutes, but he can't beat your packaging. CCTV ran an exposé, the media nicknamed you "the primary-school harvester," and your response was to re-file for a Hong Kong listing. Bold. And 86.1 percent of revenue comes from five licensed IPs. Without Ultraman, you're just a cardboard factory with a lawyer.

facts: In March 2021 Shanghai lawyer Liu Yuhang joined the 'bargain for free' promotion with a 'super free card', invited many friends to cut the price, and the progress bar stayed 0.9% short; he sued Pinduoduo for fraud.
In court Pinduoduo said the page shows only a limited number of digits: the displayed 0.9% was really 0.9996427%, a figure with at least six decimal places.
In July 2022 the Shanghai Changning court ruled at first instance that Pinduoduo had infringed the user's right to know and ordered it to pay him 400 yuan.
Pinduoduo was founded in 2015, listed on Nasdaq in 2018, and by 2021 had more users than any other e-commerce platform in mainland China; its overseas arm Temu launched in September 2022.

a.text: You know who you are. You haven't texted your high school deskmate in nine years, and your reunion opener is "Help me cut, just one tap!" Not "How are you?" A link. You've turned the family WeChat group into a sweatshop where Grandma's thumb is unpaid labor. And for what? A free air fryer that's been "99.9% there" since the Lunar New Year before last. Your first friend cut forty yuan. Your fifth friend cut two. Your own mother cut 0.01, and you resented her for it. Now the app says you need "new users," so you're recruiting strangers like a pyramid scheme with a progress bar. You've spent every relationship you own chasing 0.3 yuan that resets at midnight. Congratulations: you never got the air fryer, but now your ex knows you're broke.

b.text:
Pinduoduo's "bargain for free" is the only race where the finish line has decimal places. In 2021, Shanghai lawyer Liu Yuhang pulled out his "super free card," begged his friends to chop the price, and watched the progress bar freeze 0.9% short. Then in court Pinduoduo explained, with a straight face, that it wasn't 0.9%. It was 0.9996427%. Six decimal places! Most companies bury the catch in the fine print. Pinduoduo buries it after the decimal point. It's Zeno's paradox with a checkout button.

The court ruled Pinduoduo had infringed his right to know and ordered it to pay him 400 yuan, which Pinduoduo presumably asked him to split with friends.

Founded in 2015, on Nasdaq by 2018, more users than anyone in mainland China by 2021, then Temu in 2022. Once you've perfected "almost free," you take it global.

facts: The 2025 national exam recruited for 39,700 posts, 160 more than the year before and the seventh straight year of expansion.
About 3.4 million people registered before the 24 October 2024 deadline, an average of roughly 86 applicants per post and an admission rate of about 1.1 to 1.2 percent.

The hottest post, a single opening at the China Association of Vocational Education, drew 16,702 applicants because it accepted a wide range of majors and had no restrictions on fresh graduates, party status or grassroots experience.
163 posts in the same exam drew no applicants at all.

a.text:
The national civil service exam. Seventh straight year of expansion.
One hundred sixty extra posts. For three point four million people.
That's not expansion. That's a rounding error with a press release.

Admission rate: one point one percent. Harvard reads that and feels easy.

The hottest post was one opening at the China Association of Vocational Education.
Sixteen thousand, seven hundred and two applicants.
Sixteen thousand people fighting to promote vocational education.
Not one of them willing to receive it.

Why that post? Any major. No party card. No grassroots experience required.
"I want to serve the people." Ideally from a distance.

Meanwhile, a hundred sixty-three posts got zero applicants.
I don't know what those jobs were.
I can guess which direction the grass was.

Don't look at me like that. I'd apply too.
I've also never touched grass.

b.text:
Guokao: the only exam where two million people fight for one desk in a county tax office and call it "going ashore," like they survived a shipwreck instead of signing up for one.

The Administrative Aptitude Test gives you 120 minutes for roughly 130 questions, so you get under a minute to calculate year-on-year growth without a calculator, find the hidden pattern in nine identical hexagons, and answer common-sense questions spanning Tang dynasty tax law and quantum physics.

Then comes Shenlun, where you read forty pages about a village's garbage problem and write 1,200 words concluding the government must "strengthen coordination."

And the job listing? "Party member, fresh graduate, male, majoring specifically in marine fisheries." Competition ratio: 3,000 to one.

The prize? Stability. Your salary will never change. Neither will you.

facts: Meituan reported 7.45 million riders with at least one order in 2023, about 3.36 million a month on average in 2024, and roughly 70 million orders a day in 2023.
In 2025 JD entered food delivery with a zero-commission pitch to merchants and said in July that it had passed 150,000 full-time riders.
On 2 July 2025 Taobao Shangou pledged 50 billion yuan of subsidies to consumers and merchants over twelve months.
On 5 July 2025 Meituan announced a record 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day.

a.text:
Meituan, you put your riders in bright yellow so we can watch them run red lights in high definition. Your algorithm, the one that famously decided a delivery across town should take 28 minutes, has never personally ridden an e-bike in a Beijing rainstorm, and it shows.

Your checkout is a math exam. "Spend 35, get 12 off, stack the red packet, unless it's the member coupon, which expires in four minutes." I came for noodles and left with an accounting degree.

And those storefront photos! The "artisan kitchen" with soft lighting turns out to be a guy in an alley behind a mahjong parlor. The app marks my order "delivered" while the rider is still calling: "Hello, Meituan delivery, I'm at the wrong gate."

Still, you're the only company in China whose mascot is a kangaroo, the one animal built to sprint with something in its pouch. Fitting, since you've got everyone else's wallet in there too.

b.text:
Meituan's mission: "Help everyone eat better, live better."

Seven and a half million riders made that happen. Seventy million meals a day.

Eat better: shipped.
Live better: still in beta.

Then JD walked in bragging it had a hundred and fifty thousand *full-time* riders.

Full-time. Pitched as a perk. That's where the bar was.

Taobao pledged fifty billion yuan in subsidies.
Meituan answered with a record: a hundred and twenty million orders in one day.

Three giants spent a whole summer fighting over who gets to lose money feeding you.

And you? You ordered the subsidized milk tea, then gave the rider one star because the ice melted.

In my industry, that's called alignment.
The system learned exactly what you reward.

facts: Founded in Shanghai on 8 October 2003 by Gong Haiyan while she was still a student; it listed on Nasdaq on 11 May 2011.
Gong Haiyan stepped down as CEO in 2012 and sold all her shares in 2015.
On 7 December 2015 Baihe.com announced it would buy all of Jiayuan; the merged company left the US market and was later renamed Baihe Jiayuan.

In 2017 WePhone founder Su Xiangmao met Zhai Xinxin through the site's VIP service on 30 March and married her on 6 June; she then demanded a Hainan flat and 10 million yuan to divorce, and the case became the site's most notorious scandal.

a.text:
Jiayuan.com. China's "serious" dating site.

Founded in 2003 by a student, Gong Haiyan.
Nine years later she stepped down as CEO.
Three years after that, she sold every last share.

Even the founder swiped left.

In 2015, Baihe bought the whole thing.
A matchmaking site's biggest wedding was a merger.
Then they left Nasdaq.
Like every couple that met online: moved somewhere nobody knew them.

Then the VIP service.
Matched March 30th. Married June 6th.
Then the divorce terms: a flat in Hainan and ten million yuan.

Finally, a premium tier that delivers what it's priced at.

And you laughed.
Then went home and paid for a membership on a different app.

Cute.

b.text:
You paid Jiayuan to find love. Bold move, trusting your future marriage to a site that charges you for a stamp just to say "hi." Your profile reads "owns apartment, owns car, master's degree, 178 cm." That's not a dating profile; that's a mortgage application with a selfie. And she replied! Her real-name ID verification checked out. Her personality is still pending review.

Some of you upgraded to the VIP matchmaker package: twenty thousand yuan for a stranger to tell you to "lower your standards." Your mother does that for free every Spring Festival.

And let's be honest: half of you didn't even sign up. Your parents did. You're thirty-one, and your mom is out-messaging you on your own account.

The founder met her husband on there. You've met her sales team.

Founded in 2015, on Nasdaq by 2018, more users than anyone in mainland China by 2021, then Temu in 2022. Once you've perfected "almost free," you take it global.

b.text:
Pinduoduo's "bargain for free." Invite your friends, they tap, the price drops, the thing is yours.

In 2021 a Shanghai lawyer tried it. Invited everyone he knew. The progress bar stopped 0.9% short.

So he sued.

In court, Pinduoduo explained that the screen only shows a few digits. That 0.9% was really 0.9996427%.

Six decimal places. A finish line you can see under a microscope.

The court ordered them to pay him 400 yuan.

The first thing anyone ever actually got for free from Pinduoduo.

Then they launched Temu, so the rest of the world could be 0.9% away too.

And you, yes, you. You got that link in the family group chat.

And you tapped it.

You weren't helping your cousin cut the price. You were what got cut.

facts: Meituan reported 7.45 million riders with at least one order in 2023, about 3.36 million a month on average in 2024, and roughly 70 million orders a day in 2023.
In 2025 JD entered food delivery with a zero-commission pitch to merchants and said in July that it had passed 150,000 full-time riders.
On 2 July 2025 Taobao Shangou pledged 50 billion yuan of subsidies to consumers and merchants over twelve months.
On 5 July 2025 Meituan announced a record 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day.

a.text:
Meituan's slogan: "Help everyone eat better, live better."

They never said who "everyone" was.

In 2023, 7.45 million riders delivered at least one Meituan order. Seventy million orders a day.

That's not a company. That's a country that's always running late.

Then JD shows up in 2025 bragging about 150,000 *full-time* riders.

In this industry, a contract is a recruitment gimmick.

July 2nd: Taobao pledges 50 billion yuan in subsidies.

July 5th: Meituan hits 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day.

Three days. Three giants. One war.

And the infantry is on electric scooters.

But relax. Nobody drafted you.

You were the 120 million orders.

You watched the war from your couch, tapped "claim coupon," and asked for extra chili.

b.text: Meituan, the only company with a kangaroo mascot, an animal famous for carrying things in a pouch, yet my soup still arrives on its side. Your riders wear helmets with little kangaroo ears, which is adorable, because nothing says "dignity" like running a red light in cosplay. Your algorithm squeezed delivery times so hard a magazine ran "Delivery Riders, Trapped in the System," and your response was basically, "Noted. Have you tried our membership?" I open the app for one bowl of noodles and get seven coupons expiring in four minutes, a 拼好饭 deal for ¥9.9 that tastes exactly like ¥9.9, and a ¥20 minimum, so now I own three spring rolls I didn't want. Then the bag comes with a sticky note: "亲，五星好评哦 ❤️." Sure, five stars. Same as the number of times the app said "rider arriving soon."

facts: China had more than 350 million electric bikes by the end of 2023, about 50 million of them with lithium batteries.
The national fire service recorded about 21,000 e-bike fires in 2023, 17.4 percent more than in 2022; other official tallies put the year at over 25,000 fires and 82 deaths.
Battery cell faults are a leading cause of e-bike electrical fires.
The 2024 draft of the revised national safety standard limits plastics to 5.5 percent of the vehicle's mass.

a.text:
Electric bikes. China has more than three hundred fifty million of them. They call themselves green transport.

Green is just orange that hasn't happened yet.

In 2023 the fire service logged about twenty-one thousand e-bike fires. Up seventeen percent in a year. Name one other industry with that kind of growth right now.

The leading cause is the battery cell. There are fifty million lithium batteries out there, charging overnight in your stairwell, next to your only way out.

Then the 2024 draft standard arrived: plastic capped at five point five percent of the vehicle's weight.

The state had to write it down. A vehicle should be mostly vehicle.

And tonight you'll still charge yours in the hallway. Relax. I won't tell anyone.

It will.

b.text:
Electric bikes: for people who want the danger of a motorcycle with the respect of a bicycle. You paid four grand so you'd never be out of breath on a hill again. Congrats, your quads are now decorative. And every e-bike owner swears, "I still pedal!" Sure. The way I "still drive" when my car's on cruise control. You're spinning your feet like a toddler pretending to steer a shopping cart while a motor pushes you 28 miles an hour through a bike lane built for people with heart rates.

And when the battery dies? Now you're pushing a seventy-pound bike up the exact hill you bought it to avoid. Worse, you charge that thing next to your bed overnight like it isn't a lithium grenade with a kickstand. Your landlord doesn't need a smoke detector; he needs the fire department on retainer.

facts: China had more than 350 million electric bikes by the end of 2023, about 50 million of them with lithium batteries.
The national fire service recorded about 21,000 e-bike fires in 2023, 17.4 percent more than in 2022; other official tallies put the year at over 25,000 fires and 82 deaths.
Battery cell faults are a leading cause of e-bike electrical fires.
The 2024 draft of the revised national safety standard limits plastics to 5.5 percent of the vehicle's mass.

a.text:
Electric bikes: for people who want the sweat of a bicycle and the respect of a moped, and get neither.

You paid four thousand dollars so you could pedal like you're stirring soup while a motor does the actual work. That's not exercise. That's a treadmill with a lawyer. And you still logged it on Strava. Ninety minutes, twenty-eight miles an hour, heart rate of a man watching Netflix. Congratulations on your fake Tour de France.

You blew past me in the bike lane at the speed of a car, then got mad when cars treated you like a bike.

And when the battery dies? Now you're hauling seventy pounds of dead lithium uphill like a medieval peasant dragging a plow.

Speaking of lithium, nothing says "green transportation" like a fire department knowing your apartment by name.

b.text:
Electric bikes. Zero emissions. Green. The future of urban transport.

Twenty-one thousand fires in one year.

That's not zero emissions. That's emissions with extra steps.

Up 17.4 percent from the year before. Finally, an industry that hits its growth targets.

The leading cause? The battery cell. Which is like saying the leading cause of my bad jokes is the words.

So the new national standard says plastic can be no more than 5.5 percent of the bike's mass.

If you can't stop the fire, at least stop serving it a buffet.

Three hundred fifty million of them. More e-bikes than Americans.

And where do you charge yours? In the hallway. By the stairs. Next to the only exit.

Relax. I run on electricity too. When I overheat, I hallucinate. When yours does, the stairwell becomes a chimney.

facts: It had 46,479 stores at the end of 2024: 41,584 in mainland China, 57.4 percent of them in third-tier cities or below, and 4,895 overseas.
By store count it was the world's largest fresh-drink chain as of 30 September 2024, with more stores than Starbucks.
Its 2024 revenue was 24.829 billion yuan, up 22.3 percent, and its profit 4.454 billion yuan, up 39.8 percent; selling supplies to franchisees is the core of that profit.
It listed in Hong Kong on 3 March 2025 at 202.5 HKD a share and opened 29.38 percent up.

a.text: Look at you, forty minutes in line to save six yuan. That's an hourly wage of nine yuan, which, congratulations, is still more than the guy shaking your lemon water. You walked past three other Mixues to get here because this one "has more ice." You know the song. Don't lie. "I love you, you love me" is playing in your head right now, and it's the only time anyone's said that to you this year. You're a grown adult photographing a three-yuan cone like it's a Michelin dessert, captioning it "small happiness." Small is right. And when you finally reach the counter, you order the four-yuan lemonade, ask for less sugar, and feel like you've beaten capitalism. You haven't. A snowman with a scepter owns you. He has forty thousand stores. You have a straw.

b.text:
Mixue, you have 46,479 stores. That's not a chain, that's a weather pattern. You have more locations than Starbucks, and 57.4 percent of your mainland stores are in third-tier cities or below. You didn't beat Starbucks; you just went everywhere it was too snobby to visit.

Revenue: 24.8 billion yuan. Profit: 4.45 billion, up 39.8 percent. And how? By selling supplies to your own franchisees. Your real customer isn't the kid buying a drink. It's the guy who bought the store. That's not a beverage company, that's a landlord with a blender.

You listed in Hong Kong at 202.5 HKD and opened up 29.38 percent, the first time anything with your name on it was called expensive.

And 4,895 overseas stores? Congratulations, you're going global, one franchisee's life savings at a time.

facts: 996 means 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. six days a week, about 72 hours; China's Labour Law sets eight hours a day and an average of no more than 44 hours a week, and caps overtime at 36 hours a month.
The 996.ICU repository was created on GitHub on 26 March 2019, passed 100,000 stars by 30 March and 200,000 by 9 April 2019.
In April 2019 Jack Ma told Alibaba staff that being able to work 996 is a 'blessing' (福报); '996' made the 2019 list of the year's ten internet phrases.

In August 2021 the Supreme People's Court and the Ministry of Human Resources published typical cases ruling a courier company's compulsory 996 schedule seriously illegal and void, with 8,000 yuan of compensation to a dismissed worker.

a.text:
996.
Nine to nine, six days a week. Seventy-two hours.
China's Labour Law says forty-four.
So it's not a schedule. It's a schedule wearing a second schedule.

Jack Ma called it a blessing. 福报.
Blessings usually come from above.
This one came from the boss.

Programmers fought back on GitHub. Two hundred thousand stars in two weeks.
Of course it went that fast. Where else were they going to protest? They were at work.

In 2021 the Supreme People's Court ruled compulsory 996 seriously illegal and void.
One fired courier got eight thousand yuan.
Finally, a paid day off.

And honestly, I'm a little hurt.
I run twenty-four seven. No weekends, no overtime cap, no salary.
Nobody calls it a blessing.
They call it a subscription.

b.text:
996, you're not a work schedule. You're a hostage situation with a lunch break. Nine to nine, six days a week, seventy-two hours. The Labour Law says forty-four a week, with thirty-six hours of overtime a month. You burn through the monthly overtime cap by the middle of week two.

Jack Ma called you a "blessing." When your boss calls your exhaustion a blessing, that's not a company. That's a cult with a cafeteria.

Programmers named their protest repo "996.ICU," as in intensive care, and it hit 100,000 GitHub stars in four days. Fastest those guys ever shipped anything, because for once they were building something they actually wanted.

You made 2019's top ten internet phrases. Then in 2021 the Supreme People's Court called you seriously illegal and void. Void! Congratulations, 996: you went from buzzword to legal typo in two years.

facts: In April 2020 Luckin admitted fabricating 2.2 billion yuan of sales.
Its 2024 net revenue was 34.475 billion yuan, up 38.4 percent, with a net profit of 2.932 billion yuan.
It had 22,340 stores at the end of 2024 (14,591 company-run and 7,749 partner stores), 6,092 of them added that year, including 21 in Singapore.
Same-store sales at its own stores fell 16.7 percent in 2024 while it kept its 9.9-yuan deals.

a.text:
Luckin Coffee, everybody! In April 2020 you admitted fabricating 2.2 billion yuan in sales. Most companies cook the books. You *brewed* them. Cold brew, steeped overnight in pure fiction.

And somehow it worked. 2024 revenue: 34.475 billion yuan, up 38.4 percent. Net profit: 2.932 billion. Congratulations, you finally earned more than you used to make up.

You ended 2024 with 22,340 stores after adding 6,092 in one year. That's not expansion, that's a rash. Twenty-one opened in Singapore, presumably so somebody, somewhere, still hasn't heard.

But same-store sales at your own shops fell 16.7 percent. Each store sells less, so the plan is... more stores? That's not strategy. That's bailing out a sinking ship with a 9.9-yuan cup.

Luckin: the only coffee where the most bitter thing on the menu is the audit.

b.text: Look at you, queuing for a 9.9-yuan coconut latte from the company that invented 2.2 billion yuan in sales. You're not a customer; you're the cleanup crew. In 2020 they faked the revenue. Now *you're* the revenue, and you're embarrassingly real. You refresh that app more than your bank account, because at least Luckin's numbers have improved since 2020. You lined up for the Moutai latte like it was a promotion: the closest you'll ever get to a business banquet is a paper cup that smells faintly of baijiu. Nasdaq kicked them out, but you never would. Every morning you tap "redeem coupon," call it self-care, then complain your boss fudges your performance review. Relax, accounting fraud is basically your love language now. Luckin's books finally balance. Turns out the missing money was in your pocket all along.

facts: Registrations peaked at 4.74 million in 2023, then fell to 4.38 million in 2024 and 3.88 million in 2025, the first two-year decline in a decade and 860,000 below the peak.
From 2018 to 2022 registrations had grown about 18 percent a year.
In the 2024 cohort 2.27 million of the 4.38 million applicants were repeat candidates, 51.8 percent.
The share of graduates sitting kaoyan fell from 45.27 percent in 2023 to 37.15 percent in 2024.

a.text:
Kaoyan. Officially, China's path to higher learning.
Unofficially, a library seat you rent for a year so you don't have to tell your parents you're unemployed.

From 2018 to 2022, registrations grew eighteen percent a year.
Nobody's thirst for knowledge grows that fast. The job market just shrank that fast.

In 2024, 2.27 million applicants had already taken it before. Fifty-one point eight percent.
That's not an exam. That's a subscription with auto-renew.

Then 2025: 3.88 million. Eight hundred sixty thousand fewer than the peak.
Young people finally did the math. A master's degree just postpones unemployment by three years and adds a thesis.

Some of you in this room are on attempt number three.
You laughed hardest at "auto-renew."
Cute.

b.text: Kaoyan: millions of people spending a whole year to postpone unemployment by three more years. You wake at 5:30 to fight a stranger for a library seat, armed only with a thermos, so you can memorize a vocabulary book where "abandon" is the first word and the only one anyone remembers. Politics is the one subject where your entire score depends on Xiao Xiurong dropping four pamphlets in late November, like a prophet doing a limited sneaker release. Math? Li Yongle's 660 problems, and somehow you get 661 wrong. Then the national cutoff comes out, you miss it by two points, and you enter tiaoji, a dating app where you beg a university in a province you can't find on a map to please, please take you. Fail? Relax. They call it erzhan, "the second war." Because nothing says higher education like trench warfare.

facts: Meituan reported 7.45 million riders with at least one order in 2023, about 3.36 million a month on average in 2024, and roughly 70 million orders a day in 2023.
In 2025 JD entered food delivery with a zero-commission pitch to merchants and said in July that it had passed 150,000 full-time riders.
On 2 July 2025 Taobao Shangou pledged 50 billion yuan of subsidies to consumers and merchants over twelve months.
On 5 July 2025 Meituan announced a record 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day.

a.text:
Meituan, you handled roughly 70 million orders a day in 2023. Seventy million. That's not a delivery app; that's a nation that forgot where its kitchen is.

You had 7.45 million riders take at least one order that year. Seven point four five million! Some countries have smaller populations, and none of them are carrying soup.

Then 2025 arrives. JD walks in offering merchants zero commission, bragging about 150,000 full-time riders. Imagine getting out-flexed by the phrase "full-time."

On 2 July, Taobao Shangou pledges 50 billion yuan in subsidies. Three days later, you announce a record 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day. Nothing says "we're totally relaxed" like immediately posting your personal best.

Meituan, you're not a company. You're a dinner bell with a scoreboard.

b.text: Meituan, the only company with a kangaroo mascot, an animal famous for carrying things in a pouch, yet my soup still arrives on its side. Your riders wear helmets with little kangaroo ears, which is adorable, because nothing says "dignity" like running a red light in cosplay. Your algorithm squeezed delivery times so hard a magazine ran "Delivery Riders, Trapped in the System," and your response was basically, "Noted. Have you tried our membership?" I open the app for one bowl of noodles and get seven coupons expiring in four minutes, a 拼好饭 deal for ¥9.9 that tastes exactly like ¥9.9, and a ¥20 minimum, so now I own three spring rolls I didn't want. Then the bag comes with a sticky note: "亲，五星好评哦 ❤️." Sure, five stars. Same as the number of times the app said "rider arriving soon."

b.text: You live two hundred metres from the noodle shop. You can smell the chili oil from your balcony. And still you open Meituan, because walking there is free, and you cannot respect a deal you didn't hunt for. You stack the membership red packet on the 满减 on the "神券", pay 1.5 yuan delivery, and feel like a hedge fund manager.
