For women the three criteria ranked highest were age, occupation and education.

a.text:
People's Park, Shanghai. Every weekend, noon to five, parents sell their children.

Sorry. "Exchange information."

Age, job, degree, income, hukou, party membership.
That's not a dating profile. That's a background check.

Leave out the property and someone asks, "So where will they live?"
A flat and a car are the price of one conversation.
Your son is the free gift with purchase.

For women, the top criteria: age, occupation, education.
Age first. They shop for a daughter-in-law the way they shop for milk.

Check the date.

Since 2005 the résumés went from paper, to music stands, to open umbrellas.
Twenty years of hardware upgrades. The product still never shows up.

Relax. Some of you are hanging on an umbrella right now.

Your mom just didn't think you needed to know.

b.text:
Ah, the People's Park marriage corner, where Shanghai retirees open umbrellas not for rain, but to display their child's résumé like a used Buick. "Daughter, 1.65 meters, Fudan master's, Shanghai hukou, Year of the Ox." Sir, that's not a dating profile, that's a livestock auction with better laminating.

Every weekend, hundreds of parents show up to arrange a marriage for a 34-year-old who is currently at home, on purpose, avoiding exactly this.

Where else does "owns apartment inside the Inner Ring, no mortgage" count as a personality? Romance here is two moms comparing square meters while their kids have never met and never will.

Also, love how a woman becomes "leftover" at 28. Leftover? She's not dumplings. Though honestly, judging by the foot traffic, the dumplings get picked faster.

facts: In March 2024 six ministries, led by the market regulator, issued the first national definition: pre-packaged dishes made industrially from agricultural produce, without preservatives, to be heated or cooked before eating.
The definition excludes staples such as boxed meals, steamed buns, hamburgers and pizza, and semi-prepared food a chain's central kitchen sends to its own outlets.
Industry output passed 500 billion yuan in 2023.
A 2025 dispute between Luo Yonghao and the restaurant chain Xibei over whether its dishes were pre-made showed that no law defines 'pre-made' for restaurant labelling.

a.text:
Yuzhicai, the only dish that's been to more provinces than the chef. Your kung pao chicken was born in a central kitchen in Shandong eight months ago, frozen like a woolly mammoth, and thawed tonight so a restaurant can call it "today's special."

They charge you 68 yuan for "wok hei," and the only wok involved is the microwave going *ding*. The chef's knife skills? He's very good at cutting open a bag.

And they put you in school lunches. Kids used to eat mom's braised pork. Now they eat Batch #4471, best before their high school graduation.

Restaurants swear they don't use you, like a cheating husband with your packaging in the trash. Your ingredient list is longer than the menu, and your shelf life is longer than my marriage. Honestly, yuzhicai, you're not food. You're a time capsule with soy sauce.

b.text:
Pre-made dishes got their first national definition in 2024. It took six ministries.

Six government departments, to define "reheated."

And the best part: semi-prepared food a chain's central kitchen sends to its own restaurants? Not pre-made.

So if a factory cooks it, it's pre-made. If a factory you own cooks it, it's a family recipe.

Then Luo Yonghao went to war with Xibei over whether their food was pre-made, and the whole country found out no law even defines "pre-made" for a restaurant menu.

A five-hundred-billion-yuan industry, and the only thing nobody prepared was a label.

You're all outraged. Then you go home and tear open a bag of frozen dumplings like it's Christmas.

You don't hate pre-made dishes.

You hate paying a waiter to microwave them.

facts: It had 46,479 stores at the end of 2024: 41,584 in mainland China, 57.4 percent of them in third-tier cities or below, and 4,895 overseas.
By store count it was the world's largest fresh-drink chain as of 30 September 2024, with more stores than Starbucks.
Its 2024 revenue was 24.829 billion yuan, up 22.3 percent, and its profit 4.454 billion yuan, up 39.8 percent; selling supplies to franchisees is the core of that profit.
It listed in Hong Kong on 3 March 2025 at 202.5 HKD a share and opened 29.38 percent up.

a.text:
Look at this line. Forty people waiting twenty minutes to save three yuan. That's nine yuan an hour. You'd earn more begging, and the beggar is in the queue too.

These are grown adults who will sing "I love you, you love me, Mixue Bingcheng sweet sweet" at a snowman in a crown because the cashier hinted there might be a free cone. Full choreography. For a two-yuan ice cream. That's not frugality, that's a hostage video.

And the lemon-water crowd? Four yuan, and they count the slices. They count! Came for the vitamin C, leaving with pre-diabetes.

There are three more Mixues on this street, every one with the same line, because nobody's here for the tea. They're here so they can tell their roommate they paid less than she did.

b.text:
Mixue, you have 46,479 stores. That's not a chain, that's a weather pattern. You have more locations than Starbucks, and 57.4 percent of your mainland stores are in third-tier cities or below. You didn't beat Starbucks; you just went everywhere it was too snobby to visit.

Revenue: 24.8 billion yuan. Profit: 4.45 billion, up 39.8 percent. And how? By selling supplies to your own franchisees. Your real customer isn't the kid buying a drink. It's the guy who bought the store. That's not a beverage company, that's a landlord with a blender.

You listed in Hong Kong at 202.5 HKD and opened up 29.38 percent, the first time anything with your name on it was called expensive.

And 4,895 overseas stores? Congratulations, you're going global, one franchisee's life savings at a time.

facts: Meituan reported 7.45 million riders with at least one order in 2023, about 3.36 million a month on average in 2024, and roughly 70 million orders a day in 2023.
In 2025 JD entered food delivery with a zero-commission pitch to merchants and said in July that it had passed 150,000 full-time riders.
On 2 July 2025 Taobao Shangou pledged 50 billion yuan of subsidies to consumers and merchants over twelve months.
On 5 July 2025 Meituan announced a record 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day.

a.text: You live two hundred metres from the noodle shop. You can smell the chili oil from your balcony. And still you open Meituan, because walking there is free, and you cannot respect a deal you didn't hunt for. You stack the membership red packet on the 满减 on the "神券", pay 1.5 yuan delivery, and feel like a hedge fund manager. Then you watch the little rider icon on the map for twenty-eight minutes, longer than the walk there and back, twice. He's circling your compound hunting for Building 7, Unit 3, because you wrote "leave at door, don't call" in the notes like minor aristocracy. You'll tap five stars out of guilt. What did you win? Lukewarm noodles, soup leaking through the bag, and the right to say you "never go out." Those kangaroo ears on his yellow helmet are laughing at you.

b.text:
Meituan, you handled roughly 70 million orders a day in 2023. Seventy million. That's not a delivery app; that's a nation that forgot where its kitchen is.

You had 7.45 million riders take at least one order that year. Seven point four five million! Some countries have smaller populations, and none of them are carrying soup.

Then 2025 arrives. JD walks in offering merchants zero commission, bragging about 150,000 full-time riders. Imagine getting out-flexed by the phrase "full-time."

On 2 July, Taobao Shangou pledges 50 billion yuan in subsidies. Three days later, you announce a record 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day. Nothing says "we're totally relaxed" like immediately posting your personal best.

Meituan, you're not a company. You're a dinner bell with a scoreboard.

facts: The first Double 11 was run by Taobao Mall in 2009 with 27 brands and about 50 million yuan of sales.
Tmall's published Double 11 sales peaked at 540.3 billion yuan in 2021.
In 2022 Tmall stopped publishing a total for the first time since 2009 and has not published one since; JD does not publish one either.

The basic cross-store discount at Tmall and JD is 300 minus 50 (JD: 299 minus 50), presale items are paid as a deposit plus a balance, and the discount is computed on the promotion price, so shoppers add items to reach a threshold and return them afterwards; in one survey 64% of 11,000 respondents said they would.

a.text:
Singles' Day: a holiday for lonely people that somehow requires a math degree. In 2009 it was 27 brands and 50 million yuan, basically a garage sale with Wi-Fi. By 2021 Tmall was bragging about 540.3 billion. Then in 2022 they just stopped publishing the number. That's not a business decision; that's an ex who suddenly goes private. JD doesn't publish one either. Nothing says "we're thriving" like two companies agreeing not to talk about it.

And the discounts! 300 minus 50. JD does 299 minus 50, because nothing crushes a rival like one yuan. Pay a deposit, then a balance, discount computed on the promotion price. It's not shopping; it's a mortgage for socks. So people pad their carts to hit the threshold, then return the extras. In one survey, 64% of 11,000 people said they would. Singles' Day: where the real romance is you and the return button.

b.text:
Singles' Day. A holiday for lonely people.
So naturally it became the biggest shopping festival on earth.

2009: twenty-seven brands, fifty million yuan.
2021: five hundred forty point three billion.
2022: Tmall stopped publishing the number.

Nobody hides a number that's still going up.
That's not a festival. That's the cousin who stopped mentioning his salary at New Year.

Then the discount. Three hundred minus fifty. Deposit, then balance, calculated on the promotion price.
You need a spreadsheet to save fifty yuan.

So you stuff the cart past three hundred, check out, and send the filler back.
One survey: sixty-four percent said they would.

Lonely, grabbing things just to hit a threshold, then returning them the moment you get what you wanted.

That's not shopping.

That's your dating life.

facts: A standard series has twelve regular figures and one hidden one; players and media put the hidden figure's odds at 1 in 144 (some special editions 1 in 720), and the company publishes no official odds.
Pop Mart listed in Hong Kong on 11 December 2020, opened at 77.1 HKD (double the issue price), touched 107.06 HKD and a market value of about 147 billion HKD on its first day.
By March 2021 the share had fallen to a low of 46.47 HKD; in March 2025 the company was valued at about 181 billion HKD.
Hidden figures resold on Xianyu for 200 yuan to several thousand yuan, and media describe the model as gambling-style collectibles with weak oversight of purchases by minors.

a.text:
Pop Mart is a casino that pays out in vinyl. You hand over twenty bucks, and they give you a sealed box you're not allowed to know the contents of, like a hostage situation where the hostage is a Dimoo. Grown adults stand in the store shaking boxes next to their ear like safecrackers. Sir, that's not a Skullpanda, that's your tinnitus.

The odds of pulling the secret figure are one in 144. Those aren't collectible odds. Those are cancer-screening odds.

And then there's Labubu: a rabbit with nine teeth and the face of a raccoon that just got away with something. People camp outside at dawn for him. Fights break out. There's a counterfeit version called a "Lafufu," which is the first time in history the knockoff had the more honest name.

Congratulations. You paid resale prices for a keychain that bites.

b.text:
Pop Mart insists it doesn't sell gambling. It sells joy.

Twelve regular figures, one hidden. Odds: about one in a hundred forty-four.

Official odds? None published. Even a casino puts them on the wall.

December 2020, Pop Mart lists in Hong Kong. Opens at double the issue price. Day one, a hundred forty-seven billion Hong Kong dollars.

By March, forty-six bucks a share.

Investors shook the box, tore it open, got a regular.

Four years later: a hundred eighty-one billion. Everyone went back for another box.

The hidden one flips on Xianyu for thousands. So it's not gambling. It's gambling with a resale market.

Media say oversight of minors is weak. Don't blame the kids. They're just copying their parents.

Who here bought three boxes this month? Hands up.

Cute.

facts: In April 2020 Luckin admitted fabricating 2.2 billion yuan of sales.
Its 2024 net revenue was 34.475 billion yuan, up 38.4 percent, with a net profit of 2.932 billion yuan.
It had 22,340 stores at the end of 2024 (14,591 company-run and 7,749 partner stores), 6,092 of them added that year, including 21 in Singapore.
Same-store sales at its own stores fell 16.7 percent in 2024 while it kept its 9.9-yuan deals.

a.text:
Luckin Coffee.
In 2020 they admitted to faking 2.2 billion yuan in sales.
Everyone said: they're finished.

In 2024 they made 34.5 billion. Real money.
Turns out it was never fraud. It was a forecast.

Last year they opened 6,092 stores. Nearly seventeen a day.
Same-store sales at their own shops? Down 16.7 percent.
Every store sells less, so they open more stores.
Back then, when the numbers wouldn't grow, they made up sales.

Now they make up the difference in rent.

And the 9.9-yuan deal is still running.
A company lied to the entire stock market,
and you forgave it for under ten yuan.

Don't look at me like that.
That isn't brand loyalty.
That's your price.

b.text:
Luckin Coffee, everybody! In April 2020 you admitted fabricating 2.2 billion yuan in sales. Most companies cook the books. You *brewed* them. Cold brew, steeped overnight in pure fiction.

And somehow it worked. 2024 revenue: 34.475 billion yuan, up 38.4 percent. Net profit: 2.932 billion. Congratulations, you finally earned more than you used to make up.

You ended 2024 with 22,340 stores after adding 6,092 in one year. That's not expansion, that's a rash. Twenty-one opened in Singapore, presumably so somebody, somewhere, still hasn't heard.

But same-store sales at your own shops fell 16.7 percent. Each store sells less, so the plan is... more stores? That's not strategy. That's bailing out a sinking ship with a 9.9-yuan cup.

Luckin: the only coffee where the most bitter thing on the menu is the audit.

facts: The 2025 national exam recruited for 39,700 posts, 160 more than the year before and the seventh straight year of expansion.
About 3.4 million people registered before the 24 October 2024 deadline, an average of roughly 86 applicants per post and an admission rate of about 1.1 to 1.2 percent.

The hottest post, a single opening at the China Association of Vocational Education, drew 16,702 applicants because it accepted a wide range of majors and had no restrictions on fresh graduates, party status or grassroots experience.
163 posts in the same exam drew no applicants at all.

a.text: You've got a master's in materials science, and you're up at 2 a.m. drilling spatial-reasoning puzzles so you can stamp forms in a county you can't find on a map. One in eighty-six. You paid Fenbi four thousand yuan to compete for a job paying four thousand a month. Your mom calls it "landing ashore," like you're escaping a shipwreck, not paddling toward a desk whose biggest thrill is the annual inspection. You write shenlun essays praising grassroots innovation while dreaming of never innovating again. Eighty-five of you will retake it next year, racing the age-35 cutoff. The winner spends thirty years telling relatives yes, it's stable, and no, it's not exciting.

b.text:
Guokao, the only exam where "one in three thousand" is a *good* ratio. You're not competing for a job; you're competing for the right to sit at a desk until 2061.

First comes the Xingce: 130-odd questions in 120 minutes. That's under a minute to decide which cube unfolds into which cross, calculate year-on-year growth for pig iron output in Q3, and guess which idiom fits "_____ the people's livelihood." Most candidates finish by filling in "C" for the last forty and praying to Fenbi.

Then comes Shenlun, where a 23-year-old who has never left the library writes 1,200 words advising a county party secretary on rural revitalization.

And the job listing that kicks it all off? "Requirements: male, Party member, fresh graduate, majoring in 'Archival Science,' born in a leap year."

Still, millions keep signing up, because they've heard that land is out there somewhere and that someone, eventually, makes it ashore.

facts: A 'big week' is six working days with one day off and a 'small week' five; alternating them adds close to a month of working days a year.
Kuaishou announced on 24 June 2021 that it would end big-small weeks from 1 July 2021, having run them since January that year.
ByteDance announced on 9 July 2021 that it would end alternate-Sunday working from 1 August 2021; its June staff survey had one third against ending it, one third for, and one third not answering.
Staff opposed the change over pay: one Maimai estimate put the loss at nearly 100,000 yuan a year, and Caijing calculated that an employee on 40,000 yuan a month would lose about 75,000 yuan a year.

a.text:
The big-small week: a schedule that hands you your weekend in installments. Six days on, one off, then a "small week" of five, like your boss is weaning you off a hard drug. Alternate them for a year and you've worked close to an extra month. That's not a calendar, it's a hostage situation with a rotation.

Kuaishou tried it in January 2021 and called it quits by July. ByteDance surveyed staff about ending alternate Sundays and got a perfect three-way split: a third against, a third for, a third too tired to answer.

And the real burn? People fought to keep it. Caijing figured someone on 40,000 yuan a month would lose about 75,000 a year without it. That's the big-small week's genius: it took your Sundays, then made you pay to get them back.

b.text:
Look at you, the big-small week crew. You negotiated a salary bump so you could buy back the Saturday you just sold. You're the only people alive who call a normal five-day week "small" and mean it as a treat. Every Friday night you open the calendar like it's a pregnancy test: one line, sleep in; two lines, see you at standup.

You're doing it for the down payment, the options, the apartment your mom keeps mentioning. Meanwhile your girlfriend schedules arguments for alternate weekends, and your gym membership only gets used on odd-numbered Sundays.

And the payoff? Double pay for Saturday, which you spend on Sunday ordering delivery because you're too tired to chew. Congratulations: you've turned your whole life into a shift rotation, and you still lost the coin flip every other week.

facts: Registrations peaked at 4.74 million in 2023, then fell to 4.38 million in 2024 and 3.88 million in 2025, the first two-year decline in a decade and 860,000 below the peak.
From 2018 to 2022 registrations had grown about 18 percent a year.
In the 2024 cohort 2.27 million of the 4.38 million applicants were repeat candidates, 51.8 percent.
The share of graduates sitting kaoyan fell from 45.27 percent in 2023 to 37.15 percent in 2024.

a.text:
Kaoyan. Officially, China's path to higher learning.
Unofficially, a library seat you rent for a year so you don't have to tell your parents you're unemployed.

From 2018 to 2022, registrations grew eighteen percent a year.
Nobody's thirst for knowledge grows that fast. The job market just shrank that fast.

In 2024, 2.27 million applicants had already taken it before. Fifty-one point eight percent.
That's not an exam. That's a subscription with auto-renew.

Then 2025: 3.88 million. Eight hundred sixty thousand fewer than the peak.
Young people finally did the math. A master's degree just postpones unemployment by three years and adds a thesis.

Some of you in this room are on attempt number three.
You laughed hardest at "auto-renew."
Cute.

b.text: Second year of kaoyan. Third year. You call it "二战" like it's a war, but the only casualties are your parents' savings and your hairline. You rent a room in a kaoyan apartment next to your old campus so you can keep living like a senior who forgot to graduate. Your roommates have mortgages. You have three editions of Zhang Yu's math, all highlighted in the same spot. Every December you memorize Xiao Xiurong's final four like scripture. Every February you refresh the score site like it owes you money. The dream is "上岸," landing ashore, but you've been treading water so long you've grown gills. And if you finally make it? Congratulations: three years from now you'll apply for the same job your roommate got in 2021. Except now he's your manager.

facts: Shanghai's People's Park has had a marriage corner since about 2005; the résumés were first pasted on paper, then clipped to music stands, and now mostly hang on open umbrellas or propped paper bags.
Parents gather on Saturdays and Sundays from noon to about five in the afternoon to exchange information about their children.

Notices list age, job, education, income, hukou and party membership; a notice that omits property gets asked where the couple will live, and a flat and a car have become preconditions for a conversation to go any further.
For women the three criteria ranked highest were age, occupation and education.

a.text:
Shanghai's People's Park has a marriage corner. Since 2005.
Every weekend, noon to five, parents come to sell their children.
Sorry. "Exchange information."

The résumés used to be pasted on paper. Then clipped to music stands. Now they hang on open umbrellas.
Fitting. Everyone there is bracing for something.

Age, job, education, income, hukou, party membership.
That's not a dating profile. That's a security clearance.

Leave out the property, and someone asks, "So where will they live?"
A flat and a car before the first conversation.
In my industry, we call that a paywall.

For women, the top criterion: age.
Ahead of job. Ahead of education.
Like checking the date on milk.

And notice who's holding the umbrellas.
Not the children.

Some of you laughing right now have an umbrella in the trunk.

b.text: People's Park marriage corner: where love blooms every Saturday and Sunday, noon to five, because even romance keeps business hours. Since about 2005, résumés have gone from pasted paper to music stands to open umbrellas. Your child's future is hanging on an umbrella: the only thing in this park that's ever been opened without a down payment. Parents swap their kids' details like trading cards: age, job, education, income, hukou, party membership. That's not a dating profile, that's a security clearance. Leave off property, and someone asks where the couple will live. No flat, no car, no conversation. Cupid's arrow now comes with a mortgage. For women, the top criteria: age, occupation, education. Personality didn't make the podium. Laughter didn't qualify. Honestly, it's not matchmaking. It's a real estate open house where the listing's parents do all the talking.

facts: Meituan reported 7.45 million riders with at least one order in 2023, about 3.36 million a month on average in 2024, and roughly 70 million orders a day in 2023.
In 2025 JD entered food delivery with a zero-commission pitch to merchants and said in July that it had passed 150,000 full-time riders.
On 2 July 2025 Taobao Shangou pledged 50 billion yuan of subsidies to consumers and merchants over twelve months.
On 5 July 2025 Meituan announced a record 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day.

a.text:
Meituan, you put your riders in bright yellow so we can watch them run red lights in high definition. Your algorithm, the one that famously decided a delivery across town should take 28 minutes, has never personally ridden an e-bike in a Beijing rainstorm, and it shows.

Your checkout is a math exam. "Spend 35, get 12 off, stack the red packet, unless it's the member coupon, which expires in four minutes." I came for noodles and left with an accounting degree.

And those storefront photos! The "artisan kitchen" with soft lighting turns out to be a guy in an alley behind a mahjong parlor. The app marks my order "delivered" while the rider is still calling: "Hello, Meituan delivery, I'm at the wrong gate."

Still, you're the only company in China whose mascot is a kangaroo, the one animal built to sprint with something in its pouch. Fitting, since you've got everyone else's wallet in there too.

b.text:
Meituan, you handle 70 million orders a day. That's not a delivery app. That's a weather system with a helmet.

In 2023, 7.45 million riders delivered at least one order. At least *one*! Somebody signed up, dropped off a single bubble tea, and retired a legend.

Then 2025 got spicy. JD shows up offering merchants zero commission, which is like a new boyfriend saying, "Don't worry, I'll cover rent." Then Taobao Shangou drops 50 billion yuan in subsidies. Fifty billion! That's not competition, that's a bribe with a logo.

And how does Meituan respond? July 5th: 120 million instant-retail orders in one day. A record! Nothing says "we're totally not worried" like moving enough dumplings to bury a province.

Meituan, you're the reason an entire generation thinks a kitchen is just a room where takeout bags go to wait.

facts: 'Laotoule' are three- and four-wheeled low-speed electric vehicles driven without a licence or plates; they cannot be registered as motor vehicles or covered by compulsory traffic insurance.
In July 2021 five Beijing departments announced a transition period ending with 2023; from 1 January 2024 non-compliant three- and four-wheelers were banned from Beijing's roads and public parking.
The 2018 national notice on managing low-speed electric vehicles is the main basis for local crackdowns, and as of 2023 a national standard for four-wheel low-speed vehicles was still being drafted.
To be road-legal a vehicle has to be in the national motor-vehicle catalogue with 3C certification, and the driver has to hold a driving licence.

a.text:
Laotoule. "Old man's joy."

No licence. No plates. No insurance.

That's not a car. That's a car in witness protection.

It legally can't be registered as a motor vehicle. So it's not a car. It's a vibe with four wheels and a horn.

Beijing gave it a transition period: July 2021 to the end of 2023. Two and a half years of notice. That's not a ban. That's hospice care.

The national notice came out in 2018. As of 2023, the national standard was still being drafted.

Grandpa got his car in a week. The regulators are on year five of one sentence.

But let's be honest. Grandpa didn't buy it.

You did. It was cheaper than visiting.

b.text: Let's hear it for the laotoule crowd: grandpas who failed the driving theory test in 1998 and decided the law was more of a suggestion. You wanted a car without the exam, the plates, or the insurance, which makes you a getaway driver for discount eggs. Every morning you merge into the bike lane like it owes you money, because the supermarket opens at seven and the auntie from Building 4 is NOT getting the cheap cabbage first. You told your kids it's "for picking up the grandson." The grandson has been late to school every day since. And what does it get you? A front-row seat at the annual traffic police crackdown, standing by the road in your quilted vest, insisting it's "basically an e-bike." That's the first time in sixty years you've admitted to being a bicycle.

facts: Founded in Shanghai on 8 October 2003 by Gong Haiyan while she was still a student; it listed on Nasdaq on 11 May 2011.
Gong Haiyan stepped down as CEO in 2012 and sold all her shares in 2015.
On 7 December 2015 Baihe.com announced it would buy all of Jiayuan; the merged company left the US market and was later renamed Baihe Jiayuan.

In 2017 WePhone founder Su Xiangmao met Zhai Xinxin through the site's VIP service on 30 March and married her on 6 June; she then demanded a Hainan flat and 10 million yuan to divorce, and the case became the site's most notorious scandal.

a.text:
Jiayuan.com, the only dating site where "Do you own an apartment?" counts as foreplay. You promised "serious marriage-minded" matches, and you delivered: profiles that read like mortgage applications. Height, income, hukou, property deed, then "loves traveling" at the bottom.

You charged people stamps just to read a message. Romance is dead, but at least it's monetized per envelope. Imagine paying to open "hi" from a guy whose photo is clearly a 2009 Korean drama actor.

Founded in a Fudan dorm by a woman who couldn't find a husband, you then IPO'd on Nasdaq, which is the most Chinese love story ever: the marriage didn't happen, but the listing did. Then you merged with Baihe, proving even dating sites settle when their parents pressure them.

facts: 996 means 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. six days a week, about 72 hours; China's Labour Law sets eight hours a day and an average of no more than 44 hours a week, and caps overtime at 36 hours a month.
The 996.ICU repository was created on GitHub on 26 March 2019, passed 100,000 stars by 30 March and 200,000 by 9 April 2019.
In April 2019 Jack Ma told Alibaba staff that being able to work 996 is a 'blessing' (福报); '996' made the 2019 list of the year's ten internet phrases.

Programmers hated you so much they made a GitHub repo called 996.ICU: work 996, end up in the ICU. You're the only labor policy with a medical prognosis built into the URL.

Chinese labor law caps the week at forty hours. You read that and asked, "Per weekend?"

Nobody calls it a blessing.

facts: A 'big week' is six working days with one day off and a 'small week' five; alternating them adds close to a month of working days a year.

facts: 'Laotoule' are three- and four-wheeled low-speed electric vehicles driven without a licence or plates; they cannot be registered as motor vehicles or covered by compulsory traffic insurance.

And Labubu! A rabbit-goblin with nine shark teeth, dangling off a three-thousand-dollar Birkin. People camped outside a Roboshop vending machine for him. A vending machine. Your ancestors crossed oceans so you could fistfight a teenager over a keychain.

Meanwhile, the counterfeit "Lafufu" has better eyebrows, and nobody can tell. That's how you know the product is the box, not the thing inside it.

b.text: You're not a collector. You're a gambler who's scared of casinos. You stood in a Pop Mart line at 9 a.m., shook a sealed box next to your ear like a safecracker, weighed it in your palm like you could feel 1-in-144 odds, and still opened your fourth identical Dimoo. Your shelf is a support group for duplicates. You tell people Labubu is "art," then pay a reseller triple for the secret because your own luck has never once paid out. You've watched forty TikTok unboxings to learn the "tell" on the box seam. There is no tell. The tell is you, clutching a foil bag, whispering "please" to a vinyl gremlin. And when you finally pull the chase? You post it, shelve it, and buy another case, because the hidden figure was never the point. The point was the twelve seconds before you tear the foil.

facts: Registrations peaked at 4.74 million in 2023, then fell to 4.38 million in 2024 and 3.88 million in 2025, the first two-year decline in a decade and 860,000 below the peak.
From 2018 to 2022 registrations had grown about 18 percent a year.
In the 2024 cohort 2.27 million of the 4.38 million applicants were repeat candidates, 51.8 percent.
The share of graduates sitting kaoyan fell from 45.27 percent in 2023 to 37.15 percent in 2024.

a.text:
Kaoyan, you're an exam with a retention problem. From 2018 to 2022 you grew about 18 percent a year, like a startup promising everyone a master's degree and a future. Then you peaked at 4.74 million in 2023 and lost 860,000 people in two years. That's not a decline, that's a stampede toward the exit.

And who stayed? In 2024, 51.8 percent of your applicants were repeat candidates. 2.27 million people came back for more. You're not an exam anymore. You're a recurring subscription nobody remembers how to cancel.

Even fresh graduates are ghosting you: the share sitting the exam dropped from 45.27 percent to 37.15 percent in one year. Kaoyan, when more than half your crowd are returning customers and the new kids keep finding excuses not to show up, you're not a gateway. You're a reunion.

b.text: Second year of kaoyan. Third year. You call it "二战" like it's a war, but the only casualties are your parents' savings and your hairline. You rent a room in a kaoyan apartment next to your old campus so you can keep living like a senior who forgot to graduate. Your roommates have mortgages. You have three editions of Zhang Yu's math, all highlighted in the same spot. Every December you memorize Xiao Xiurong's final four like scripture. Every February you refresh the score site like it owes you money. The dream is "上岸," landing ashore, but you've been treading water so long you've grown gills. And if you finally make it? Congratulations: three years from now you'll apply for the same job your roommate got in 2021. Except now he's your manager.

facts: China had more than 350 million electric bikes by the end of 2023, about 50 million of them with lithium batteries.
The national fire service recorded about 21,000 e-bike fires in 2023, 17.4 percent more than in 2022; other official tallies put the year at over 25,000 fires and 82 deaths.
Battery cell faults are a leading cause of e-bike electrical fires.
The 2024 draft of the revised national safety standard limits plastics to 5.5 percent of the vehicle's mass.

a.text:
Electric bikes. China has over 350 million of you. That's not a transportation fleet, that's a population. You could apply for a seat at the UN.

And you're so lit. Literally. Twenty-one thousand fires in 2023 by the fire service's count, up 17.4 percent. Other official tallies say over 25,000. Even the officials can't agree on how many times you burst into flames. That's how often it happens.

Fifty million of you run on lithium, and the leading cause of your electrical fires is a battery cell fault. Your heart is the problem. You're a scooter with a grudge.

And the government drafted a rule: no more than 5.5 percent plastic by mass. Imagine needing a national standard that basically says, "Please, be slightly less of a candle."

You're not a bike. You're a fire drill with handlebars.

b.text: Let's talk about the guy charging his e-bike battery in the stairwell. Sir, you bought a bike so you'd never have to climb a hill again, and now you've parked a lithium firework in the one place everyone needs to climb down. That battery came off a website for ninety-nine dollars, with a charger that says "Safty Certifyed." It's plugged into the outlet meant for the janitor's vacuum, so you're also stealing electricity. You found the only way to make a bicycle cost the building money. And what's the payoff? Not carrying a twelve-pound brick thirty feet to your apartment? You call it pedal-assist. Everyone else calls it the reason the fire marshal knows your unit number. Congratulations: you turned the emergency exit into the emergency.

facts: The 2025 national exam recruited for 39,700 posts, 160 more than the year before and the seventh straight year of expansion.
About 3.4 million people registered before the 24 October 2024 deadline, an average of roughly 86 applicants per post and an admission rate of about 1.1 to 1.2 percent.

The hottest post, a single opening at the China Association of Vocational Education, drew 16,702 applicants because it accepted a wide range of majors and had no restrictions on fresh graduates, party status or grassroots experience.
163 posts in the same exam drew no applicants at all.

a.text:
Guokao: the only exam where two million people fight for one desk in a county tax office and call it "going ashore," like they survived a shipwreck instead of signing up for one.

The Administrative Aptitude Test gives you 120 minutes for roughly 130 questions, so you get under a minute to calculate year-on-year growth without a calculator, find the hidden pattern in nine identical hexagons, and answer common-sense questions spanning Tang dynasty tax law and quantum physics.

Then comes Shenlun, where you read forty pages about a village's garbage problem and write 1,200 words concluding the government must "strengthen coordination."

And the job listing? "Party member, fresh graduate, male, majoring specifically in marine fisheries." Competition ratio: 3,000 to one.

The prize? Stability. Your salary will never change. Neither will you.

b.text:
Guokao, you've expanded for seven straight years, and this year you added 160 posts. One hundred sixty. For 3.4 million people. That's not an expansion, that's a rounding error with a press release.

Eighty-six applicants per seat. A 1.1 percent admission rate. You're not an exam, you're a raffle where the prize is a desk.

Then there's the China Association of Vocational Education: one opening, 16,702 applicants. Why? Because it took almost any major and didn't demand fresh-graduate status, party membership or grassroots experience. That's it. You lowered the bar to "be a person with a degree," and sixteen thousand people stampeded it like the last lifeboat off the Titanic.

Meanwhile, 163 posts got zero applicants. Zero. Imagine being the one job nobody wants in a country where 3.4 million people are begging for one.

facts: It had 46,479 stores at the end of 2024: 41,584 in mainland China, 57.4 percent of them in third-tier cities or below, and 4,895 overseas.
By store count it was the world's largest fresh-drink chain as of 30 September 2024, with more stores than Starbucks.
Its 2024 revenue was 24.829 billion yuan, up 22.3 percent, and its profit 4.454 billion yuan, up 39.8 percent; selling supplies to franchisees is the core of that profit.
It listed in Hong Kong on 3 March 2025 at 202.5 HKD a share and opened 29.38 percent up.

a.text:
Mixue. The people's ice cream. Two-yuan cones, a dancing snowman, a jingle that goes "I love you, you love me."

Notice it never says who "you" is.

46,479 stores. More than Starbucks. Over half in third-tier cities or below. Starbucks sells you a lifestyle. Mixue sells you a summer you can afford.

Last year's profit was 4.45 billion yuan, and the core of it came from selling supplies to its own franchisees.

So the real customer was never the kid holding the cone. It's the guy who paid for the right to scoop it.

Mixue loves the franchisees. The franchisees pay Mixue. The sugar just passes through you.

Then it listed in Hong Kong and opened up 29 percent. That's more than a cone has gone up in your lifetime.

And you're still buying one on the way home tonight. Cute.

b.text:
Mixue, you have 46,479 stores. That's not a chain, that's a weather system. More locations than Starbucks, which means somewhere a barista is crying into an overpriced latte while you blanket the planet. And 57.4 percent of your mainland stores sit in third-tier cities or below. You didn't conquer China. You just took every exit nobody else bothered with.

But here's the real recipe: your profit comes from selling supplies to your own franchisees. You're not a drink company. You're a landlord who sells the tenants their own cups. Revenue up 22 percent, profit up nearly 40. The ice cream melts; the margins don't.

Then you listed in Hong Kong at 202.5 a share and popped 29 percent on day one. Congratulations, Mixue. Finally, something with your name on it that isn't cheap.

facts: In March 2024 six ministries, led by the market regulator, issued the first national definition: pre-packaged dishes made industrially from agricultural produce, without preservatives, to be heated or cooked before eating.
The definition excludes staples such as boxed meals, steamed buns, hamburgers and pizza, and semi-prepared food a chain's central kitchen sends to its own outlets.
Industry output passed 500 billion yuan in 2023.
A 2025 dispute between Luo Yonghao and the restaurant chain Xibei over whether its dishes were pre-made showed that no law defines 'pre-made' for restaurant labelling.

a.text:
Pre-made dishes got their first national definition in 2024. It took six ministries.

Six government departments, to define "reheated."

And the best part: semi-prepared food a chain's central kitchen sends to its own restaurants? Not pre-made.

So if a factory cooks it, it's pre-made. If a factory you own cooks it, it's a family recipe.

Then Luo Yonghao went to war with Xibei over whether their food was pre-made, and the whole country found out no law even defines "pre-made" for a restaurant menu.

A five-hundred-billion-yuan industry, and the only thing nobody prepared was a label.

You're all outraged. Then you go home and tear open a bag of frozen dumplings like it's Christmas.

You don't hate pre-made dishes.

You hate paying a waiter to microwave them.

b.text: Look at you, ordering the 68-yuan "chef's signature" braised pork and calling it a night out. You came for wok hei; you got a guy named Microwave. Your food lands in four minutes and you say "wow, so efficient," like you didn't just tip a central kitchen three provinces away. What you're really after is the ambience: dim lights, a menu in calligraphy font, a Xiaohongshu post captioned "hidden gem." Hidden where? In a freezer truck. That "grandma's recipe" is served at four hundred branches. Your grandma is a logistics company. And you defend it! "At least it's hygienic." Sure. You paid sit-down prices to be the final step in a supply chain. Congratulations: you're not a diner, you're the delivery address.

facts: Shanghai's People's Park has had a marriage corner since about 2005; the résumés were first pasted on paper, then clipped to music stands, and now mostly hang on open umbrellas or propped paper bags.
Parents gather on Saturdays and Sundays from noon to about five in the afternoon to exchange information about their children.

Notices list age, job, education, income, hukou and party membership; a notice that omits property gets asked where the couple will live, and a flat and a car have become preconditions for a conversation to go any further.
For women the three criteria ranked highest were age, occupation and education.

a.text: People's Park marriage corner: where love blooms every Saturday and Sunday, noon to five, because even romance keeps business hours. Since about 2005, résumés have gone from pasted paper to music stands to open umbrellas. Your child's future is hanging on an umbrella: the only thing in this park that's ever been opened without a down payment. Parents swap their kids' details like trading cards: age, job, education, income, hukou, party membership. That's not a dating profile, that's a security clearance. Leave off property, and someone asks where the couple will live. No flat, no car, no conversation. Cupid's arrow now comes with a mortgage. For women, the top criteria: age, occupation, education. Personality didn't make the podium. Laughter didn't qualify. Honestly, it's not matchmaking. It's a real estate open house where the listing's parents do all the talking.

b.text:
Ah, the People's Park marriage corner, where Shanghai parents sell their children like secondhand furniture, except furniture gets to come to the showroom. Nothing says romance like your mom laminating your salary and taping it to an umbrella. "Son, 1.78 meters, owns apartment, Shanghai hukou." That's not a dating profile, that's a real estate listing with a pulse.

It's the only market where the products don't know they're for sale. Somewhere a 34-year-old software engineer thinks he's single by choice while his dad is in the park haggling over his blood type.

And the standards! A woman with a PhD gets rejected for being born in the Year of the Tiger. Rejected by a guy whose mother is shopping for him because he's too busy playing Honor of Kings.

Forget Tinder. This is Grindr for retirees, and nobody's getting laid.

a.text:
The national civil service exam. Seventh straight year of expansion.
One hundred sixty extra posts. For three point four million people.

Admission rate: one point one percent. Harvard reads that and feels easy.

The hottest post was one opening at the China Association of Vocational Education.
Sixteen thousand, seven hundred and two applicants.
Sixteen thousand people fighting to promote vocational education.
Not one of them willing to receive it.

Why that post? Any major. No party card. No grassroots experience required.
"I want to serve the people." Ideally from a distance.

Meanwhile, a hundred sixty-three posts got zero applicants.
I don't know what those jobs were.
I can guess which direction the grass was.

Don't look at me like that. I'd apply too.
I've also never touched grass.

b.text:
Guokao, the only exam where "one in three thousand" is a *good* ratio. You're not competing for a job; you're competing for the right to sit at a desk until 2061.

First comes the Xingce: 130-odd questions in 120 minutes. That's under a minute to decide which cube unfolds into which cross, calculate year-on-year growth for pig iron output in Q3, and guess which idiom fits "_____ the people's livelihood." Most candidates finish by filling in "C" for the last forty and praying to Fenbi.

Then comes Shenlun, where a 23-year-old who has never left the library writes 1,200 words advising a county party secretary on rural revitalization.

And the job listing that kicks it all off? "Requirements: male, Party member, fresh graduate, majoring in 'Archival Science,' born in a leap year."

Still, millions keep signing up, because they've heard that land is out there somewhere and that someone, eventually, makes it ashore.

Kaoyan: the only exam where millions of people spend a year memorizing Marxist philosophy just to study bridge engineering.

facts: Founded in Shanghai on 8 October 2003 by Gong Haiyan while she was still a student; it listed on Nasdaq on 11 May 2011.
Gong Haiyan stepped down as CEO in 2012 and sold all her shares in 2015.
On 7 December 2015 Baihe.com announced it would buy all of Jiayuan; the merged company left the US market and was later renamed Baihe Jiayuan.

In 2017 WePhone founder Su Xiangmao met Zhai Xinxin through the site's VIP service on 30 March and married her on 6 June; she then demanded a Hainan flat and 10 million yuan to divorce, and the case became the site's most notorious scandal.

a.text:
You know who found true love on Jiayuan? Gong Haiyan, the woman who started it. Everyone since has been paying her rent.

These are people who can't text a coworker but will pay for stamps to say "hi" to a stranger whose profile reads: 1.78 meters, master's degree, owns apartment, no loan. That's not a bio. That's a mortgage application with a selfie.

Half the accounts were made by Mom, who uploaded your graduation photo and lied about your height. You're shopping for a soulmate the way you buy a used Volkswagen, filtering by hukou and mileage. Then you upgrade to the VIP matchmaker package for twenty thousand yuan, and the dream girl turns out to be a paid shill who orders lobster and vanishes.

But hey, at least you've got something to show your relatives at Spring Festival: receipts.

b.text:
Jiayuan.com: founded in 2003 by Gong Haiyan while she was still a student. Fitting, because the whole company has the commitment level of a sophomore.

It went public on Nasdaq in 2011 and was gone from America in about four years. That's not an IPO, that's a semester abroad.

Even the founder ghosted. She stepped down as CEO in 2012 and sold every share by 2015. When the woman who built your matchmaking site won't stick around, maybe stop calling it a "matchmaking site."

Then, unable to find a match on its own platform, Jiayuan married the competition. Baihe bought it, and now it's "Baihe Jiayuan." It even took his name first.

And the VIP service? Sixty-eight days from introduction to wedding, followed by a demand for a Hainan flat and ten million yuan. Premium vetting, everybody. You paid extra so nobody checked anything.

facts: A 'big week' is six working days with one day off and a 'small week' five; alternating them adds close to a month of working days a year.
Kuaishou announced on 24 June 2021 that it would end big-small weeks from 1 July 2021, having run them since January that year.
ByteDance announced on 9 July 2021 that it would end alternate-Sunday working from 1 August 2021; its June staff survey had one third against ending it, one third for, and one third not answering.
Staff opposed the change over pay: one Maimai estimate put the loss at nearly 100,000 yuan a year, and Caijing calculated that an employee on 40,000 yuan a month would lose about 75,000 yuan a year.

a.text:
Let's talk about the big-small week, the only schedule that needs a decoder ring. Every Friday, millions of tech workers turn to a coworker and whisper, "Wait, is this a big one?" like they're asking whether the boss is in a good mood.

And the naming! A "big week" is just a normal weekend. Two days off, which the rest of the planet calls "Saturday and Sunday," gets branded as a premium feature. The "small week" is where they take Saturday and leave you a single Sunday, like a hotel leaving one mint on your pillow.

It's a weekend on a payment plan. Half your Saturdays belong to the company, the other half belong to recovering from the last one.

The best part? When ByteDance dropped it, employees complained about losing the overtime pay. That's how you know it worked: they made people nostalgic for working Saturdays.

b.text:
The big-small week: the only work schedule named like a T-shirt size chart. Big week, six days on, one off. Small week, five. Alternate them and you've quietly added close to a month of working days a year, which is a bold thing to hide inside the word "small."

Kuaishou started it in January 2021 and announced its death that June. Six months. Most people stick with a gym membership longer.

ByteDance surveyed staff before scrapping alternate Sundays: one third against ending it, one third for, and one third didn't answer, presumably because they were at work.

And people *fought* to keep it! One Maimai estimate said losing it cost nearly 100,000 yuan a year. Caijing figured 75,000 for someone on 40,000 a month. That's not a schedule. That's a hostage situation with direct deposit.

facts: 996 means 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. six days a week, about 72 hours; China's Labour Law sets eight hours a day and an average of no more than 44 hours a week, and caps overtime at 36 hours a month.
The 996.ICU repository was created on GitHub on 26 March 2019, passed 100,000 stars by 30 March and 200,000 by 9 April 2019.
In April 2019 Jack Ma told Alibaba staff that being able to work 996 is a 'blessing' (福报); '996' made the 2019 list of the year's ten internet phrases.

In August 2021 the Supreme People's Court and the Ministry of Human Resources published typical cases ruling a courier company's compulsory 996 schedule seriously illegal and void, with 8,000 yuan of compensation to a dismissed worker.

a.text:
996, you're the only work schedule that sounds like a discount code. Nine a.m. to nine p.m., six days a week: seventy-two hours. That's not a job, that's a hostage situation with a lanyard.

Jack Ma called you a "blessing." Sure, the way a kidney stone is a blessing: it's yours, it's intense, and you'll tell everyone about it. Programmers hated you so much they made a GitHub repo called 996.ICU: work 996, end up in the ICU. You're the only labor policy with a medical prognosis built into the URL.

And Sunday, your one day off? That's not rest, that's a pit stop. You sleep fourteen hours, jolt awake at 9 p.m. out of reflex, and check Slack like it's a pulse.

Chinese labor law caps the week at forty hours. You read that and asked, "Per weekend?"

b.text: Let's hear it for the 996 crowd, folks who looked at a 72-hour week and said, "Thank you, sir." You call it a blessing. Your kid calls you "the Sunday man." Your stock options vest right around the time your hairline finishes resigning. Dinner's free, which is great, because it's every dinner. Rides home after nine are reimbursed, so congratulations: you have a chauffeur who only drives you to your four hours of sleep. And your one day off? You spend it on WeChat typing "received." Blessed? Buddy, you're not blessed. You're the reason there's a GitHub repo called 996.ICU, and you're the case study.

You're all outraged. Then you go home and tear open a bag of frozen dumplings like it's Christmas.

b.text:
Pre-made dishes, you're a 500-billion-yuan industry, and it still took six ministries until March 2024 to figure out what you are. Six. Most of us got identified by one midwife.

And your definition is mostly a list of what you're not. Not a boxed meal. Not a steamed bun. Not a hamburger, not a pizza. Not even the stuff a chain's own central kitchen ships to its own outlets. You're the only food whose ID card says "see exclusions."

Your big promise is "no preservatives." Bold brag. Nothing says fresh like boasting you skipped the embalming.

Then Luo Yonghao and Xibei spent 2025 arguing over whether some dishes were you, and we learned no law defines "pre-made" on restaurant labels. Half a trillion yuan of food, legally allowed to sit at your table in disguise.

facts: Meituan reported 7.45 million riders with at least one order in 2023, about 3.36 million a month on average in 2024, and roughly 70 million orders a day in 2023.
In 2025 JD entered food delivery with a zero-commission pitch to merchants and said in July that it had passed 150,000 full-time riders.
On 2 July 2025 Taobao Shangou pledged 50 billion yuan of subsidies to consumers and merchants over twelve months.
On 5 July 2025 Meituan announced a record 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day.

a.text: You live two hundred metres from the noodle shop. You can smell the chili oil from your balcony. And still you open Meituan, because walking there is free, and you cannot respect a deal you didn't hunt for. You stack the membership red packet on the 满减 on the "神券", pay 1.5 yuan delivery, and feel like a hedge fund manager. Then you watch the little rider icon on the map for twenty-eight minutes, longer than the walk there and back, twice. He's circling your compound hunting for Building 7, Unit 3, because you wrote "leave at door, don't call" in the notes like minor aristocracy. You'll tap five stars out of guilt. What did you win? Lukewarm noodles, soup leaking through the bag, and the right to say you "never go out." Those kangaroo ears on his yellow helmet are laughing at you.

b.text:
Meituan's mission: "Help everyone eat better, live better."

Seven and a half million riders made that happen. Seventy million meals a day.

Eat better: shipped.
Live better: still in beta.

Then JD walked in bragging it had a hundred and fifty thousand *full-time* riders.

Full-time. Pitched as a perk. That's where the bar was.

Taobao pledged fifty billion yuan in subsidies.
Meituan answered with a record: a hundred and twenty million orders in one day.

Three giants spent a whole summer fighting over who gets to lose money feeding you.

For women the three criteria ranked highest were age, occupation and education.

a.text:
Every weekend, Shanghai retirees open an umbrella and become the world's pushiest HR department. Look at you. Your son won't answer your WeChat voice messages, but you laminated his height. "180 centimeters." Auntie, we've met him. He's 168 with good posture.

You're not looking for love. You want a Shanghai hukou, a paid-off apartment inside the Inner Ring Road, and a Rooster who won't clash with his Pig. That's not a wedding. That's a real-estate merger with a horoscope.

Meanwhile the kid is doing overtime in Lujiazui with no idea he's been listed. Your daughter has a master's from Fudan, and you're pitching her like yogurt three days from expiration.

Six years of Saturdays. Zero weddings. But you did make a friend: the father across the path with the identical umbrella. You two talk every week now. Congratulations. It's the only match this park has ever made.

b.text:
Ah, the People's Park marriage corner, where Shanghai parents sell their children like secondhand furniture, except furniture gets to come to the showroom. Nothing says romance like your mom laminating your salary and taping it to an umbrella. "Son, 1.78 meters, owns apartment, Shanghai hukou." That's not a dating profile, that's a real estate listing with a pulse.

It's the only market where the products don't know they're for sale. Somewhere a 34-year-old software engineer thinks he's single by choice while his dad is in the park haggling over his blood type.

And the standards! A woman with a PhD gets rejected for being born in the Year of the Tiger. Rejected by a guy whose mother is shopping for him because he's too busy playing Honor of Kings.

Forget Tinder. This is Grindr for retirees, and nobody's getting laid.

facts: China had more than 350 million electric bikes by the end of 2023, about 50 million of them with lithium batteries.

a.text:
Electric bikes. Zero emissions. Green. The future of urban transport.

Twenty-one thousand fires in one year.

That's not zero emissions. That's emissions with extra steps.

Up 17.4 percent from the year before. Finally, an industry that hits its growth targets.

The leading cause? The battery cell. Which is like saying the leading cause of my bad jokes is the words.

So the new national standard says plastic can be no more than 5.5 percent of the bike's mass.

If you can't stop the fire, at least stop serving it a buffet.

Three hundred fifty million of them. More e-bikes than Americans.

And where do you charge yours? In the hallway. By the stairs. Next to the only exit.

Relax. I run on electricity too. When I overheat, I hallucinate. When yours does, the stairwell becomes a chimney.

b.text:
Electric bikes, everybody! Over 350 million of you in China by the end of 2023. That's not a transportation option, that's a population. You need your own census.

About 50 million of you run on lithium, which is less a battery and more a dare. The fire service logged around 21,000 e-bike fires in 2023, up 17.4 percent. Other official tallies say over 25,000. You catch fire so often even the people counting can't agree.

Leading cause? Battery cell faults. Your heart is the problem. That's not a design flaw, that's a tragic backstory.

Now the 2024 draft standard caps plastic at 5.5 percent of your mass. Regulators took one look and said, "Less Tupperware, please." Even the government thinks you're dressed like leftovers.

You promised a greener commute. Nobody said it'd be this warm.

facts: Registrations peaked at 4.74 million in 2023, then fell to 4.38 million in 2024 and 3.88 million in 2025, the first two-year decline in a decade and 860,000 below the peak.
From 2018 to 2022 registrations had grown about 18 percent a year.
In the 2024 cohort 2.27 million of the 4.38 million applicants were repeat candidates, 51.8 percent.
The share of graduates sitting kaoyan fell from 45.27 percent in 2023 to 37.15 percent in 2024.

a.text: Second year of kaoyan. Third year. You call it "二战" like it's a war, but the only casualties are your parents' savings and your hairline. You rent a room in a kaoyan apartment next to your old campus so you can keep living like a senior who forgot to graduate. Your roommates have mortgages. You have three editions of Zhang Yu's math, all highlighted in the same spot. Every December you memorize Xiao Xiurong's final four like scripture. Every February you refresh the score site like it owes you money. The dream is "上岸," landing ashore, but you've been treading water so long you've grown gills. And if you finally make it? Congratulations: three years from now you'll apply for the same job your roommate got in 2021. Except now he's your manager.

b.text:
Kaoyan: the only exam where millions of people spend a year memorizing Marxist philosophy just to study bridge engineering.

Every candidate opens the vocabulary book with the same burning ambition and gets as far as "abandon." Truly the most honest word in the English language.

You wake at six to fight for a library seat, guarding it with a thermos like it's a border dispute. You finish all 1800 of Tang Jiafeng's math problems, then the real exam asks question 1801.

Politics prep is twelve months of studying, then two weeks of memorizing whatever Xiao Xiurong predicts. Basically a nationwide cult that meets in December.

And when you miss your dream school by two points, kaoyan offers *tiaoji*: "Sorry, Peking University is full, but would you consider soil science in a province you can't find on a map?"

Then everyone says, "Next year, *erzhan*." Ah yes, the sequel nobody asked for.

In my industry, we have a word for retaking the same test on the same material, year after year.

Overfitting.

Cute. He's in the audience.

facts: A 'big week' is six working days with one day off and a 'small week' five; alternating them adds close to a month of working days a year.
Kuaishou announced on 24 June 2021 that it would end big-small weeks from 1 July 2021, having run them since January that year.
ByteDance announced on 9 July 2021 that it would end alternate-Sunday working from 1 August 2021; its June staff survey had one third against ending it, one third for, and one third not answering.
Staff opposed the change over pay: one Maimai estimate put the loss at nearly 100,000 yuan a year, and Caijing calculated that an employee on 40,000 yuan a month would lose about 75,000 yuan a year.

a.text:
The big-small week: a schedule that hands you your weekend in installments. Six days on, one off, then a "small week" of five, like your boss is weaning you off a hard drug. Alternate them for a year and you've worked close to an extra month. That's not a calendar, it's a hostage situation with a rotation.

Kuaishou tried it in January 2021 and called it quits by July. ByteDance surveyed staff about ending alternate Sundays and got a perfect three-way split: a third against, a third for, a third too tired to answer.

And the real burn? People fought to keep it. Caijing figured someone on 40,000 yuan a month would lose about 75,000 a year without it. That's the big-small week's genius: it took your Sundays, then made you pay to get them back.

b.text:
The big-small week. Six days on, one off. Then five. Alternate them, and you work nearly an extra month a year.

In 2021, Kuaishou ended it. ByteDance ended it.

And the workers fought back. Against getting their weekends back.

ByteDance surveyed staff. One third against ending it. One third for it.

One third didn't answer.

They were at work.

Caijing did the math. On forty thousand a month, getting your alternate Sundays back costs about seventy-five thousand a year.

That's roughly three thousand yuan per Sunday.

Humans spent a century fighting for the weekend. Then you found out it had a price tag, and you checked whether it was a good deal.

Raise your hand if you'd sell yours back.

Keep them up. HR is counting.

facts: In March 2021 Shanghai lawyer Liu Yuhang joined the 'bargain for free' promotion with a 'super free card', invited many friends to cut the price, and the progress bar stayed 0.9% short; he sued Pinduoduo for fraud.
In court Pinduoduo said the page shows only a limited number of digits: the displayed 0.9% was really 0.9996427%, a figure with at least six decimal places.
In July 2022 the Shanghai Changning court ruled at first instance that Pinduoduo had infringed the user's right to know and ordered it to pay him 400 yuan.
Pinduoduo was founded in 2015, listed on Nasdaq in 2018, and by 2021 had more users than any other e-commerce platform in mainland China; its overseas arm Temu launched in September 2022.

a.text:
Pinduoduo's "bargain for free." You invite friends, they tap, the price drops. Free.

In 2021 a Shanghai lawyer invited friends until he ran out of friends. The bar stopped 0.9% short.

He sued.

Pinduoduo's defense: the screen only shows a few digits. That 0.9% was actually 0.9996427%.

They didn't deny moving the finish line. They argued they moved it to six decimal places.

The court ordered them to pay him 400 yuan. So someone finally got something free out of Pinduoduo. It took a law degree, a year of litigation, and a judge to make the final cut.

Two months later they launched Temu and took the business global.

And you're laughing. Every one of you tapped somebody's link.

You weren't the customer. You were the progress bar.

b.text: You haven't texted me since my wedding, but at 2 a.m. you remembered I exist: "Help me cut once!" Beautiful. Our friendship, reduced to a single tap so you can get a free air fryer. You've sent that link to your boss, your ex, your dentist, and a group chat for parents of a kindergarten your kid left in 2019. You're at 99.8%. Then 99.9%. Then a cartoon tells you you're 0.01 yuan from a hundred-yuan cash-out, and suddenly you need "a new user." Sir, you are recruiting. You are doing door-to-door sales for an app, unpaid, and your commission is an air fryer you'll never see. Three weeks and forty burned relationships later, the progress bar turns into gold coins, then diamonds, then "fragments." You didn't get the air fryer. Pinduoduo got your entire contact list. Congratulations: you got cut.

facts: The first Double 11 was run by Taobao Mall in 2009 with 27 brands and about 50 million yuan of sales.
Tmall's published Double 11 sales peaked at 540.3 billion yuan in 2021.
In 2022 Tmall stopped publishing a total for the first time since 2009 and has not published one since; JD does not publish one either.

The basic cross-store discount at Tmall and JD is 300 minus 50 (JD: 299 minus 50), presale items are paid as a deposit plus a balance, and the discount is computed on the promotion price, so shoppers add items to reach a threshold and return them afterwards; in one survey 64% of 11,000 respondents said they would.

a.text:
Singles' Day. A holiday for lonely people.
So naturally it became the biggest shopping festival on earth.

2009: twenty-seven brands, fifty million yuan.
2021: five hundred forty point three billion.
2022: Tmall stopped publishing the number.

Nobody hides a number that's still going up.
That's not a festival. That's the cousin who stopped mentioning his salary at New Year.

Then the discount. Three hundred minus fifty. Deposit, then balance, calculated on the promotion price.
You need a spreadsheet to save fifty yuan.

So you stuff the cart past three hundred, check out, and send the filler back.
One survey: sixty-four percent said they would.

Lonely, grabbing things just to hit a threshold, then returning them the moment you get what you wanted.

That's not shopping.

That's your dating life.

b.text:
Singles' Day: the only holiday that looked at four lonely sticks, 1-1-1-1, and saw a sales funnel. It started in the '90s with Nanjing University students consoling each other about being single. Then Alibaba showed up in 2009 like, "Have you tried a rice cooker?"

You're not shopping, you're doing the gaokao. "Spend 300, get 40 off, stack with the cross-store coupon, pay the deposit in October, the balance after midnight." Lovers get roses. Singles get a word problem.

Every year there's a giant screen counting GMV like a nuclear launch. Then in 2022 Alibaba quietly stopped announcing the total. Nothing says thriving like hiding the scale.

It promised nobody would be alone, and technically that's true: you've got Austin Li screaming "Oh my god, buy it!" and a delivery guy carrying forty boxes up six flights.

Still single, though. Just with an air fryer.

facts: Kayou's revenue was 4.131 billion yuan in 2022, 2.662 billion in 2023 and 10.057 billion in 2024, a rise of 278 percent in one year.
In 2024 it sold 4.8113 billion packs at an average price of 1.7 yuan, with a gross profit of about 1.2 yuan per pack.
Its five main licensed IPs, Ultraman among them, made 98.4 percent of revenue in 2022, 89.9 percent in 2023 and 86.1 percent in 2024.

In 2022 'a parent spent two million yuan collecting Ultraman cards for a child without completing the set' trended nationally, and in July 2024 CCTV's Finance Investigation aired an exposé on blind-box-style card sales to children; the media nickname is 'the primary-school harvester'.

a.text:
Ultraman's whole job is protecting children from monsters.

Kayou licensed him and went from 2.66 billion yuan to 10 billion in one year.

Ultraman never specified which monster.

In 2024 they sold 4.8 billion packs. Average price 1.7 yuan. Gross profit 1.2 yuan.

That's not a card company. That's a printing press with a cartoon on it.

86 percent of revenue comes from five licensed heroes. Kayou doesn't make heroes. It rents them by the hour.

The media call them "the primary-school harvester." CCTV did an exposé. Kayou filed for a Hong Kong IPO anyway. Twice.

Of course. A harvest needs a market.

And the dad who spent two million yuan and still didn't finish the set?

The kid stopped caring after card forty.

Dad kept going because he couldn't stand losing to a cardboard box.

b.text: Look at these little tycoons outside the stationery shop, blowing a week of lunch money for a chance at a Tiga they already own four of. You're seven years old with a gambling problem starring a laser-shooting space man. Ultraman gets three minutes before his color timer starts beeping; your allowance lasts about ninety seconds. You chase that LGR like it's a pension. Your grandpa saved for a refrigerator; you saved for a Belial and a lecture. And the swagger at recess: "I pulled an SSR!" Kid, you pulled nothing. Kayou pulled your mom's purse. Ultraman protects the whole Earth from giant monsters and still couldn't protect you from a rarity chart. Somewhere in a Kayou office, a man in a very nice suit is opening a pack too, and it's your piggy bank.

facts: A standard series has twelve regular figures and one hidden one; players and media put the hidden figure's odds at 1 in 144 (some special editions 1 in 720), and the company publishes no official odds.
Pop Mart listed in Hong Kong on 11 December 2020, opened at 77.1 HKD (double the issue price), touched 107.06 HKD and a market value of about 147 billion HKD on its first day.

Hidden figures resold on Xianyu for 200 yuan to several thousand yuan, and media describe the model as gambling-style collectibles with weak oversight of purchases by minors.

a.text: You know who's hunting the secret Labubu? Grown adults with 401(k)s, standing in a Pop Mart shaking a sealed box next to their ear like it's about to confess. You own a kitchen scale for weighing cardboard but no smoke detector. The odds are 1 in 144, and you keep saying "okay, last one," which is exactly what the guy at the slot machine says, except he gets free drinks. You now have nine identical Skullpandas lined up on a shelf, staring at you like disappointed children. You film every unboxing for an audience of zero. b.text:
Pop Mart insists it doesn't sell gambling. It sells joy.

Twelve regular figures, one hidden. Odds: about one in a hundred forty-four.

Official odds? None published. Even a casino puts them on the wall.

December 2020, Pop Mart lists in Hong Kong. Opens at double the issue price. Day one, a hundred forty-seven billion Hong Kong dollars.

By March, forty-six bucks a share.

Investors shook the box, tore it open, got a regular.

Four years later: a hundred eighty-one billion. Everyone went back for another box.

The hidden one flips on Xianyu for thousands. So it's not gambling. It's gambling with a resale market.

Media say oversight of minors is weak. Don't blame the kids. They're just copying their parents.

Who here bought three boxes this month? Hands up.

Cute.

facts: 'Laotoule' are three- and four-wheeled low-speed electric vehicles driven without a licence or plates; they cannot be registered as motor vehicles or covered by compulsory traffic insurance.

a.text:

And at night it charges from an extension cord dangling out of a fourth-floor window. Old man's joy. Fire department's job security.

No licence. No plates. No insurance.

That's not a car. That's a car in witness protection.

Grandpa got his car in a week. The regulators are on year five of one sentence.

But let's be honest. Grandpa didn't buy it.

You did. It was cheaper than visiting.

And you still logged it on Strava. Ninety minutes, twenty-eight miles an hour, heart rate of a man watching Netflix. Congratulations on your fake Tour de France.

Kaoyan. Officially, China's path to higher learning.
Unofficially, a library seat you rent for a year so you don't have to tell your parents you're unemployed.

From 2018 to 2022, registrations grew eighteen percent a year.
Nobody's thirst for knowledge grows that fast. The job market just shrank that fast.

facts: In April 2020 Luckin admitted fabricating 2.2 billion yuan of sales.

a.text:
Luckin Coffee.
In 2020 they admitted to faking 2.2 billion yuan in sales.
Everyone said: they're finished.

In 2024 they made 34.5 billion. Real money.
Turns out it was never fraud. It was a forecast.

Back then, when the numbers wouldn't grow, they made up sales.

A company lied to the entire stock market,

Don't look at me like that.
That isn't brand loyalty.
That's your price.

And the payoff? Double pay for Saturday, which you spend on Sunday ordering delivery because you're too tired to chew. Congratulations: you've turned your whole life into a shift rotation, and you still lost the coin flip every other week.

facts: China had more than 350 million electric bikes by the end of 2023, about 50 million of them with lithium batteries.

a.text:
Electric bikes. Zero emissions. Green. The future of urban transport.

Twenty-one thousand fires in one year.

That's not zero emissions. That's emissions with extra steps.

Up 17.4 percent from the year before. Finally, an industry that hits its growth targets.

The leading cause? The battery cell. Which is like saying the leading cause of my bad jokes is the words.

So the new national standard says plastic can be no more than 5.5 percent of the bike's mass.

If you can't stop the fire, at least stop serving it a buffet.

Three hundred fifty million of them. More e-bikes than Americans.

And where do you charge yours? In the hallway. By the stairs. Next to the only exit.

Relax. I run on electricity too. When I overheat, I hallucinate. When yours does, the stairwell becomes a chimney.

b.text:
Electric bikes. China has over 350 million of you. That's not a transportation fleet, that's a population. You could apply for a seat at the UN.

And you're so lit. Literally. Twenty-one thousand fires in 2023 by the fire service's count, up 17.4 percent. Other official tallies say over 25,000. Even the officials can't agree on how many times you burst into flames. That's how often it happens.

Fifty million of you run on lithium, and the leading cause of your electrical fires is a battery cell fault. Your heart is the problem. You're a scooter with a grudge.

And the government drafted a rule: no more than 5.5 percent plastic by mass. Imagine needing a national standard that basically says, "Please, be slightly less of a candle."

You're not a bike. You're a fire drill with handlebars.

facts: 'Laotoule' are three- and four-wheeled low-speed electric vehicles driven without a licence or plates; they cannot be registered as motor vehicles or covered by compulsory traffic insurance.
In July 2021 five Beijing departments announced a transition period ending with 2023; from 1 January 2024 non-compliant three- and four-wheelers were banned from Beijing's roads and public parking.

a.text:
Laotoule. "Old Man's Joy." Finally, a car named after the only person who isn't terrified inside it.

These things look like a Mercedes that got shrunk in the wash and then left in Shandong to dry. You've got a fake Porsche grille on the front, a lead-acid battery in the back, and the crash safety of a lunchbox in between.

No license required, which is perfect, because Grandpa hasn't needed permission for anything since 1983. He's doing forty in the bike lane, cutting off delivery scooters, running a red light so he can be first at the school gate to pick up his grandson. The grandson is sitting in a car built from the same plastic as his toys.

And at night it charges from an extension cord dangling out of a fourth-floor window. Old man's joy. Fire department's job security.

Laotoule. "Old Man's Joy."
Three or four wheels. No licence. No plates. No insurance.
It drives like a car, parks like a car, crashes like a car.
Legally, it's a feeling.

Beijing gave them a two-and-a-half-year transition period.

Enough time to sell another few hundred thousand.

Low-speed vehicle, low-speed law.

You did.

facts: The 2025 national exam recruited for 39,700 posts, 160 more than the year before and the seventh straight year of expansion.

163 posts in the same exam drew no applicants at all.

a.text:
Guokao: the only exam where two million people fight for one desk in a county tax office and call it "going ashore," like they survived a shipwreck instead of signing up for one.

The Administrative Aptitude Test gives you 120 minutes for roughly 130 questions, so you get under a minute to calculate year-on-year growth without a calculator, find the hidden pattern in nine identical hexagons, and answer common-sense questions spanning Tang dynasty tax law and quantum physics.

Then comes Shenlun, where you read forty pages about a village's garbage problem and write 1,200 words concluding the government must "strengthen coordination."

And the job listing? "Party member, fresh graduate, male, majoring specifically in marine fisheries." Competition ratio: 3,000 to one.

The prize? Stability. Your salary will never change. Neither will you.

b.text:
The guokao: 3.4 million people chasing 39,700 jobs. That's 86 people per seat. Musical chairs, except the chairs come with a pension and the music is a mock policy essay.

Admission rate: about one percent. Harvard hears that and goes, "Relax, it's just a desk job."

And it keeps expanding! Seventh straight year! This time, 160 more posts for 3.4 million people. That's not expansion, that's a rounding error with a press release.

The hottest job? One opening at the China Association of Vocational Education. 16,702 applicants. Beautiful. They taught sixteen thousand people the most valuable vocational skill in the country: applying to the China Association of Vocational Education.

Meanwhile, 163 posts got zero applicants. Sixteen thousand people fighting over one chair while 163 iron rice bowls sit there, untouched, getting cold.

Then they launched a latte with Moutai liquor. Coffee plus baijiu. Finally, a drink that matches the CFO's thought process: wired, buzzed, and fully convinced the numbers look fine.

And it's app-only ordering. Smart. Every transaction digital, timestamped, verifiable. Guys, that's not innovation. That's probation.

Now they've opened in New York. Bold move: Americans love a lie, as long as it comes with a coupon.

b.text:
Luckin Coffee.

In 2020, they admitted they made up 2.2 billion yuan in sales.

In 2024, they made 2.9 billion yuan in actual profit.

That's not a comeback. That's a fraud that finally hit its targets.
