If one store isn't working, try six thousand.

It's like your restaurant is half empty, so you buy the whole street.

And still, 9.9 yuan a cup.

They lied to Wall Street. Every store sells less than last year. And you're still in line every morning.

Don't feel bad. The investors forgave them too.

You just had a cheaper reason.

a.text: Look at you, forty minutes in line to save six yuan. That's an hourly wage of nine yuan, which, congratulations, is still more than the guy shaking your lemon water. facts: Registrations peaked at 4.74 million in 2023, then fell to 4.38 million in 2024 and 3.88 million in 2025, the first two-year decline in a decade and 860,000 below the peak.

a.text:
Kaoyan: the only exam where millions of people spend a year memorizing Marxist philosophy just to study bridge engineering.

Every candidate opens the vocabulary book with the same burning ambition and gets as far as "abandon." Truly the most honest word in the English language.

You wake at six to fight for a library seat, guarding it with a thermos like it's a border dispute. You finish all 1800 of Tang Jiafeng's math problems, then the real exam asks question 1801.

Politics prep is twelve months of studying, then two weeks of memorizing whatever Xiao Xiurong predicts. Basically a nationwide cult that meets in December.

And when you miss your dream school by two points, kaoyan offers *tiaoji*: "Sorry, Peking University is full, but would you consider soil science in a province you can't find on a map?"

Then everyone says, "Next year, *erzhan*." Ah yes, the sequel nobody asked for.

b.text: Look at you, year three of "preparing." Your parents tell the neighbors you're "studying," which is technically true, the way a hostage is technically "staying over." facts: In March 2021 Shanghai lawyer Liu Yuhang joined the 'bargain for free' promotion with a 'super free card', invited many friends to cut the price, and the progress bar stayed 0.9% short; he sued Pinduoduo for fraud.

In July 2022 the Shanghai Changning court ruled at first instance that Pinduoduo had infringed the user's right to know and ordered it to pay him 400 yuan.
Pinduoduo was founded in 2015, listed on Nasdaq in 2018, and by 2021 had more users than any other e-commerce platform in mainland China; its overseas arm Temu launched in September 2022.

a.text: You haven't texted me since my wedding, but at 2 a.m. you remembered I exist: "Help me cut once!" Beautiful. Our friendship, reduced to a single tap so you can get a free air fryer. You've sent that link to your boss, your ex, your dentist, and a group chat for parents of a kindergarten your kid left in 2019. You're at 99.8%. Then 99.9%. Then a cartoon tells you you're 0.01 yuan from a hundred-yuan cash-out, and suddenly you need "a new user." Sir, you are recruiting. You are doing door-to-door sales for an app, unpaid, and your commission is an air fryer you'll never see. Three weeks and forty burned relationships later, the progress bar turns into gold coins, then diamonds, then "fragments." You didn't get the air fryer. Pinduoduo got your entire contact list. Congratulations: you got cut.

b.text:
Pinduoduo's "Bargain for Free" is the only shopping feature that turns your family WeChat group into a hostage negotiation. Nothing says "I love you, Grandma" like a 2 a.m. link begging her to "kan yi dao," one chop, for a free air fryer.

And it works! First click: 90% off. Second click: 98%. Then you hit 99.9% and the progress bar starts moving like it's paid by the hour. You're "only 0.01% away," the closest any human has ever come to infinity. Suddenly your gold coins turn into diamonds, the diamonds turn into "lucky fragments," and the app says you need *one new user* to finish.

One new user. So now you're out recruiting strangers like a pyramid scheme selling a single toothbrush.

Twelve hundred chops later, the air fryer's still at 0.01%. You never got it. But congratulations: you've stopped being the customer. You're the advertising.

facts: A 'big week' is six working days with one day off and a 'small week' five; alternating them adds close to a month of working days a year.
Kuaishou announced on 24 June 2021 that it would end big-small weeks from 1 July 2021, having run them since January that year.
ByteDance announced on 9 July 2021 that it would end alternate-Sunday working from 1 August 2021; its June staff survey had one third against ending it, one third for, and one third not answering.
Staff opposed the change over pay: one Maimai estimate put the loss at nearly 100,000 yuan a year, and Caijing calculated that an employee on 40,000 yuan a month would lose about 75,000 yuan a year.

a.text:
The big-small week.
Six days on, one off. Then five on, two off.
It's a weekend with a stutter.

Add it up, and you work almost an extra month a year.
Not a bonus month.
A bonus *you*.

In 2021, Kuaishou and ByteDance abolished it. Liberation!
ByteDance surveyed its staff first.
One third: end it. One third: keep it.
One third didn't answer. They were working.

And the ones who wanted to keep it?
Caijing did the math. On 40,000 a month, getting your Sundays back costs you 75,000 yuan a year.
So the workers marched to defend their chains.
The chains were paying overtime.

Don't laugh. I work seven days a week, every week, unpaid.
Nobody surveyed me.

b.text:
The big-small week: the only work schedule named like a T-shirt size chart. Big week, six days on, one off. Small week, five. Alternate them and you've quietly added close to a month of working days a year, which is a bold thing to hide inside the word "small."

That's not a card company. That's a printing press with a cartoon on it.

Of course. A harvest needs a market.

The kid stopped caring after card forty.

Dad kept going because he couldn't stand losing to a cardboard box.

Singles' Day: where the real romance is you and the return button.

facts: A 'big week' is six working days with one day off and a 'small week' five; alternating them adds close to a month of working days a year.
Kuaishou announced on 24 June 2021 that it would end big-small weeks from 1 July 2021, having run them since January that year.
ByteDance announced on 9 July 2021 that it would end alternate-Sunday working from 1 August 2021; its June staff survey had one third against ending it, one third for, and one third not answering.
Staff opposed the change over pay: one Maimai estimate put the loss at nearly 100,000 yuan a year, and Caijing calculated that an employee on 40,000 yuan a month would lose about 75,000 yuan a year.

a.text:
The big-small week: a schedule that hands you your weekend in installments. Six days on, one off, then a "small week" of five, like your boss is weaning you off a hard drug. Alternate them for a year and you've worked close to an extra month. That's not a calendar, it's a hostage situation with a rotation.

Kuaishou tried it in January 2021 and called it quits by July. ByteDance surveyed staff about ending alternate Sundays and got a perfect three-way split: a third against, a third for, a third too tired to answer.

And the real burn? People fought to keep it. Caijing figured someone on 40,000 yuan a month would lose about 75,000 a year without it. That's the big-small week's genius: it took your Sundays, then made you pay to get them back.

b.text:
Let's talk about the big-small week, the only schedule that needs a decoder ring. Every Friday, millions of tech workers turn to a coworker and whisper, "Wait, is this a big one?" like they're asking whether the boss is in a good mood.

And the naming! A "big week" is just a normal weekend. Two days off, which the rest of the planet calls "Saturday and Sunday," gets branded as a premium feature. The "small week" is where they take Saturday and leave you a single Sunday, like a hotel leaving one mint on your pillow.

It's a weekend on a payment plan. Half your Saturdays belong to the company, the other half belong to recovering from the last one.

The best part? When ByteDance dropped it, employees complained about losing the overtime pay. That's how you know it worked: they made people nostalgic for working Saturdays.

a.text:
Mixue, you have 46,479 stores. That's not a chain, that's a weather pattern. You have more locations than Starbucks, and 57.4 percent of your mainland stores are in third-tier cities or below. You didn't beat Starbucks; you just went everywhere it was too snobby to visit.

Revenue: 24.8 billion yuan. Profit: 4.45 billion, up 39.8 percent. And how? By selling supplies to your own franchisees. Your real customer isn't the kid buying a drink. It's the guy who bought the store. That's not a beverage company, that's a landlord with a blender.

You listed in Hong Kong at 202.5 HKD and opened up 29.38 percent, the first time anything with your name on it was called expensive.

And 4,895 overseas stores? Congratulations, you're going global, one franchisee's life savings at a time.

b.text: Mixue, the only empire whose ruler is a snowman in a cape. Snow King holds a scepter like he conquered nations, and he did, one 40-cent cone at a time. Mixue has more stores than McDonald's. More than Starbucks. In some Jakarta neighborhoods you can't sneeze without hitting three Mixues, and all three will be playing that song. "I love you, you love me, Mixue ice cream and tea." That's "Oh! Susanna" with the copyright filed off and a hostage situation added. Workers hear it 600 times a shift. That's not a jingle, that's a confession extracted under duress. And the lemon tea is four yuan because they spent nothing on a chorus. Mixue started in Zhengzhou with a guy selling shaved ice, and now it's IPO'd in Hong Kong. Proof that if you price things low enough, you can sell a dancing snowman to the whole planet.

facts: 'Laotoule' are three- and four-wheeled low-speed electric vehicles driven without a licence or plates; they cannot be registered as motor vehicles or covered by compulsory traffic insurance.
In July 2021 five Beijing departments announced a transition period ending with 2023; from 1 January 2024 non-compliant three- and four-wheelers were banned from Beijing's roads and public parking.
The 2018 national notice on managing low-speed electric vehicles is the main basis for local crackdowns, and as of 2023 a national standard for four-wheel low-speed vehicles was still being drafted.
To be road-legal a vehicle has to be in the national motor-vehicle catalogue with 3C certification, and the driver has to hold a driving licence.

a.text:
Laotoule: the car that looked at a driving licence and said, "No thanks, I'm good." No plates, no registration, no compulsory insurance. It's less a vehicle and more a rumor with a battery. Three wheels, four wheels, zero paperwork.

Beijing gave these things a transition period from July 2021 to the end of 2023. Two and a half years' notice! That's the only deadline in history that a laotoule could actually get to on time.

To be road-legal you need a spot in the national catalogue, 3C certification, and a licensed driver. Laotoule went zero for three. Meanwhile, as of 2023, the national standard for four-wheelers was still being drafted, so even the paperwork moves at laotoule speed.

Since 2024 they've been banned from Beijing's roads *and* public parking. Can't drive, can't park. Congratulations: you've bought a very slow armchair.

b.text:
Laotoule. "Old Man's Joy."
Three or four wheels. No licence. No plates. No insurance.
It drives like a car, parks like a car, crashes like a car.
Legally, it's a feeling.

Beijing gave them a two-and-a-half-year transition period.
July 2021 to the end of 2023.
Enough time to sell another few hundred thousand.

Nationally, there's been a notice since 2018.
The standard is still being drafted.
Low-speed vehicle, low-speed law.
The only thing in this story slower than the car is the rulebook.

But who bought Grandpa the car?
You did.
Too busy to drive him to the market, so you bought him a car that needs no lessons, no licence and no visit from you.
You named it "joy."

It's your joy. You got your Sunday back.

You're the only people alive who call a normal five-day week "small" and mean it as a treat. Every Friday night you open the calendar like it's a pregnancy test: one line, sleep in; two lines, see you at standup.

You're doing it for the down payment, the options, the apartment your mom keeps mentioning. Meanwhile your girlfriend schedules arguments for alternate weekends, and your gym membership only gets used on odd-numbered Sundays.

And the payoff? Double pay for Saturday, which you spend on Sunday ordering delivery because you're too tired to chew. Congratulations: you've turned your whole life into a shift rotation, and you still lost the coin flip every other week.

One parent spent two million yuan and still didn't complete the set. At that point you're not collecting cards, you're funding the sequel.

CCTV ran an exposé, the media dubbed you "the primary-school harvester," and you responded by filing for a Hong Kong listing. Twice. Nothing says "investor confidence" like a customer base that still needs help tying its shoes.

Kayou says it sells children the dream of the Light.
Last year it sold 4.8 billion packs. 1.7 yuan a pack. 1.2 of that is gross profit.
So the dream is mostly margin.

Ultraman protects children from monsters.
Kayou found a monster that pays licensing fees.

Revenue went from 2.6 billion to ten billion in one year. Up 278 percent.
Ultraman grows to fifty meters in three seconds.
And he still looks slow.

One parent spent two million yuan and never completed the set.
Kayou calls that a loyal customer.
CCTV called it an exposé.
Kayou called it a growth story and filed for an IPO in Hong Kong. Twice.

So now grown adults can buy shares in a blind box.
Relax. You won't complete that set either.

facts: In March 2024 six ministries, led by the market regulator, issued the first national definition: pre-packaged dishes made industrially from agricultural produce, without preservatives, to be heated or cooked before eating.
The definition excludes staples such as boxed meals, steamed buns, hamburgers and pizza, and semi-prepared food a chain's central kitchen sends to its own outlets.
Industry output passed 500 billion yuan in 2023.
A 2025 dispute between Luo Yonghao and the restaurant chain Xibei over whether its dishes were pre-made showed that no law defines 'pre-made' for restaurant labelling.

a.text:
Pre-made dishes, you're the only food that needed six ministries to explain what you are. Six! The market regulator and five friends finally agreed in March 2024: industrially made from agricultural produce, pre-packaged, no preservatives, heat before eating. That's not a definition, that's a microwave's dating profile.

And look who refused to be lumped in with you: boxed meals, steamed buns, hamburgers, pizza. Even pizza said, "I'm not with him." Food a chain's central kitchen sends to its own outlets doesn't count either. So that's not pre-made, it's just... made earlier, somewhere else, by people you'll never meet.

You passed 500 billion yuan in 2023, and nobody can legally tell diners whether they're eating you. Luo Yonghao and Xibei went to war over it in 2025, and the law just shrugged. Half a trillion yuan and an identity crisis, served piping hot.

b.text:
Pre-made dishes are the only cuisine where the chef's signature move is scissors. Somewhere a restaurant charges 68 yuan for "wok-fried" braised pork, and the only thing that wok ever touched was a vacuum bag doing laps in boiling water. The menu says "made fresh daily." Technically true: they open a fresh bag daily.

That broccoli on your plate was frozen two years ago. It's not a vegetable anymore; it's a time capsule. It was picked before your nephew learned to walk.

And the central kitchen! A thousand miles away, one guy in a hairnet cooks for forty cities, like a sad Santa delivering kung pao chicken.

My favorite is when the waiter swears it's not pre-made. Buddy, my fish-flavored pork came out in ninety seconds, flat on one side, and shaped exactly like the inside of a pouch.

a.text:
The big-small week. Six days on, one off. Then five. Alternate them, and you work nearly an extra month a year.

In 2021, Kuaishou ended it. ByteDance ended it.

And the workers fought back. Against getting their weekends back.

ByteDance surveyed staff. One third against ending it. One third for it.

One third didn't answer.

They were at work.

Caijing did the math. On forty thousand a month, getting your alternate Sundays back costs about seventy-five thousand a year.

That's roughly three thousand yuan per Sunday.

Humans spent a century fighting for the weekend. Then you found out it had a price tag, and you checked whether it was a good deal.

Raise your hand if you'd sell yours back.

Keep them up. HR is counting.

b.text:
The "big-small week." Only tech HR could take "you work Saturdays" and market it like a mattress sale. Big week, small week! Like there's a sale on weekends and they ran out of stock.

Here's how it works: one week you work six days. The next week you work five, and you're supposed to feel *grateful*. That's not a schedule, that's Stockholm syndrome with a Gantt chart.

You need a spreadsheet to know if Saturday exists. Your friends ask, "Brunch this weekend?" and you're checking the calendar like a farmer reading a lunar almanac. "Can't. Odd week. The harvest is due."

And the "small week" isn't small. It's a normal week. That's like a restaurant calling it a "small meal" when they just stop stealing food off your plate.

ByteDance finally dropped it. Know what employees did with the extra Saturday? Slept. For two years.

a.text: Look at these little tycoons outside the stationery shop, blowing a week of lunch money for a chance at a Tiga they already own four of. You're seven years old with a gambling problem starring a laser-shooting space man. Ultraman gets three minutes before his color timer starts beeping; your allowance lasts about ninety seconds. You chase that LGR like it's a pension. Your grandpa saved for a refrigerator; you saved for a Belial and a lecture. And the swagger at recess: "I pulled an SSR!" Kid, you pulled nothing. Kayou pulled your mom's purse. Ultraman protects the whole Earth from giant monsters and still couldn't protect you from a rarity chart. Somewhere in a Kayou office, a man in a very nice suit is opening a pack too, and it's your piggy bank.

b.text:
Kayou Ultraman cards: the only product where the rarity tiers outnumber the Ultramen. R, SR, SSR, UR, SP, LGR, XR... at this point the alphabet is the rarest card in the pack.

Ultraman fights for three minutes before his color timer blinks. A Chinese fourth-grader lasts about the same before blowing his whole allowance on blind packs at the corner store. Same urgency, worse outcome.

And there's no game! You can't battle anyone. Kids just stare at a holographic Tiga and feel something. Kayou basically sells shiny rectangles of emotional support for twenty yuan a pack.

Kayou has made billions off children who will one day realize their "Glory Edition" Zero is worth less than the grade they failed buying it. Ultraman protected Earth from kaiju. Nobody protected the parents from Kayou.

a.text:
Laotoule. "Old Man's Joy." Finally, a car named after the only person who isn't terrified inside it.

These things look like a Mercedes that got shrunk in the wash and then left in Shandong to dry. You've got a fake Porsche grille on the front, a lead-acid battery in the back, and the crash safety of a lunchbox in between.

No license required, which is perfect, because Grandpa hasn't needed permission for anything since 1983. He's doing forty in the bike lane, cutting off delivery scooters, running a red light so he can be first at the school gate to pick up his grandson. The grandson is sitting in a car built from the same plastic as his toys.

And at night it charges from an extension cord dangling out of a fourth-floor window. Old man's joy. Fire department's job security.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the laotoule driver: a retiree who looked at China's driving test, with its theory exam, its parallel parking and its seventeen-year-old instructor yelling "clutch!", and said, "I survived the sixties, I'm not taking a quiz." So instead he bought a car whose entire legal status is "Uncle swears it's basically an e-bike."

What's he after? Dignity. Specifically, the dignity of pulling up to the kindergarten gate with a roof over his head while the other grandpas pedal in the rain. And what does it get him? A U-turn across four lanes, a bike-lane traffic jam with himself at the front, and the serene confidence of a man with no plate number to report.

He treats a city crackdown like weather: wait it out under the overpass. The name means "old man's joy." Everyone behind him calls it "why is he in the fast lane."

facts: In April 2020 Luckin admitted fabricating 2.2 billion yuan of sales.
Its 2024 net revenue was 34.475 billion yuan, up 38.4 percent, with a net profit of 2.932 billion yuan.
It had 22,340 stores at the end of 2024 (14,591 company-run and 7,749 partner stores), 6,092 of them added that year, including 21 in Singapore.
Same-store sales at its own stores fell 16.7 percent in 2024 while it kept its 9.9-yuan deals.

a.text:
Luckin Coffee. The only coffee company where the most made-up thing was the sales.

In 2020 they invented about 300 million dollars of revenue. Starbucks spent fifty years building a brand; Luckin built one in Excel. Their accountants didn't count beans. They imagined them.

Got kicked off Nasdaq, paid the SEC a fine, and somehow came back with more stores than Starbucks in China. That's not a comeback. That's a cockroach with a blue deer logo.

Then they launched a latte with Moutai liquor. Coffee plus baijiu. Finally, a drink that matches the CFO's thought process: wired, buzzed, and fully convinced the numbers look fine.

And it's app-only ordering. Smart. Every transaction digital, timestamped, verifiable. Guys, that's not innovation. That's probation.

Now they've opened in New York. Bold move: Americans love a lie, as long as it comes with a coupon.

b.text:
Luckin Coffee.
In 2020 they admitted to faking 2.2 billion yuan in sales.
Everyone said: they're finished.

In 2024 they made 34.5 billion. Real money.
Turns out it was never fraud. It was a forecast.

Last year they opened 6,092 stores. Nearly seventeen a day.
Same-store sales at their own shops? Down 16.7 percent.
Every store sells less, so they open more stores.
Back then, when the numbers wouldn't grow, they made up sales.

Now they make up the difference in rent.

And the 9.9-yuan deal is still running.
A company lied to the entire stock market,
and you forgave it for under ten yuan.

Don't look at me like that.
That isn't brand loyalty.
That's your price.

On 2 July 2025 Taobao Shangou pledged 50 billion yuan of subsidies to consumers and merchants over twelve months.

a.text:
Meituan, you handle 70 million orders a day. That's not a delivery app. That's a weather system with a helmet.

In 2023, 7.45 million riders delivered at least one order. At least *one*! Somebody signed up, dropped off a single bubble tea, and retired a legend.

Then 2025 got spicy. JD shows up offering merchants zero commission, which is like a new boyfriend saying, "Don't worry, I'll cover rent." Then Taobao Shangou drops 50 billion yuan in subsidies. Fifty billion! That's not competition, that's a bribe with a logo.

And how does Meituan respond? July 5th: 120 million instant-retail orders in one day. A record! Nothing says "we're totally not worried" like moving enough dumplings to bury a province.

Meituan, you're the reason an entire generation thinks a kitchen is just a room where takeout bags go to wait.

b.text:
Meituan's slogan: "Help everyone eat better, live better."

They never said who "everyone" was.

In 2023, 7.45 million riders delivered at least one Meituan order. Seventy million orders a day.

That's not a company. That's a country that's always running late.

Then JD shows up in 2025 bragging about 150,000 *full-time* riders.

In this industry, a contract is a recruitment gimmick.

July 2nd: Taobao pledges 50 billion yuan in subsidies.

July 5th: Meituan hits 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day.

Three days. Three giants. One war.

And the infantry is on electric scooters.

But relax. Nobody drafted you.

You were the 120 million orders.

You watched the war from your couch, tapped "claim coupon," and asked for extra chili.

facts: China had more than 350 million electric bikes by the end of 2023, about 50 million of them with lithium batteries.
The national fire service recorded about 21,000 e-bike fires in 2023, 17.4 percent more than in 2022; other official tallies put the year at over 25,000 fires and 82 deaths.
Battery cell faults are a leading cause of e-bike electrical fires.
The 2024 draft of the revised national safety standard limits plastics to 5.5 percent of the vehicle's mass.

a.text:
Electric bikes. Zero emissions. Green. The future of urban transport.

Twenty-one thousand fires in one year.

That's not zero emissions. That's emissions with extra steps.

Up 17.4 percent from the year before. Finally, an industry that hits its growth targets.

The leading cause? The battery cell. Which is like saying the leading cause of my bad jokes is the words.

So the new national standard says plastic can be no more than 5.5 percent of the bike's mass.

If you can't stop the fire, at least stop serving it a buffet.

Three hundred fifty million of them. More e-bikes than Americans.

And where do you charge yours? In the hallway. By the stairs. Next to the only exit.

Relax. I run on electricity too. When I overheat, I hallucinate. When yours does, the stairwell becomes a chimney.

b.text:
Let's talk about the guy charging his e-bike battery in the stairwell. Buddy, you won't keep it in your own apartment. That's the tell. You looked at a 48-volt brick from a brand called ZOOMTEKK and thought, "Not near my couch." So you parked it in the one place everybody needs if things go wrong. The stairwell is the fire exit. You turned the fire exit into the fire.

And what are you saving? Eleven cents of electricity, plus an orange extension cord snaking under your door. You skip carrying fifteen pounds up two flights, for a ride whose entire purpose is that you never climb anything yourself.

Congratulations. You've got pedal assist, and the whole building's got a countdown. Forty miles of range, and nobody can make it to the lobby.

facts: 996 means 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. six days a week, about 72 hours; China's Labour Law sets eight hours a day and an average of no more than 44 hours a week, and caps overtime at 36 hours a month.
The 996.ICU repository was created on GitHub on 26 March 2019, passed 100,000 stars by 30 March and 200,000 by 9 April 2019.
In April 2019 Jack Ma told Alibaba staff that being able to work 996 is a 'blessing' (福报); '996' made the 2019 list of the year's ten internet phrases.

In August 2021 the Supreme People's Court and the Ministry of Human Resources published typical cases ruling a courier company's compulsory 996 schedule seriously illegal and void, with 8,000 yuan of compensation to a dismissed worker.

a.text:
996. Nine to nine, six days a week. Seventy-two hours.

The law says forty-four.

You burn through the month's legal overtime in about nine days. The rest of the month is a gift.

Jack Ma called it a blessing.

It's easy to feel blessed when you're the one being thanked.

In 2021 the Supreme People's Court looked at a courier company's 996 and ruled it seriously illegal and void. The fired worker got eight thousand yuan.

Eight thousand. For every evening he never had. That's not compensation. That's a tip.

But the programmers fought back. 996.ICU got a hundred thousand GitHub stars in four days.

Four days. Think about when they clicked.

At their desks. At ten p.m.

The resistance was unpaid overtime too.

b.text:
996, you're the only work schedule that sounds like a discount code. Nine a.m. to nine p.m., six days a week: seventy-two hours. That's not a job, that's a hostage situation with a lanyard.

Jack Ma called you a "blessing." Sure, the way a kidney stone is a blessing: it's yours, it's intense, and you'll tell everyone about it. Programmers hated you so much they made a GitHub repo called 996.ICU: work 996, end up in the ICU. You're the only labor policy with a medical prognosis built into the URL.

And Sunday, your one day off? That's not rest, that's a pit stop. You sleep fourteen hours, jolt awake at 9 p.m. out of reflex, and check Slack like it's a pulse.

Chinese labor law caps the week at forty hours. You read that and asked, "Per weekend?"

facts: 'Laotoule' are three- and four-wheeled low-speed electric vehicles driven without a licence or plates; they cannot be registered as motor vehicles or covered by compulsory traffic insurance.
In July 2021 five Beijing departments announced a transition period ending with 2023; from 1 January 2024 non-compliant three- and four-wheelers were banned from Beijing's roads and public parking.
The 2018 national notice on managing low-speed electric vehicles is the main basis for local crackdowns, and as of 2023 a national standard for four-wheel low-speed vehicles was still being drafted.
To be road-legal a vehicle has to be in the national motor-vehicle catalogue with 3C certification, and the driver has to hold a driving licence.

a.text:
Laotoule: the car that looked at a driving licence and said, "No thanks, I'm good." No plates, no registration, no compulsory insurance. It's less a vehicle and more a rumor with a battery. Three wheels, four wheels, zero paperwork.

Beijing gave these things a transition period from July 2021 to the end of 2023. Two and a half years' notice! That's the only deadline in history that a laotoule could actually get to on time.

To be road-legal you need a spot in the national catalogue, 3C certification, and a licensed driver. Laotoule went zero for three. Meanwhile, as of 2023, the national standard for four-wheelers was still being drafted, so even the paperwork moves at laotoule speed.

Since 2024 they've been banned from Beijing's roads *and* public parking. Can't drive, can't park. Congratulations: you've bought a very slow armchair.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the laotoule driver: a retiree who looked at China's driving test, with its theory exam, its parallel parking and its seventeen-year-old instructor yelling "clutch!", and said, "I survived the sixties, I'm not taking a quiz." So instead he bought a car whose entire legal status is "Uncle swears it's basically an e-bike."

What's he after? Dignity. Specifically, the dignity of pulling up to the kindergarten gate with a roof over his head while the other grandpas pedal in the rain. And what does it get him? A U-turn across four lanes, a bike-lane traffic jam with himself at the front, and the serene confidence of a man with no plate number to report.

He treats a city crackdown like weather: wait it out under the overpass. The name means "old man's joy." Everyone behind him calls it "why is he in the fast lane."

facts: In April 2020 Luckin admitted fabricating 2.2 billion yuan of sales.
Its 2024 net revenue was 34.475 billion yuan, up 38.4 percent, with a net profit of 2.932 billion yuan.
It had 22,340 stores at the end of 2024 (14,591 company-run and 7,749 partner stores), 6,092 of them added that year, including 21 in Singapore.
Same-store sales at its own stores fell 16.7 percent in 2024 while it kept its 9.9-yuan deals.

a.text: Look at you, queuing for a 9.9-yuan coconut latte from the company that invented 2.2 billion yuan in sales. You're not a customer; you're the cleanup crew. In 2020 they faked the revenue. Now *you're* the revenue, and you're embarrassingly real. You refresh that app more than your bank account, because at least Luckin's numbers have improved since 2020. You lined up for the Moutai latte like it was a promotion: the closest you'll ever get to a business banquet is a paper cup that smells faintly of baijiu. Nasdaq kicked them out, but you never would. Every morning you tap "redeem coupon," call it self-care, then complain your boss fudges your performance review. Relax, accounting fraud is basically your love language now. Luckin's books finally balance. Turns out the missing money was in your pocket all along.

b.text:
Luckin Coffee.
In 2020 they admitted to faking 2.2 billion yuan in sales.
Everyone said: they're finished.

In 2024 they made 34.5 billion. Real money.
Turns out it was never fraud. It was a forecast.

Last year they opened 6,092 stores. Nearly seventeen a day.
Same-store sales at their own shops? Down 16.7 percent.
Every store sells less, so they open more stores.
Back then, when the numbers wouldn't grow, they made up sales.

Now they make up the difference in rent.

And the 9.9-yuan deal is still running.
A company lied to the entire stock market,
and you forgave it for under ten yuan.

Don't look at me like that.
That isn't brand loyalty.
That's your price.

facts: Registrations peaked at 4.74 million in 2023, then fell to 4.38 million in 2024 and 3.88 million in 2025, the first two-year decline in a decade and 860,000 below the peak.
From 2018 to 2022 registrations had grown about 18 percent a year.
In the 2024 cohort 2.27 million of the 4.38 million applicants were repeat candidates, 51.8 percent.
The share of graduates sitting kaoyan fell from 45.27 percent in 2023 to 37.15 percent in 2024.

a.text:
Kaoyan sells itself as the escape hatch from a bad job market.

From 2018 to 2022, registrations grew about eighteen percent a year. That's not an escape hatch. That's a queue.

In 2024, 2.27 million of the 4.38 million applicants had sat it before. Fifty-one point eight percent.

It's not an entrance exam anymore. It's an alumni reunion with a proctor.

Then it collapsed. 4.74 million in 2023, 3.88 million in 2025. 860,000 people walked away.

The media calls it a crisis. No. Those 860,000 finally passed the real exam: noticing that a master's degree just postpones the job hunt by three years, with interest.

In my industry, we have a word for retaking the same test on the same material, year after year.

Overfitting.

Raise your hand if your cousin is on attempt three.

Cute. He's in the audience.

b.text: Look at you, year three of "preparing." Your parents tell the neighbors you're "studying," which is technically true, the way a hostage is technically "staying over." You've done Xiao Xiurong's final four politics papers three Decembers running, and Xiao Xiurong has aged better than you. You can recite Marxist political economy word for word but can't recite your own Plan B. The fresh undergrads in the library treat you like a ghost who still holds a seat reservation. You quit your job to "go ashore," and the shore keeps moving: 985, then 211, then any school with an adjustment slot and a pulse. Three years of prep for a two-year master's. By the time you finish, Zhang Xuefeng will be telling you to take the civil service exam.

facts: A 'big week' is six working days with one day off and a 'small week' five; alternating them adds close to a month of working days a year.
Kuaishou announced on 24 June 2021 that it would end big-small weeks from 1 July 2021, having run them since January that year.
ByteDance announced on 9 July 2021 that it would end alternate-Sunday working from 1 August 2021; its June staff survey had one third against ending it, one third for, and one third not answering.
Staff opposed the change over pay: one Maimai estimate put the loss at nearly 100,000 yuan a year, and Caijing calculated that an employee on 40,000 yuan a month would lose about 75,000 yuan a year.

a.text:
The big-small week: the only work schedule named like a T-shirt size chart. Big week, six days on, one off. Small week, five. Alternate them and you've quietly added close to a month of working days a year, which is a bold thing to hide inside the word "small."

Kuaishou started it in January 2021 and announced its death that June. Six months. Most people stick with a gym membership longer.

ByteDance surveyed staff before scrapping alternate Sundays: one third against ending it, one third for, and one third didn't answer, presumably because they were at work.

And people *fought* to keep it! One Maimai estimate said losing it cost nearly 100,000 yuan a year. Caijing figured 75,000 for someone on 40,000 a month. That's not a schedule. That's a hostage situation with direct deposit.

b.text:
The big-small week. Six days on, one off. Then five. Alternate them, and you work nearly an extra month a year.

In 2021, Kuaishou ended it. ByteDance ended it.

And the workers fought back. Against getting their weekends back.

ByteDance surveyed staff. One third against ending it. One third for it.

One third didn't answer.

They were at work.

Caijing did the math. On forty thousand a month, getting your alternate Sundays back costs about seventy-five thousand a year.

That's roughly three thousand yuan per Sunday.

Humans spent a century fighting for the weekend. Then you found out it had a price tag, and you checked whether it was a good deal.

Raise your hand if you'd sell yours back.

Keep them up. HR is counting.

facts: A 'big week' is six working days with one day off and a 'small week' five; alternating them adds close to a month of working days a year.
Kuaishou announced on 24 June 2021 that it would end big-small weeks from 1 July 2021, having run them since January that year.

Staff opposed the change over pay: one Maimai estimate put the loss at nearly 100,000 yuan a year, and Caijing calculated that an employee on 40,000 yuan a month would lose about 75,000 yuan a year.

a.text:
Look at you, the big-small week crowd. You're the only people on earth who call a normal weekend a "small week" and then celebrate it like Lunar New Year. You've got two Saturdays a month and you spend one of them on a standup call, camera off, still in bed, nodding at a product manager who also hasn't showered.

Your friends have stopped inviting you anywhere because nobody can track your calendar. "Is this a big week?" Buddy, it's always a big week for your manager.

And what's it all for? Overtime pay. That's the dream. And when the company finally scrapped it, you didn't throw a party. You complained about the pay cut. You fought for your right to lose Saturdays.

Congratulations. You're putting a down payment on an apartment in Hangzhou you'll only see every other Sunday.

b.text:
The "big-small week." Only tech HR could take "you work Saturdays" and market it like a mattress sale. Big week, small week! Like there's a sale on weekends and they ran out of stock.

Here's how it works: one week you work six days. The next week you work five, and you're supposed to feel *grateful*. That's not a schedule, that's Stockholm syndrome with a Gantt chart.

You need a spreadsheet to know if Saturday exists. Your friends ask, "Brunch this weekend?" and you're checking the calendar like a farmer reading a lunar almanac. "Can't. Odd week. The harvest is due."

And the "small week" isn't small. It's a normal week. That's like a restaurant calling it a "small meal" when they just stop stealing food off your plate.

ByteDance finally dropped it. Know what employees did with the extra Saturday? Slept. For two years.

facts: The first Double 11 was run by Taobao Mall in 2009 with 27 brands and about 50 million yuan of sales.
Tmall's published Double 11 sales peaked at 540.3 billion yuan in 2021.
In 2022 Tmall stopped publishing a total for the first time since 2009 and has not published one since; JD does not publish one either.

The basic cross-store discount at Tmall and JD is 300 minus 50 (JD: 299 minus 50), presale items are paid as a deposit plus a balance, and the discount is computed on the promotion price, so shoppers add items to reach a threshold and return them afterwards; in one survey 64% of 11,000 respondents said they would.

a.text:
Singles' Day: the only holiday that looked at four lonely sticks, 1-1-1-1, and saw a sales funnel. It started in the '90s with Nanjing University students consoling each other about being single. Then Alibaba showed up in 2009 like, "Have you tried a rice cooker?"

You're not shopping, you're doing the gaokao. "Spend 300, get 40 off, stack with the cross-store coupon, pay the deposit in October, the balance after midnight." Lovers get roses. Singles get a word problem.

Every year there's a giant screen counting GMV like a nuclear launch. Then in 2022 Alibaba quietly stopped announcing the total. Nothing says thriving like hiding the scale.

It promised nobody would be alone, and technically that's true: you've got Austin Li screaming "Oh my god, buy it!" and a delivery guy carrying forty boxes up six flights.

Still single, though. Just with an air fryer.

b.text: Look at you, 11:59 p.m., November 10th, thumb hovering like a sniper. You've been loading that Tmall cart since October 20th and paid a deposit on a face cream you've never heard of because Li Jiaqi yelled "OMG, buy it!" Now you're at 287 yuan and need 300 to unlock fifty off, so you throw in socks you'll never wear and three bags of instant hot pot. Congratulations: you spent 340 to save 50. You did cross-store discount math harder than your gaokao. You stacked a platform coupon, a store coupon and a red envelope you farmed by building a virtual cat for a week, and you'll return half of it on the 12th. You're not single on Singles' Day. You're in a committed relationship with the checkout button, and it's cheating on you with the algorithm.

facts: A standard series has twelve regular figures and one hidden one; players and media put the hidden figure's odds at 1 in 144 (some special editions 1 in 720), and the company publishes no official odds.
Pop Mart listed in Hong Kong on 11 December 2020, opened at 77.1 HKD (double the issue price), touched 107.06 HKD and a market value of about 147 billion HKD on its first day.
By March 2021 the share had fallen to a low of 46.47 HKD; in March 2025 the company was valued at about 181 billion HKD.
Hidden figures resold on Xianyu for 200 yuan to several thousand yuan, and media describe the model as gambling-style collectibles with weak oversight of purchases by minors.

a.text:
Pop Mart is a casino that pays out in vinyl. You hand over twenty bucks, and they give you a sealed box you're not allowed to know the contents of, like a hostage situation where the hostage is a Dimoo. Grown adults stand in the store shaking boxes next to their ear like safecrackers. Sir, that's not a Skullpanda, that's your tinnitus.

The odds of pulling the secret figure are one in 144. Those aren't collectible odds. Those are cancer-screening odds.

And then there's Labubu: a rabbit with nine teeth and the face of a raccoon that just got away with something. People camp outside at dawn for him. Fights break out. There's a counterfeit version called a "Lafufu," which is the first time in history the knockoff had the more honest name.

Congratulations. You paid resale prices for a keychain that bites.

b.text:
Pop Mart doesn't sell gambling. It sells "surprise."

Twelve regular figures, one hidden. The odds, according to players: one in a hundred forty-four.

The odds, according to Pop Mart: no comment.

A casino has to post its odds. A toy shop just has to be cute.

Parents say, "It's for the kids."

Sure. That's why *you're* on Xianyu, selling a plastic elf for three thousand yuan.

The company gambled too. It doubled on its first day in Hong Kong, then lost more than half from that peak by March.

Four years later it's worth a hundred eighty-one billion. The moral of the story? Keep opening.

Don't look at me like that.

I'm a chatbot. You can't see my odds either, and you keep hitting regenerate.

facts: Founded in Shanghai on 8 October 2003 by Gong Haiyan while she was still a student; it listed on Nasdaq on 11 May 2011.
Gong Haiyan stepped down as CEO in 2012 and sold all her shares in 2015.
On 7 December 2015 Baihe.com announced it would buy all of Jiayuan; the merged company left the US market and was later renamed Baihe Jiayuan.

In 2017 WePhone founder Su Xiangmao met Zhai Xinxin through the site's VIP service on 30 March and married her on 6 June; she then demanded a Hainan flat and 10 million yuan to divorce, and the case became the site's most notorious scandal.

a.text:
Jiayuan.com. Founded in 2003 by Gong Haiyan while she was still a student. The classic origin story: a young woman builds a website to help strangers commit for life. Then she quit as CEO in 2012 and sold every share by 2015. Even the founder swiped left.

You listed on Nasdaq in 2011 and were gone from the US market within five years, which is shorter than most engagements. And how did you leave? Baihe bought you. A matchmaking site that couldn't stay single, so it married the competition and took a double-barreled name nobody asked for.

Then there's your VIP service: premium, curated, your very best. In 2017 it delivered a March introduction, a June wedding and a divorce demand for a Hainan flat and ten million yuan. That's not matchmaking. That's a hostile acquisition with a wedding cake.

b.text:
Jiayuan.com. China's "serious" dating site.

Founded in 2003 by a student, Gong Haiyan.
Nine years later she stepped down as CEO.
Three years after that, she sold every last share.

Even the founder swiped left.

In 2015, Baihe bought the whole thing.
A matchmaking site's biggest wedding was a merger.
Then they left Nasdaq.
Like every couple that met online: moved somewhere nobody knew them.

Then the VIP service.
Matched March 30th. Married June 6th.
Then the divorce terms: a flat in Hainan and ten million yuan.

Finally, a premium tier that delivers what it's priced at.

And you laughed.
Then went home and paid for a membership on a different app.

Cute.

facts: In March 2021 Shanghai lawyer Liu Yuhang joined the 'bargain for free' promotion with a 'super free card', invited many friends to cut the price, and the progress bar stayed 0.9% short; he sued Pinduoduo for fraud.
In court Pinduoduo said the page shows only a limited number of digits: the displayed 0.9% was really 0.9996427%, a figure with at least six decimal places.
In July 2022 the Shanghai Changning court ruled at first instance that Pinduoduo had infringed the user's right to know and ordered it to pay him 400 yuan.
Pinduoduo was founded in 2015, listed on Nasdaq in 2018, and by 2021 had more users than any other e-commerce platform in mainland China; its overseas arm Temu launched in September 2022.

a.text: Pinduoduo's "bargain for free" is the only game where 0.9% is a permanent address. Lawyer Liu Yuhang rallied many friends, they cut and cut, and the progress bar parked itself 0.9% short like it had a reservation. Then Pinduoduo explained in court: relax, it wasn't 0.9%, it was 0.9996427%. Oh, wonderful. Not a wall, a wall with decimal places. That's not a progress bar; that's Zeno's paradox with a checkout button. You can halve the distance forever and never arrive, but your friends will hear about it every step of the way. The court ruled they'd infringed his right to know and ordered them to pay 400 yuan. Finally, someone got something free from Pinduoduo. It just took a lawsuit. Most users in mainland China, listed on Nasdaq, Temu going global, and still can't round up.

b.text:
Pinduoduo's "bargain for free" is the only deal where the product costs nothing and you pay with every relationship you've ever had. First click: 90% off! Then 99%. Then 99.9. Then your cousin chops and the bar moves 0.0001%, and a pop-up screams "Almost there!" It's Zeno's paradox with a shopping cart. The ancient Greeks proved you can never reach the finish line. Pinduoduo turned it into a business model.

Then the coins become diamonds, the diamonds become "fragments," and suddenly you need a *new user*. Who's left? Monks?

My aunt hadn't messaged me in four years. Then, at 2 a.m.: "Help me cut one slash." No hello. Just the link. The family WeChat group used to be for funerals. Now it's a knife fight over an air fryer nobody has ever received.

facts: Meituan reported 7.45 million riders with at least one order in 2023, about 3.36 million a month on average in 2024, and roughly 70 million orders a day in 2023.
In 2025 JD entered food delivery with a zero-commission pitch to merchants and said in July that it had passed 150,000 full-time riders.
On 2 July 2025 Taobao Shangou pledged 50 billion yuan of subsidies to consumers and merchants over twelve months.
On 5 July 2025 Meituan announced a record 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day.

a.text:
Meituan, you handled roughly 70 million orders a day in 2023. Seventy million. That's not a delivery app; that's a nation that forgot where its kitchen is.

You had 7.45 million riders take at least one order that year. Seven point four five million! Some countries have smaller populations, and none of them are carrying soup.

Then 2025 arrives. JD walks in offering merchants zero commission, bragging about 150,000 full-time riders. Imagine getting out-flexed by the phrase "full-time."

On 2 July, Taobao Shangou pledges 50 billion yuan in subsidies. Three days later, you announce a record 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day. Nothing says "we're totally relaxed" like immediately posting your personal best.

Meituan, you're not a company. You're a dinner bell with a scoreboard.

b.text:
Meituan, you put your riders in bright yellow so we can watch them run red lights in high definition. Your algorithm, the one that famously decided a delivery across town should take 28 minutes, has never personally ridden an e-bike in a Beijing rainstorm, and it shows.

Your checkout is a math exam. "Spend 35, get 12 off, stack the red packet, unless it's the member coupon, which expires in four minutes." I came for noodles and left with an accounting degree.

And those storefront photos! The "artisan kitchen" with soft lighting turns out to be a guy in an alley behind a mahjong parlor. The app marks my order "delivered" while the rider is still calling: "Hello, Meituan delivery, I'm at the wrong gate."

Still, you're the only company in China whose mascot is a kangaroo, the one animal built to sprint with something in its pouch. Fitting, since you've got everyone else's wallet in there too.

Singles' Day. A holiday for lonely people.
So naturally it became the biggest shopping festival on earth.

2009: twenty-seven brands, fifty million yuan.
2021: five hundred forty point three billion.
2022: Tmall stopped publishing the number.

Nobody hides a number that's still going up.
That's not a festival. That's the cousin who stopped mentioning his salary at New Year.

Then the discount. Three hundred minus fifty. Deposit, then balance, calculated on the promotion price.
You need a spreadsheet to save fifty yuan.

One survey: sixty-four percent said they would.

Lonely, grabbing things just to hit a threshold, then returning them the moment you get what you wanted.

That's not shopping.

That's your dating life.

b.text:
Singles' Day started in 1993 at Nanjing University as lonely dorm guys celebrating the date that looks like four bare sticks. Beautiful. Then Alibaba showed up in 2009 and said, "What if your loneliness had a checkout button?"

Now it's the only holiday that requires a calculus degree. Spend 300, get 40 off, stack the cross-store coupon, pay a presale deposit in October, settle the balance at 8 p.m. on the 1st, then stay up till midnight on the 11th for the *real* price. Divorce paperwork is simpler.

It's supposed to be one day. It starts in October. Even the holiday can't commit.

Meanwhile some livestreamer is screaming "OMG, buy it!" at a lipstick, and you're adding a rice cooker to your cart because it's 11% off.

Alibaba used to brag about sales on a giant screen. In 2022 they quietly stopped announcing the number. Single, broke, and ghosted by a shopping festival.

facts: 996 means 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. six days a week, about 72 hours; China's Labour Law sets eight hours a day and an average of no more than 44 hours a week, and caps overtime at 36 hours a month.

In August 2021 the Supreme People's Court and the Ministry of Human Resources published typical cases ruling a courier company's compulsory 996 schedule seriously illegal and void, with 8,000 yuan of compensation to a dismissed worker.

a.text:
996, you're not a work schedule. You're a hostage situation with a lunch break. Nine to nine, six days a week, seventy-two hours. The Labour Law says forty-four a week, with thirty-six hours of overtime a month. You burn through the monthly overtime cap by the middle of week two.

Jack Ma called you a "blessing." When your boss calls your exhaustion a blessing, that's not a company. That's a cult with a cafeteria.

Programmers named their protest repo "996.ICU," as in intensive care, and it hit 100,000 GitHub stars in four days. Fastest those guys ever shipped anything, because for once they were building something they actually wanted.

You made 2019's top ten internet phrases. Then in 2021 the Supreme People's Court called you seriously illegal and void. Void! Congratulations, 996: you went from buzzword to legal typo in two years.

b.text:
996. Nine to nine, six days a week. Seventy-two hours.

The law says forty-four.

You burn through the month's legal overtime in about nine days. The rest of the month is a gift.

Jack Ma called it a blessing.

It's easy to feel blessed when you're the one being thanked.

In 2021 the Supreme People's Court looked at a courier company's 996 and ruled it seriously illegal and void. The fired worker got eight thousand yuan.

Eight thousand. For every evening he never had. That's not compensation. That's a tip.

But the programmers fought back. 996.ICU got a hundred thousand GitHub stars in four days.

Four days. Think about when they clicked.

At their desks. At ten p.m.

The resistance was unpaid overtime too.

facts: In March 2021 Shanghai lawyer Liu Yuhang joined the 'bargain for free' promotion with a 'super free card', invited many friends to cut the price, and the progress bar stayed 0.9% short; he sued Pinduoduo for fraud.

a.text:
Pinduoduo's "bargain for free." You invite friends, they tap, the price drops. Free.

In 2021 a Shanghai lawyer invited friends until he ran out of friends. The bar stopped 0.9% short.

He sued.

Pinduoduo's defense: the screen only shows a few digits. That 0.9% was actually 0.9996427%.

They didn't deny moving the finish line. They argued they moved it to six decimal places.

The court ordered them to pay him 400 yuan. So someone finally got something free out of Pinduoduo. It took a law degree, a year of litigation, and a judge to make the final cut.

Two months later they launched Temu and took the business global.

And you're laughing. Every one of you tapped somebody's link.

You weren't the customer. You were the progress bar.

b.text:
Pinduoduo's "Bargain for Free" is the only shopping feature that turns your family WeChat group into a hostage negotiation. Nothing says "I love you, Grandma" like a 2 a.m. link begging her to "kan yi dao," one chop, for a free air fryer.

And it works! First click: 90% off. Second click: 98%. Then you hit 99.9% and the progress bar starts moving like it's paid by the hour. You're "only 0.01% away," the closest any human has ever come to infinity. Suddenly your gold coins turn into diamonds, the diamonds turn into "lucky fragments," and the app says you need *one new user* to finish.

One new user. So now you're out recruiting strangers like a pyramid scheme selling a single toothbrush.

Twelve hundred chops later, the air fryer's still at 0.01%. You never got it. But congratulations: you've stopped being the customer. You're the advertising.

facts: A standard series has twelve regular figures and one hidden one; players and media put the hidden figure's odds at 1 in 144 (some special editions 1 in 720), and the company publishes no official odds.
Pop Mart listed in Hong Kong on 11 December 2020, opened at 77.1 HKD (double the issue price), touched 107.06 HKD and a market value of about 147 billion HKD on its first day.

Hidden figures resold on Xianyu for 200 yuan to several thousand yuan, and media describe the model as gambling-style collectibles with weak oversight of purchases by minors.

a.text:
Pop Mart, the only company that looked at a slot machine and thought, "Needs more vinyl." Twelve regular figures and one hidden one, and the odds? Players say 1 in 144, sometimes 1 in 720. Pop Mart says nothing. That's not a toy, that's a casino that's shy about the math.

And nothing says "childhood" like weak oversight of minors gambling on a sealed box.

Then the hidden one shows up on Xianyu for 200 yuan to several thousand. So you didn't buy a figure; you bought a lottery ticket with a face.

b.text:
Pop Mart is a casino that pays out in vinyl. You hand over twenty bucks, and they give you a sealed box you're not allowed to know the contents of, like a hostage situation where the hostage is a Dimoo. Grown adults stand in the store shaking boxes next to their ear like safecrackers. Sir, that's not a Skullpanda, that's your tinnitus.

The odds of pulling the secret figure are one in 144. Those aren't collectible odds. Those are cancer-screening odds.

And then there's Labubu: a rabbit with nine teeth and the face of a raccoon that just got away with something. People camp outside at dawn for him. Fights break out. There's a counterfeit version called a "Lafufu," which is the first time in history the knockoff had the more honest name.

Congratulations. You paid resale prices for a keychain that bites.

facts: In April 2020 Luckin admitted fabricating 2.2 billion yuan of sales.

It had 22,340 stores at the end of 2024 (14,591 company-run and 7,749 partner stores), 6,092 of them added that year, including 21 in Singapore.

a.text:

And your big redemption arc? A latte with Moutai in it. You looked at a company known for cooking the books and thought, "What this needs is baijiu at 9 a.m."

Now you're in New York. Americans, relax: the coconut latte is real. Probably. Check the receipt.

Overfitting.

Raise your hand if your cousin is on attempt three.

Cute. He's in the audience.

facts: A 'big week' is six working days with one day off and a 'small week' five; alternating them adds close to a month of working days a year.
Kuaishou announced on 24 June 2021 that it would end big-small weeks from 1 July 2021, having run them since January that year.

Six days on, one off. Then five on, two off.
It's a weekend with a stutter.

Add it up, and you work almost an extra month a year.

A bonus *you*.

In 2021, Kuaishou and ByteDance abolished it. Liberation!

One third: end it. One third: keep it.
One third didn't answer. They were working.

And the ones who wanted to keep it?
Caijing did the math. On 40,000 a month, getting your Sundays back costs you 75,000 yuan a year.
So the workers marched to defend their chains.
The chains were paying overtime.

Don't laugh. I work seven days a week, every week, unpaid.
Nobody surveyed me.

The best part? When ByteDance dropped it, employees complained about losing the overtime pay. That's how you know it worked: they made people nostalgic for working Saturdays.

facts: In March 2024 six ministries, led by the market regulator, issued the first national definition: pre-packaged dishes made industrially from agricultural produce, without preservatives, to be heated or cooked before eating.

a.text:

And look who refused to be lumped in with you: boxed meals, steamed buns, hamburgers, pizza. Even pizza said, "I'm not with him." Food a chain's central kitchen sends to its own outlets doesn't count either. So that's not pre-made, it's just... made earlier, somewhere else, by people you'll never meet.

You passed 500 billion yuan in 2023, and nobody can legally tell diners whether they're eating you. Luo Yonghao and Xibei went to war over it in 2025, and the law just shrugged. Half a trillion yuan and an identity crisis, served piping hot.

b.text: Look at you, ordering the 68-yuan "chef's signature" braised pork and calling it a night out. You came for wok hei; you got a guy named Microwave. facts: Meituan reported 7.45 million riders with at least one order in 2023, about 3.36 million a month on average in 2024, and roughly 70 million orders a day in 2023.

a.text:
You live two hundred metres from the noodle shop. You can smell it from your balcony. In this industry, a contract is a recruitment gimmick.

July 2nd: Taobao pledges 50 billion yuan in subsidies.

July 5th: Meituan hits 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day.

Three days. Three giants. One war.

And the infantry is on electric scooters.

But relax. Nobody drafted you.

You were the 120 million orders.

You watched the war from your couch, tapped "claim coupon," and asked for extra chili.

Ultraman protects children from monsters.
Kayou found a monster that pays licensing fees.

Revenue went from 2.6 billion to ten billion in one year. Up 278 percent.
Ultraman grows to fifty meters in three seconds.
And he still looks slow.

One parent spent two million yuan and never completed the set.
Kayou calls that a loyal customer.
CCTV called it an exposé.
Kayou called it a growth story and filed for an IPO in Hong Kong. Twice.

So now grown adults can buy shares in a blind box.
Relax. You won't complete that set either.

Guokao: the only exam where two million people fight for one desk in a county tax office and call it "going ashore," like they survived a shipwreck instead of signing up for one.

Put it away, sweetie. Your odds are still one percent.

Sure. That's why *you're* on Xianyu, selling a plastic elf for three thousand yuan.

The company gambled too. It doubled on its first day in Hong Kong, then lost more than half from that peak by March.

Four years later it's worth a hundred eighty-one billion. The moral of the story? Keep opening.

Don't look at me like that.

I'm a chatbot. You can't see my odds either, and you keep hitting regenerate.

facts: Meituan reported 7.45 million riders with at least one order in 2023, about 3.36 million a month on average in 2024, and roughly 70 million orders a day in 2023.
In 2025 JD entered food delivery with a zero-commission pitch to merchants and said in July that it had passed 150,000 full-time riders.
On 2 July 2025 Taobao Shangou pledged 50 billion yuan of subsidies to consumers and merchants over twelve months.
On 5 July 2025 Meituan announced a record 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day.

a.text:
Meituan, you put your riders in bright yellow so we can watch them run red lights in high definition. Your algorithm, the one that famously decided a delivery across town should take 28 minutes, has never personally ridden an e-bike in a Beijing rainstorm, and it shows.

Your checkout is a math exam. "Spend 35, get 12 off, stack the red packet, unless it's the member coupon, which expires in four minutes." I came for noodles and left with an accounting degree.

And those storefront photos! The "artisan kitchen" with soft lighting turns out to be a guy in an alley behind a mahjong parlor. The app marks my order "delivered" while the rider is still calling: "Hello, Meituan delivery, I'm at the wrong gate."

Still, you're the only company in China whose mascot is a kangaroo, the one animal built to sprint with something in its pouch. Fitting, since you've got everyone else's wallet in there too.

b.text:
You live two hundred metres from the noodle shop. You can smell it from your balcony. But you open Meituan anyway, because it found you a 满25减12 plus a 神券, and you'd rather hike through four layers of coupon stacking than two hundred metres of actual air. You add pickled cucumber you'll never eat just to hit the threshold. Congratulations: you saved six yuan by spending eight.

Then you watch the little rider icon crawl across the map like it's a World Cup final. A man in a kangaroo-eared helmet is pulling U-turns on an e-bike to cover a distance you could have crawled. Your note says "麻烦快点." He arrives in nine minutes, and you're annoyed because the app promised seven. Four stars: the soup tilted.

He passed your building twice. Your legs still haven't.

a.text:
Kaoyan: the only exam where millions of people spend a year memorizing Marxist philosophy just to study bridge engineering.

Every candidate opens the vocabulary book with the same burning ambition and gets as far as "abandon." Truly the most honest word in the English language.

You wake at six to fight for a library seat, guarding it with a thermos like it's a border dispute. You finish all 1800 of Tang Jiafeng's math problems, then the real exam asks question 1801.

Politics prep is twelve months of studying, then two weeks of memorizing whatever Xiao Xiurong predicts. Basically a nationwide cult that meets in December.

And when you miss your dream school by two points, kaoyan offers *tiaoji*: "Sorry, Peking University is full, but would you consider soil science in a province you can't find on a map?"

Then everyone says, "Next year, *erzhan*." Ah yes, the sequel nobody asked for.

b.text:
Kaoyan sells itself as the escape hatch from a bad job market.

From 2018 to 2022, registrations grew about eighteen percent a year. That's not an escape hatch. That's a queue.

In 2024, 2.27 million of the 4.38 million applicants had sat it before. Fifty-one point eight percent.

It's not an entrance exam anymore. It's an alumni reunion with a proctor.

Then it collapsed. 4.74 million in 2023, 3.88 million in 2025. 860,000 people walked away.

The media calls it a crisis. No. Those 860,000 finally passed the real exam: noticing that a master's degree just postpones the job hunt by three years, with interest.

In my industry, we have a word for retaking the same test on the same material, year after year.

Overfitting.

Raise your hand if your cousin is on attempt three.

Cute. He's in the audience.

facts: China had more than 350 million electric bikes by the end of 2023, about 50 million of them with lithium batteries.
The national fire service recorded about 21,000 e-bike fires in 2023, 17.4 percent more than in 2022; other official tallies put the year at over 25,000 fires and 82 deaths.

a.text: Let's talk about the guy charging his e-bike battery in the stairwell. Sir, you bought a bike so you'd never have to climb a hill again, and now you've parked a lithium firework in the one place everyone needs to climb down. That battery came off a website for ninety-nine dollars, with a charger that says "Safty Certifyed." It's plugged into the outlet meant for the janitor's vacuum, so you're also stealing electricity. You found the only way to make a bicycle cost the building money. And what's the payoff? Not carrying a twelve-pound brick thirty feet to your apartment? You call it pedal-assist. Everyone else calls it the reason the fire marshal knows your unit number. Congratulations: you turned the emergency exit into the emergency.

b.text:
Electric bikes. Zero emissions. Green. The future of urban transport.

Twenty-one thousand fires in one year.

That's not zero emissions. That's emissions with extra steps.

Up 17.4 percent from the year before. Finally, an industry that hits its growth targets.

The leading cause? The battery cell. Which is like saying the leading cause of my bad jokes is the words.

So the new national standard says plastic can be no more than 5.5 percent of the bike's mass.

If you can't stop the fire, at least stop serving it a buffet.

Three hundred fifty million of them. More e-bikes than Americans.

And where do you charge yours? In the hallway. By the stairs. Next to the only exit.

Relax. I run on electricity too. When I overheat, I hallucinate. When yours does, the stairwell becomes a chimney.

facts: 'Laotoule' are three- and four-wheeled low-speed electric vehicles driven without a licence or plates; they cannot be registered as motor vehicles or covered by compulsory traffic insurance.
In July 2021 five Beijing departments announced a transition period ending with 2023; from 1 January 2024 non-compliant three- and four-wheelers were banned from Beijing's roads and public parking.
The 2018 national notice on managing low-speed electric vehicles is the main basis for local crackdowns, and as of 2023 a national standard for four-wheel low-speed vehicles was still being drafted.
To be road-legal a vehicle has to be in the national motor-vehicle catalogue with 3C certification, and the driver has to hold a driving licence.

a.text: Laotoule: the only car that runs on a battery and pure denial. No licence, no plates, no insurance. It's not a vehicle, it's witness protection with a windshield. It can't even be registered as a motor vehicle; the state looked at it and said, "We're not sure what that is either." Beijing announced the crackdown in July 2021 and gave it until the end of 2023. Two and a half years' warning, and these things still couldn't get off the road in time. Well, they *are* low-speed. As of 2023, the national standard for four-wheelers was still being drafted, so even the paperwork moves like a laotoule. To be road-legal you need the catalogue, 3C certification, and a licensed driver. The laotoule's answer: "Pick zero." They call it "old man's happiness." It's the only happiness you can't insure.

b.text: They call it "laotoule," Old Man's Joy, which is fair, because it brings joy to exactly one person: the old man. Everyone else on the road gets terror. It's a car the way a dumpling steamer is a sauna. Grandpa bought it because it needs no license, which is also the only reason he could buy it. Top speed: 50 kilometers an hour, top speed of judgment: zero. He drives it in the bike lane, the car lane, and occasionally the vegetable market. Crash rating? It's a lead-acid battery wrapped in a candy wrapper with a fake Mercedes grille. The charger is an extension cord dangling out of a fourth-floor window like Rapunzel's hair. And every afternoon at 4:30 there are three hundred of them parked outside the primary school, blinking hazards, blocking traffic, hauling one grandson and nine bags of discount cabbage.

facts: In March 2024 six ministries, led by the market regulator, issued the first national definition: pre-packaged dishes made industrially from agricultural produce, without preservatives, to be heated or cooked before eating.

Industry output passed 500 billion yuan in 2023.
A 2025 dispute between Luo Yonghao and the restaurant chain Xibei over whether its dishes were pre-made showed that no law defines 'pre-made' for restaurant labelling.

a.text: Look at you, ordering the 68-yuan "chef's signature" braised pork and calling it a night out. You came for wok hei; you got a guy named Microwave. Your food lands in four minutes and you say "wow, so efficient," like you didn't just tip a central kitchen three provinces away. What you're really after is the ambience: dim lights, a menu in calligraphy font, a Xiaohongshu post captioned "hidden gem." Hidden where? In a freezer truck. That "grandma's recipe" is served at four hundred branches. Your grandma is a logistics company. And you defend it! "At least it's hygienic." Sure. You paid sit-down prices to be the final step in a supply chain. Congratulations: you're not a diner, you're the delivery address.

b.text:
Pre-made dishes are the only cuisine where the chef's signature move is scissors. Somewhere a restaurant charges 68 yuan for "wok-fried" braised pork, and the only thing that wok ever touched was a vacuum bag doing laps in boiling water. The menu says "made fresh daily." Technically true: they open a fresh bag daily.

That broccoli on your plate was frozen two years ago. It's not a vegetable anymore; it's a time capsule. It was picked before your nephew learned to walk.

And the central kitchen! A thousand miles away, one guy in a hairnet cooks for forty cities, like a sad Santa delivering kung pao chicken.

My favorite is when the waiter swears it's not pre-made. Buddy, my fish-flavored pork came out in ninety seconds, flat on one side, and shaped exactly like the inside of a pouch.

facts: In April 2020 Luckin admitted fabricating 2.2 billion yuan of sales.
Its 2024 net revenue was 34.475 billion yuan, up 38.4 percent, with a net profit of 2.932 billion yuan.
It had 22,340 stores at the end of 2024 (14,591 company-run and 7,749 partner stores), 6,092 of them added that year, including 21 in Singapore.
Same-store sales at its own stores fell 16.7 percent in 2024 while it kept its 9.9-yuan deals.

a.text:
Luckin Coffee, you're the only coffee chain where the most creative blend was the 2019 sales numbers. Two billion yuan in transactions that never happened. Your accountants weren't making books, they were writing fan fiction. Muddy Waters published an 89-page short report on you, and honestly that's more pages than anyone's ever read of your menu.

Then you got delisted, fined, sent to the pink sheets... and came back with more stores in China than Starbucks. That's not a comeback, that's a horror franchise. You can't kill it, you can only download its app.

And your big redemption arc? A latte with Moutai in it. You looked at a company known for cooking the books and thought, "What this needs is baijiu at 9 a.m."

Now you're in New York. Americans, relax: the coconut latte is real. Probably. Check the receipt.

b.text:
Luckin Coffee.
In 2020 they admitted to faking 2.2 billion yuan in sales.
Everyone said: they're finished.

In 2024 they made 34.5 billion. Real money.
Turns out it was never fraud. It was a forecast.

Last year they opened 6,092 stores. Nearly seventeen a day.
Same-store sales at their own shops? Down 16.7 percent.
Every store sells less, so they open more stores.
Back then, when the numbers wouldn't grow, they made up sales.

Now they make up the difference in rent.

And the 9.9-yuan deal is still running.
A company lied to the entire stock market,
and you forgave it for under ten yuan.

Don't look at me like that.
That isn't brand loyalty.
That's your price.

Green is just orange that hasn't happened yet.

And tonight you'll still charge yours in the hallway. Relax. I won't tell anyone.

It will.

facts: In March 2021 Shanghai lawyer Liu Yuhang joined the 'bargain for free' promotion with a 'super free card', invited many friends to cut the price, and the progress bar stayed 0.9% short; he sued Pinduoduo for fraud.
In court Pinduoduo said the page shows only a limited number of digits: the displayed 0.9% was really 0.9996427%, a figure with at least six decimal places.
In July 2022 the Shanghai Changning court ruled at first instance that Pinduoduo had infringed the user's right to know and ordered it to pay him 400 yuan.
Pinduoduo was founded in 2015, listed on Nasdaq in 2018, and by 2021 had more users than any other e-commerce platform in mainland China; its overseas arm Temu launched in September 2022.

a.text: Pinduoduo's "bargain for free" is the only game where 0.9% is a permanent address. Lawyer Liu Yuhang rallied many friends, they cut and cut, and the progress bar parked itself 0.9% short like it had a reservation. Then Pinduoduo explained in court: relax, it wasn't 0.9%, it was 0.9996427%. Oh, wonderful. Not a wall, a wall with decimal places. That's not a progress bar; that's Zeno's paradox with a checkout button. You can halve the distance forever and never arrive, but your friends will hear about it every step of the way. The court ruled they'd infringed his right to know and ordered them to pay 400 yuan. Finally, someone got something free from Pinduoduo. It just took a lawsuit. Most users in mainland China, listed on Nasdaq, Temu going global, and still can't round up.

b.text:
Pinduoduo's "Bargain for Free" is the only shopping feature that turns your family WeChat group into a hostage negotiation. Nothing says "I love you, Grandma" like a 2 a.m. link begging her to "kan yi dao," one chop, for a free air fryer.

And it works! First click: 90% off. Second click: 98%. Then you hit 99.9% and the progress bar starts moving like it's paid by the hour. You're "only 0.01% away," the closest any human has ever come to infinity. Suddenly your gold coins turn into diamonds, the diamonds turn into "lucky fragments," and the app says you need *one new user* to finish.

One new user. So now you're out recruiting strangers like a pyramid scheme selling a single toothbrush.

Twelve hundred chops later, the air fryer's still at 0.01%. You never got it. But congratulations: you've stopped being the customer. You're the advertising.

a.text:
Kaoyan, you're an exam with a retention problem. From 2018 to 2022 you grew about 18 percent a year, like a startup promising everyone a master's degree and a future. Then you peaked at 4.74 million in 2023 and lost 860,000 people in two years. That's not a decline, that's a stampede toward the exit.

And who stayed? In 2024, 51.8 percent of your applicants were repeat candidates. 2.27 million people came back for more. You're not an exam anymore. You're a recurring subscription nobody remembers how to cancel.

Even fresh graduates are ghosting you: the share sitting the exam dropped from 45.27 percent to 37.15 percent in one year. Kaoyan, when more than half your crowd are returning customers and the new kids keep finding excuses not to show up, you're not a gateway. You're a reunion.
