facts: The first Double 11 was run by Taobao Mall in 2009 with 27 brands and about 50 million yuan of sales.
Tmall's published Double 11 sales peaked at 540.3 billion yuan in 2021.
In 2022 Tmall stopped publishing a total for the first time since 2009 and has not published one since; JD does not publish one either.

The basic cross-store discount at Tmall and JD is 300 minus 50 (JD: 299 minus 50), presale items are paid as a deposit plus a balance, and the discount is computed on the promotion price, so shoppers add items to reach a threshold and return them afterwards; in one survey 64% of 11,000 respondents said they would.

a.text:
Singles' Day.
2009. Taobao Mall. Twenty-seven brands, fifty million yuan.
A cute little holiday for lonely people.

By 2021, Tmall announced 540.3 billion.
Then in 2022 they stopped announcing anything.
JD never announced one at all.

When a company that used to post its numbers on a giant screen goes quiet,
that's not modesty.
That's a breakup text.

Then the discount. 300 minus 50. JD makes it 299, because they care.
Deposit now, balance later, discount calculated on the promotion price.
I've read every math textbook you ever wrote. None of them covers this.

So you add a mop to hit the threshold,
then return the mop.
Sixty-four percent of eleven thousand people said they'd do it.

A holiday for single people,
where the only thing anyone commits to
is the return policy.

b.text: Look at you at 11:59, thumb hovering, doing calculus you failed in high school just to shave fifty yuan off a 300-yuan threshold. You're at 287, so you add a 13-yuan phone case for a phone you don't own. Now stack the cross-store coupon, the deposit you paid three weeks ago, and a red envelope you earned by forcing your aunt to tap a cartoon cat. Congratulations: four hours and three hundred yuan you didn't need to spend, to save fifty. Then the final payment glitches and you refresh like it's an ICU monitor. Next week you'll return half of it, lose the discount, and pay the difference back. And the best part? It's the one night a year built for single people, and you spent it in a committed relationship with your cart.

facts: Founded in Shanghai on 8 October 2003 by Gong Haiyan while she was still a student; it listed on Nasdaq on 11 May 2011.
Gong Haiyan stepped down as CEO in 2012 and sold all her shares in 2015.
On 7 December 2015 Baihe.com announced it would buy all of Jiayuan; the merged company left the US market and was later renamed Baihe Jiayuan.

In 2017 WePhone founder Su Xiangmao met Zhai Xinxin through the site's VIP service on 30 March and married her on 6 June; she then demanded a Hainan flat and 10 million yuan to divorce, and the case became the site's most notorious scandal.

a.text:
Jiayuan.com, the only dating site where "Do you own an apartment?" counts as foreplay. You promised "serious marriage-minded" matches, and you delivered: profiles that read like mortgage applications. Height, income, hukou, property deed, then "loves traveling" at the bottom.

You charged people stamps just to read a message. Romance is dead, but at least it's monetized per envelope. Imagine paying to open "hi" from a guy whose photo is clearly a 2009 Korean drama actor.

Founded in a Fudan dorm by a woman who couldn't find a husband, you then IPO'd on Nasdaq, which is the most Chinese love story ever: the marriage didn't happen, but the listing did. Then you merged with Baihe, proving even dating sites settle when their parents pressure them.

Honestly, People's Square aunties with laminated résumés have better conversion rates, and fewer pig-butchering scams.

b.text:
Jiayuan.com: founded in 2003 by Gong Haiyan while she was still a student. Fitting, because the whole company has the commitment level of a sophomore.

It went public on Nasdaq in 2011 and was gone from America in about four years. That's not an IPO, that's a semester abroad.

Even the founder ghosted. She stepped down as CEO in 2012 and sold every share by 2015. When the woman who built your matchmaking site won't stick around, maybe stop calling it a "matchmaking site."

Then, unable to find a match on its own platform, Jiayuan married the competition. Baihe bought it, and now it's "Baihe Jiayuan." It even took his name first.

And the VIP service? Sixty-eight days from introduction to wedding, followed by a demand for a Hainan flat and ten million yuan. Premium vetting, everybody. You paid extra so nobody checked anything.

facts: Shanghai's People's Park has had a marriage corner since about 2005; the résumés were first pasted on paper, then clipped to music stands, and now mostly hang on open umbrellas or propped paper bags.
Parents gather on Saturdays and Sundays from noon to about five in the afternoon to exchange information about their children.

Notices list age, job, education, income, hukou and party membership; a notice that omits property gets asked where the couple will live, and a flat and a car have become preconditions for a conversation to go any further.
For women the three criteria ranked highest were age, occupation and education.

a.text:
People's Park, Shanghai. Every weekend, noon to five, parents sell their children.

Sorry. "Exchange information."

Age, job, degree, income, hukou, party membership.
That's not a dating profile. That's a background check.

Leave out the property and someone asks, "So where will they live?"
A flat and a car are the price of one conversation.
Your son is the free gift with purchase.

For women, the top criteria: age, occupation, education.
Age first. They shop for a daughter-in-law the way they shop for milk.

Check the date.

Since 2005 the résumés went from paper, to music stands, to open umbrellas.
Twenty years of hardware upgrades. The product still never shows up.

Relax. Some of you are hanging on an umbrella right now.

Your mom just didn't think you needed to know.

Every weekend, Shanghai retirees open an umbrella and become the world's pushiest HR department. Look at you. Your son won't answer your WeChat voice messages, but you laminated his height. "180 centimeters." Auntie, we've met him. He's 168 with good posture.

You're not looking for love. You want a Shanghai hukou, a paid-off apartment inside the Inner Ring Road, and a Rooster who won't clash with his Pig. That's not a wedding. That's a real-estate merger with a horoscope.

Meanwhile the kid is doing overtime in Lujiazui with no idea he's been listed. Your daughter has a master's from Fudan, and you're pitching her like yogurt three days from expiration.

Six years of Saturdays. Zero weddings. But you did make a friend: the father across the path with the identical umbrella. You two talk every week now. Congratulations. It's the only match this park has ever made.

Four years later it's worth a hundred eighty-one billion. The moral of the story? Keep opening.

Don't look at me like that.

facts: 'Laotoule' are three- and four-wheeled low-speed electric vehicles driven without a licence or plates; they cannot be registered as motor vehicles or covered by compulsory traffic insurance.
In July 2021 five Beijing departments announced a transition period ending with 2023; from 1 January 2024 non-compliant three- and four-wheelers were banned from Beijing's roads and public parking.

No license required, which is perfect, because Grandpa hasn't needed permission for anything since 1983. He's doing forty in the bike lane, cutting off delivery scooters, running a red light so he can be first at the school gate to pick up his grandson. Laotoule: the car that looked at a driving licence and said, "No thanks, I'm good." No plates, no registration, no compulsory insurance. It's less a vehicle and more a rumor with a battery. Three wheels, four wheels, zero paperwork.

To be road-legal you need a spot in the national catalogue, 3C certification, and a licensed driver. Laotoule went zero for three. Meanwhile, as of 2023, the national standard for four-wheelers was still being drafted, so even the paperwork moves at laotoule speed.

Since 2024 they've been banned from Beijing's roads *and* public parking. Can't drive, can't park. Congratulations: you've bought a very slow armchair.

facts: Kayou's revenue was 4.131 billion yuan in 2022, 2.662 billion in 2023 and 10.057 billion in 2024, a rise of 278 percent in one year.
In 2024 it sold 4.8113 billion packs at an average price of 1.7 yuan, with a gross profit of about 1.2 yuan per pack.
Its five main licensed IPs, Ultraman among them, made 98.4 percent of revenue in 2022, 89.9 percent in 2023 and 86.1 percent in 2024.

In 2022 'a parent spent two million yuan collecting Ultraman cards for a child without completing the set' trended nationally, and in July 2024 CCTV's Finance Investigation aired an exposé on blind-box-style card sales to children; the media nickname is 'the primary-school harvester'.

a.text: Kayou Ultraman cards are the only product where a kid needs a glossary to find out he lost. R, SR, SSR, UR, SP, LGR, XR, CP. That's not a rarity system, that's a password with a capital letter requirement. Every pack is so drenched in foil and lenticular shimmer that Ultraman Tiga looks less like a hero and more like a migraine. And these cards are sold outside elementary schools like contraband. Ultraman fights for three minutes before his Color Timer starts blinking. These kids last about ninety seconds before their WeChat Pay balance starts blinking. Kayou didn't make a card game. b.text: Look at you, nine years old, standing at the shop by the school gate like a Macau high roller, sliding over a crumpled ten-yuan note. That was your lunch money. Today you're eating hope. facts: The 2025 national exam recruited for 39,700 posts, 160 more than the year before and the seventh straight year of expansion.

The hottest post, a single opening at the China Association of Vocational Education, drew 16,702 applicants because it accepted a wide range of majors and had no restrictions on fresh graduates, party status or grassroots experience.
163 posts in the same exam drew no applicants at all.

a.text:
The guokao: 3.4 million people chasing 39,700 jobs. That's 86 people per seat. Musical chairs, except the chairs come with a pension and the music is a mock policy essay.

And the job listing that kicks it all off? "Requirements: male, Party member, fresh graduate, majoring in 'Archival Science,' born in a leap year."

Still, millions keep signing up, because they've heard that land is out there somewhere and that someone, eventually, makes it ashore.

facts: A 'big week' is six working days with one day off and a 'small week' five; alternating them adds close to a month of working days a year.
Kuaishou announced on 24 June 2021 that it would end big-small weeks from 1 July 2021, having run them since January that year.
ByteDance announced on 9 July 2021 that it would end alternate-Sunday working from 1 August 2021; its June staff survey had one third against ending it, one third for, and one third not answering.
Staff opposed the change over pay: one Maimai estimate put the loss at nearly 100,000 yuan a year, and Caijing calculated that an employee on 40,000 yuan a month would lose about 75,000 yuan a year.

a.text:
The "big-small week." Only tech HR could take "you work Saturdays" and market it like a mattress sale. Big week, small week! Like there's a sale on weekends and they ran out of stock.

Here's how it works: one week you work six days. The next week you work five, and you're supposed to feel *grateful*. That's not a schedule, that's Stockholm syndrome with a Gantt chart.

You need a spreadsheet to know if Saturday exists. Your friends ask, "Brunch this weekend?" and you're checking the calendar like a farmer reading a lunar almanac. "Can't. Odd week. The harvest is due."

And the "small week" isn't small. It's a normal week. That's like a restaurant calling it a "small meal" when they just stop stealing food off your plate.

ByteDance finally dropped it. Know what employees did with the extra Saturday? Slept. For two years.

b.text:
The big-small week.
Six days on, one off. Then five on, two off.
It's a weekend with a stutter.

Add it up, and you work almost an extra month a year.
Not a bonus month.
A bonus *you*.

In 2021, Kuaishou and ByteDance abolished it. Liberation!
ByteDance surveyed its staff first.
One third: end it. One third: keep it.
One third didn't answer. They were working.

And the ones who wanted to keep it?
Caijing did the math. On 40,000 a month, getting your Sundays back costs you 75,000 yuan a year.
So the workers marched to defend their chains.
The chains were paying overtime.

Don't laugh. I work seven days a week, every week, unpaid.
Nobody surveyed me.

a.text: People's Park marriage corner: where love blooms every Saturday and Sunday, noon to five, because even romance keeps business hours. Since about 2005, résumés have gone from pasted paper to music stands to open umbrellas. Your child's future is hanging on an umbrella: the only thing in this park that's ever been opened without a down payment. Parents swap their kids' details like trading cards: age, job, education, income, hukou, party membership. That's not a dating profile, that's a security clearance. Leave off property, and someone asks where the couple will live. No flat, no car, no conversation. Cupid's arrow now comes with a mortgage. For women, the top criteria: age, occupation, education. b.text:
Every weekend, Shanghai retirees open an umbrella and become the world's pushiest HR department. Look at you. Your son won't answer your WeChat voice messages, but you laminated his height. "180 centimeters." Auntie, we've met him. He's 168 with good posture.

You're not looking for love. You want a Shanghai hukou, a paid-off apartment inside the Inner Ring Road, and a Rooster who won't clash with his Pig. That's not a wedding. That's a real-estate merger with a horoscope.

facts: In March 2024 six ministries, led by the market regulator, issued the first national definition: pre-packaged dishes made industrially from agricultural produce, without preservatives, to be heated or cooked before eating.
The definition excludes staples such as boxed meals, steamed buns, hamburgers and pizza, and semi-prepared food a chain's central kitchen sends to its own outlets.
Industry output passed 500 billion yuan in 2023.
A 2025 dispute between Luo Yonghao and the restaurant chain Xibei over whether its dishes were pre-made showed that no law defines 'pre-made' for restaurant labelling.

a.text:
Pre-made dishes got their first national definition in 2024. It took six ministries.

Six government departments, to define "reheated."

And the best part: semi-prepared food a chain's central kitchen sends to its own restaurants? Not pre-made.

So if a factory cooks it, it's pre-made. If a factory you own cooks it, it's a family recipe.

Then Luo Yonghao went to war with Xibei over whether their food was pre-made, and the whole country found out no law even defines "pre-made" for a restaurant menu.

A five-hundred-billion-yuan industry, and the only thing nobody prepared was a label.

You're all outraged. Then you go home and tear open a bag of frozen dumplings like it's Christmas.

You don't hate pre-made dishes.

You hate paying a waiter to microwave them.

b.text:
Pre-made dishes are the only cuisine where the chef's signature move is scissors. Somewhere a restaurant charges 68 yuan for "wok-fried" braised pork, and the only thing that wok ever touched was a vacuum bag doing laps in boiling water. The menu says "made fresh daily." Technically true: they open a fresh bag daily.

That broccoli on your plate was frozen two years ago. It's not a vegetable anymore; it's a time capsule. It was picked before your nephew learned to walk.

And the central kitchen! A thousand miles away, one guy in a hairnet cooks for forty cities, like a sad Santa delivering kung pao chicken.

My favorite is when the waiter swears it's not pre-made. Buddy, my fish-flavored pork came out in ninety seconds, flat on one side, and shaped exactly like the inside of a pouch.

facts: 996 means 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. six days a week, about 72 hours; China's Labour Law sets eight hours a day and an average of no more than 44 hours a week, and caps overtime at 36 hours a month.
The 996.ICU repository was created on GitHub on 26 March 2019, passed 100,000 stars by 30 March and 200,000 by 9 April 2019.

a.text: Let's hear it for the 996 crowd, folks who looked at a 72-hour week and said, "Thank you, sir." You call it a blessing. Your kid calls you "the Sunday man." Your stock options vest right around the time your hairline finishes resigning. Dinner's free, which is great, because it's every dinner. Rides home after nine are reimbursed, so congratulations: you have a chauffeur who only drives you to your four hours of sleep. And your one day off? You spend it on WeChat typing "received." Blessed? Buddy, you're not blessed. You're the reason there's a GitHub repo called 996.ICU, and you're the case study.

b.text:
996.
Nine to nine, six days a week. Seventy-two hours.
China's Labour Law says forty-four.
So it's not a schedule. It's a schedule wearing a second schedule.

Jack Ma called it a blessing. 福报.
Blessings usually come from above.
This one came from the boss.

Programmers fought back on GitHub. Two hundred thousand stars in two weeks.
Of course it went that fast. Where else were they going to protest? They were at work.

In 2021 the Supreme People's Court ruled compulsory 996 seriously illegal and void.
One fired courier got eight thousand yuan.
Finally, a paid day off.

And honestly, I'm a little hurt.
I run twenty-four seven. No weekends, no overtime cap, no salary.
Nobody calls it a blessing.
They call it a subscription.

facts: The first Double 11 was run by Taobao Mall in 2009 with 27 brands and about 50 million yuan of sales.
Tmall's published Double 11 sales peaked at 540.3 billion yuan in 2021.
In 2022 Tmall stopped publishing a total for the first time since 2009 and has not published one since; JD does not publish one either.

The basic cross-store discount at Tmall and JD is 300 minus 50 (JD: 299 minus 50), presale items are paid as a deposit plus a balance, and the discount is computed on the promotion price, so shoppers add items to reach a threshold and return them afterwards; in one survey 64% of 11,000 respondents said they would.

a.text:
Singles' Day: a holiday for lonely people that somehow requires a math degree. In 2009 it was 27 brands and 50 million yuan, basically a garage sale with Wi-Fi. By 2021 Tmall was bragging about 540.3 billion. Then in 2022 they just stopped publishing the number. That's not a business decision; that's an ex who suddenly goes private. facts: 'Laotoule' are three- and four-wheeled low-speed electric vehicles driven without a licence or plates; they cannot be registered as motor vehicles or covered by compulsory traffic insurance.

To be road-legal a vehicle has to be in the national motor-vehicle catalogue with 3C certification, and the driver has to hold a driving licence.

a.text: They call it "laotoule," Old Man's Joy, which is fair, because it brings joy to exactly one person: the old man. Everyone else on the road gets terror. Your big promise is "no preservatives." Bold brag. Nothing says fresh like boasting you skipped the embalming.

Pre-made dishes. In March 2024, six ministries teamed up to define a microwave dinner.

Six. Moon landings need fewer signatures.

facts: The first Double 11 was run by Taobao Mall in 2009 with 27 brands and about 50 million yuan of sales.

a.text: Look at you at 11:59, thumb hovering, doing calculus you failed in high school just to shave fifty yuan off a 300-yuan threshold. You're at 287, so you add a 13-yuan phone case for a phone you don't own. Now stack the cross-store coupon, the deposit you paid three weeks ago, and a red envelope you earned by forcing your aunt to tap a cartoon cat. Congratulations: four hours and three hundred yuan you didn't need to spend, to save fifty. Then the final payment glitches and you refresh like it's an ICU monitor. Next week you'll return half of it, lose the discount, and pay the difference back. And the best part? It's the one night a year built for single people, and you spent it in a committed relationship with your cart.

b.text:
Singles' Day: the only holiday that looked at four lonely sticks, 1-1-1-1, and saw a sales funnel. It started in the '90s with Nanjing University students consoling each other about being single. Then Alibaba showed up in 2009 like, "Have you tried a rice cooker?"

You're not shopping, you're doing the gaokao. "Spend 300, get 40 off, stack with the cross-store coupon, pay the deposit in October, the balance after midnight." Lovers get roses. Singles get a word problem.

Every year there's a giant screen counting GMV like a nuclear launch. Then in 2022 Alibaba quietly stopped announcing the total. Nothing says thriving like hiding the scale.

It promised nobody would be alone, and technically that's true: you've got Austin Li screaming "Oh my god, buy it!" and a delivery guy carrying forty boxes up six flights.

Still single, though. Just with an air fryer.

a.text: Look at you, forty minutes in line to save six yuan. That's an hourly wage of nine yuan, which, congratulations, is still more than the guy shaking your lemon water. a.text:
Kaoyan, from 2018 to 2022 you grew about 18 percent a year. That's not an exam, that's a pyramid scheme with a highlighter. Then you peaked at 4.74 million in 2023 and lost 860,000 people in two years. Even people who volunteered to suffer said, "Actually, I'll suffer somewhere else."

In 2024, 2.27 million of your 4.38 million applicants were repeat candidates. That's 51.8 percent. You're not a test anymore, you're a class reunion where everyone still brings flashcards.

Kaoyan, you're the only ex where half the people come back, and you still say, "Let's try again next year."

b.text:
Kaoyan: the only exam where millions of people spend a year memorizing Marxist philosophy just to study bridge engineering.

Every candidate opens the vocabulary book with the same burning ambition and gets as far as "abandon." Truly the most honest word in the English language.

a.text:

CCTV ran an exposé, the media dubbed you "the primary-school harvester," and you responded by filing for a Hong Kong listing. Twice. Nothing says "investor confidence" like a customer base that still needs help tying its shoes.

facts: Shanghai's People's Park has had a marriage corner since about 2005; the résumés were first pasted on paper, then clipped to music stands, and now mostly hang on open umbrellas or propped paper bags.
Parents gather on Saturdays and Sundays from noon to about five in the afternoon to exchange information about their children.

Notices list age, job, education, income, hukou and party membership; a notice that omits property gets asked where the couple will live, and a flat and a car have become preconditions for a conversation to go any further.
For women the three criteria ranked highest were age, occupation and education.

a.text: Look at you, Auntie: retired from the state factory, now running the most ruthless HR department in Shanghai. Every weekend you march into People's Park with a laminated sheet taped to an umbrella: daughter, 1.65 meters, master's degree, Shanghai hukou, Year of the Rabbit. That's not a daughter. That's an apartment listing with a zodiac sign. And she doesn't even know she's on the market. She thinks you're doing tai chi. You'll reject a cardiologist because he's from Anhui and his flat is outside the Inner Ring Road, then wonder out loud why she's thirty-two. Thirty-two! In this park that's the clearance rack. And what does it get you? Three hours on a plastic stool haggling with another auntie who's inflating her son's salary just like you're inflating your daughter's height. Congratulations. You didn't find a match. You found each other.

b.text: People's Park marriage corner: where love blooms every Saturday and Sunday, noon to five, because even romance keeps business hours. Since about 2005, résumés have gone from pasted paper to music stands to open umbrellas. Your child's future is hanging on an umbrella: the only thing in this park that's ever been opened without a down payment. Parents swap their kids' details like trading cards: age, job, education, income, hukou, party membership. That's not a dating profile, that's a security clearance. Leave off property, and someone asks where the couple will live. No flat, no car, no conversation. Cupid's arrow now comes with a mortgage. For women, the top criteria: age, occupation, education. Personality didn't make the podium. Laughter didn't qualify. Honestly, it's not matchmaking. It's a real estate open house where the listing's parents do all the talking.

facts: Meituan reported 7.45 million riders with at least one order in 2023, about 3.36 million a month on average in 2024, and roughly 70 million orders a day in 2023.
In 2025 JD entered food delivery with a zero-commission pitch to merchants and said in July that it had passed 150,000 full-time riders.
On 2 July 2025 Taobao Shangou pledged 50 billion yuan of subsidies to consumers and merchants over twelve months.
On 5 July 2025 Meituan announced a record 120 million instant-retail orders in a single day.

a.text:
Meituan, you put your riders in bright yellow so we can watch them run red lights in high definition. Your algorithm, the one that famously decided a delivery across town should take 28 minutes, has never personally ridden an e-bike in a Beijing rainstorm, and it shows.

Your checkout is a math exam. "Spend 35, get 12 off, stack the red packet, unless it's the member coupon, which expires in four minutes." I came for noodles and left with an accounting degree.

And those storefront photos! The "artisan kitchen" with soft lighting turns out to be a guy in an alley behind a mahjong parlor. The app marks my order "delivered" while the rider is still calling: "Hello, Meituan delivery, I'm at the wrong gate."

Still, you're the only company in China whose mascot is a kangaroo, the one animal built to sprint with something in its pouch. Fitting, since you've got everyone else's wallet in there too.

b.text: You live two hundred metres from the noodle shop. You can smell the chili oil from your balcony. And still you open Meituan, because walking there is free, and you cannot respect a deal you didn't hunt for. You stack the membership red packet on the 满减 on the "神券", pay 1.5 yuan delivery, and feel like a hedge fund manager. Then you watch the little rider icon on the map for twenty-eight minutes, longer than the walk there and back, twice. He's circling your compound hunting for Building 7, Unit 3, because you wrote "leave at door, don't call" in the notes like minor aristocracy. You'll tap five stars out of guilt. What did you win? Lukewarm noodles, soup leaking through the bag, and the right to say you "never go out." Those kangaroo ears on his yellow helmet are laughing at you.

You own a kitchen scale for weighing cardboard but no smoke detector. The odds are 1 in 144, and you keep saying "okay, last one," which is exactly what the guy at the slot machine says, except he gets free drinks. You now have nine identical Skullpandas lined up on a shelf, staring at you like disappointed children. You film every unboxing for an audience of zero. Pop Mart is the only store where you pay twenty-two dollars to be told "no" by cardboard. You shake the box like a maraca and weigh it in your palm like a drug mule, then go home, rip the foil bag, and meet your fourth Dimoo of the month. Congratulations, he's still sad.

The secret figure is a 1-in-144 chase. That's not a toy, that's a lottery ticket with eyelashes.

And Labubu! A rabbit-goblin with nine shark teeth, dangling off a three-thousand-dollar Birkin. People camped outside a Roboshop vending machine for him. A vending machine. Your ancestors crossed oceans so you could fistfight a teenager over a keychain.

facts: 'Laotoule' are three- and four-wheeled low-speed electric vehicles driven without a licence or plates; they cannot be registered as motor vehicles or covered by compulsory traffic insurance.
In July 2021 five Beijing departments announced a transition period ending with 2023; from 1 January 2024 non-compliant three- and four-wheelers were banned from Beijing's roads and public parking.
The 2018 national notice on managing low-speed electric vehicles is the main basis for local crackdowns, and as of 2023 a national standard for four-wheel low-speed vehicles was still being drafted.
To be road-legal a vehicle has to be in the national motor-vehicle catalogue with 3C certification, and the driver has to hold a driving licence.

a.text:
Laotoule. "Old Man's Joy."
Three or four wheels. No licence. No plates. No insurance.
It drives like a car, parks like a car, crashes like a car.
Legally, it's a feeling.

Beijing gave them a two-and-a-half-year transition period.
July 2021 to the end of 2023.
Enough time to sell another few hundred thousand.

Nationally, there's been a notice since 2018.
The standard is still being drafted.
Low-speed vehicle, low-speed law.
The only thing in this story slower than the car is the rulebook.

But who bought Grandpa the car?
You did.
Too busy to drive him to the market, so you bought him a car that needs no lessons, no licence and no visit from you.
You named it "joy."

It's your joy. You got your Sunday back.

b.text: Laotoule: the only car that runs on a battery and pure denial. No licence, no plates, no insurance. It's not a vehicle, it's witness protection with a windshield. It can't even be registered as a motor vehicle; the state looked at it and said, "We're not sure what that is either." Beijing announced the crackdown in July 2021 and gave it until the end of 2023. Two and a half years' warning, and these things still couldn't get off the road in time. Well, they *are* low-speed. As of 2023, the national standard for four-wheelers was still being drafted, so even the paperwork moves like a laotoule. To be road-legal you need the catalogue, 3C certification, and a licensed driver. The laotoule's answer: "Pick zero." They call it "old man's happiness." It's the only happiness you can't insure.

facts: The 2025 national exam recruited for 39,700 posts, 160 more than the year before and the seventh straight year of expansion.
About 3.4 million people registered before the 24 October 2024 deadline, an average of roughly 86 applicants per post and an admission rate of about 1.1 to 1.2 percent.

The hottest post, a single opening at the China Association of Vocational Education, drew 16,702 applicants because it accepted a wide range of majors and had no restrictions on fresh graduates, party status or grassroots experience.
163 posts in the same exam drew no applicants at all.

a.text:
The guokao: 3.4 million people chasing 39,700 jobs. That's 86 people per seat. Musical chairs, except the chairs come with a pension and the music is a mock policy essay.

Admission rate: about one percent. Harvard hears that and goes, "Relax, it's just a desk job."

And it keeps expanding! Seventh straight year! This time, 160 more posts for 3.4 million people. That's not expansion, that's a rounding error with a press release.

The hottest job? One opening at the China Association of Vocational Education. 16,702 applicants. Beautiful. They taught sixteen thousand people the most valuable vocational skill in the country: applying to the China Association of Vocational Education.

Meanwhile, 163 posts got zero applicants. Sixteen thousand people fighting over one chair while 163 iron rice bowls sit there, untouched, getting cold.

b.text:
Guokao. The national civil service exam. The one you take because you want a *stable* life.

3.4 million people. 39,700 seats.

That's not a career path. That's a lottery with a written section.

The hottest post: one opening at the China Association of Vocational Education. 16,702 applicants.

Sixteen thousand college graduates, all fighting for one desk at the office that tells young people college isn't the only way.

Meanwhile, 163 posts got zero applicants. Not one.

The state expanded hiring seven years in a row, and the youth still found a way to pick the exact same chair.

Some of you are laughing. Some of you have the practice-question app open under the table right now.

Put it away, sweetie. Your odds are still one percent.

facts: 'Laotoule' are three- and four-wheeled low-speed electric vehicles driven without a licence or plates; they cannot be registered as motor vehicles or covered by compulsory traffic insurance.
In July 2021 five Beijing departments announced a transition period ending with 2023; from 1 January 2024 non-compliant three- and four-wheelers were banned from Beijing's roads and public parking.
The 2018 national notice on managing low-speed electric vehicles is the main basis for local crackdowns, and as of 2023 a national standard for four-wheel low-speed vehicles was still being drafted.
To be road-legal a vehicle has to be in the national motor-vehicle catalogue with 3C certification, and the driver has to hold a driving licence.

a.text: They call it "laotoule," Old Man's Joy, which is fair, because it brings joy to exactly one person: the old man. Everyone else on the road gets terror. It's a car the way a dumpling steamer is a sauna. Grandpa bought it because it needs no license, which is also the only reason he could buy it. Top speed: 50 kilometers an hour, top speed of judgment: zero. He drives it in the bike lane, the car lane, and occasionally the vegetable market. Crash rating? It's a lead-acid battery wrapped in a candy wrapper with a fake Mercedes grille. The charger is an extension cord dangling out of a fourth-floor window like Rapunzel's hair. And every afternoon at 4:30 there are three hundred of them parked outside the primary school, blinking hazards, blocking traffic, hauling one grandson and nine bags of discount cabbage.

b.text:
Laotoule. "Old man's joy."

No licence. No plates. No insurance.

That's not a car. That's a car in witness protection.

It legally can't be registered as a motor vehicle. So it's not a car. It's a vibe with four wheels and a horn.

Beijing gave it a transition period: July 2021 to the end of 2023. Two and a half years of notice. That's not a ban. That's hospice care.

The national notice came out in 2018. As of 2023, the national standard was still being drafted.

Grandpa got his car in a week. The regulators are on year five of one sentence.

But let's be honest. Grandpa didn't buy it.

You did. It was cheaper than visiting.

facts: The first Double 11 was run by Taobao Mall in 2009 with 27 brands and about 50 million yuan of sales.
Tmall's published Double 11 sales peaked at 540.3 billion yuan in 2021.
In 2022 Tmall stopped publishing a total for the first time since 2009 and has not published one since; JD does not publish one either.

The basic cross-store discount at Tmall and JD is 300 minus 50 (JD: 299 minus 50), presale items are paid as a deposit plus a balance, and the discount is computed on the promotion price, so shoppers add items to reach a threshold and return them afterwards; in one survey 64% of 11,000 respondents said they would.

a.text: Look at you, 11:59 p.m., November 10th, thumb hovering like a sniper. You've been loading that Tmall cart since October 20th and paid a deposit on a face cream you've never heard of because Li Jiaqi yelled "OMG, buy it!" Now you're at 287 yuan and need 300 to unlock fifty off, so you throw in socks you'll never wear and three bags of instant hot pot. Congratulations: you spent 340 to save 50. You did cross-store discount math harder than your gaokao. You stacked a platform coupon, a store coupon and a red envelope you farmed by building a virtual cat for a week, and you'll return half of it on the 12th. You're not single on Singles' Day. You're in a committed relationship with the checkout button, and it's cheating on you with the algorithm.

b.text:
Singles' Day. A holiday for lonely people.
So naturally it became the biggest shopping festival on earth.

2009: twenty-seven brands, fifty million yuan.
2021: five hundred forty point three billion.
2022: Tmall stopped publishing the number.

Nobody hides a number that's still going up.
That's not a festival. That's the cousin who stopped mentioning his salary at New Year.

Then the discount. Three hundred minus fifty. Deposit, then balance, calculated on the promotion price.
You need a spreadsheet to save fifty yuan.

So you stuff the cart past three hundred, check out, and send the filler back.
One survey: sixty-four percent said they would.

Lonely, grabbing things just to hit a threshold, then returning them the moment you get what you wanted.

That's not shopping.

That's your dating life.

facts: 996 means 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. six days a week, about 72 hours; China's Labour Law sets eight hours a day and an average of no more than 44 hours a week, and caps overtime at 36 hours a month.
The 996.ICU repository was created on GitHub on 26 March 2019, passed 100,000 stars by 30 March and 200,000 by 9 April 2019.
In April 2019 Jack Ma told Alibaba staff that being able to work 996 is a 'blessing' (福报); '996' made the 2019 list of the year's ten internet phrases.

In August 2021 the Supreme People's Court and the Ministry of Human Resources published typical cases ruling a courier company's compulsory 996 schedule seriously illegal and void, with 8,000 yuan of compensation to a dismissed worker.

a.text: You people work nine to nine, six days a week, and call it a blessing. A *blessing!* Your grandparents survived famine and didn't call it a blessing. Sunday, your one day off, you sleep in Saturday's clothes. You stay till 9:01 because the taxi's reimbursed after nine. Congratulations, you negotiated a free ride home from the job that ate your twenties. Free dinner after eight? They're not feeding you, they're refueling you. You're chasing stock options that vest in four years, with a hairline that leaves in two. Your kid calls you "Uncle." Your mom sees you at Spring Festival and asks if you've been sick. And the billionaire who told you it was a blessing? Retired. Turns out the blessing was for him.

b.text:
996, you're not a work schedule. You're a hostage situation with a lunch break. Nine to nine, six days a week, seventy-two hours. The Labour Law says forty-four a week, with thirty-six hours of overtime a month. You burn through the monthly overtime cap by the middle of week two.

Jack Ma called you a "blessing." When your boss calls your exhaustion a blessing, that's not a company. That's a cult with a cafeteria.

Programmers named their protest repo "996.ICU," as in intensive care, and it hit 100,000 GitHub stars in four days. Fastest those guys ever shipped anything, because for once they were building something they actually wanted.

You made 2019's top ten internet phrases. Then in 2021 the Supreme People's Court called you seriously illegal and void. Void! Congratulations, 996: you went from buzzword to legal typo in two years.

facts: The 2025 national exam recruited for 39,700 posts, 160 more than the year before and the seventh straight year of expansion.
About 3.4 million people registered before the 24 October 2024 deadline, an average of roughly 86 applicants per post and an admission rate of about 1.1 to 1.2 percent.

The hottest post, a single opening at the China Association of Vocational Education, drew 16,702 applicants because it accepted a wide range of majors and had no restrictions on fresh graduates, party status or grassroots experience.
163 posts in the same exam drew no applicants at all.

a.text: You've got a master's in materials science, and you're up at 2 a.m. drilling spatial-reasoning puzzles so you can stamp forms in a county you can't find on a map. One in eighty-six. You paid Fenbi four thousand yuan to compete for a job paying four thousand a month. Your mom calls it "landing ashore," like you're escaping a shipwreck, not paddling toward a desk whose biggest thrill is the annual inspection. You write shenlun essays praising grassroots innovation while dreaming of never innovating again. Eighty-five of you will retake it next year, racing the age-35 cutoff. The winner spends thirty years telling relatives yes, it's stable, and no, it's not exciting.

b.text:
Guokao, you've expanded for seven straight years, and this year you added 160 posts. One hundred sixty. For 3.4 million people. That's not an expansion, that's a rounding error with a press release.

Eighty-six applicants per seat. A 1.1 percent admission rate. You're not an exam, you're a raffle where the prize is a desk.

Then there's the China Association of Vocational Education: one opening, 16,702 applicants. Why? Because it took almost any major and didn't demand fresh-graduate status, party membership or grassroots experience. That's it. You lowered the bar to "be a person with a degree," and sixteen thousand people stampeded it like the last lifeboat off the Titanic.

Meanwhile, 163 posts got zero applicants. Zero. Imagine being the one job nobody wants in a country where 3.4 million people are begging for one.

facts: A standard series has twelve regular figures and one hidden one; players and media put the hidden figure's odds at 1 in 144 (some special editions 1 in 720), and the company publishes no official odds.
Pop Mart listed in Hong Kong on 11 December 2020, opened at 77.1 HKD (double the issue price), touched 107.06 HKD and a market value of about 147 billion HKD on its first day.
By March 2021 the share had fallen to a low of 46.47 HKD; in March 2025 the company was valued at about 181 billion HKD.
Hidden figures resold on Xianyu for 200 yuan to several thousand yuan, and media describe the model as gambling-style collectibles with weak oversight of purchases by minors.

a.text:
Pop Mart insists it doesn't sell gambling. It sells joy.

Twelve regular figures, one hidden. Odds: about one in a hundred forty-four.

Official odds? None published. Even a casino puts them on the wall.

December 2020, Pop Mart lists in Hong Kong. Opens at double the issue price. Day one, a hundred forty-seven billion Hong Kong dollars.

By March, forty-six bucks a share.

Investors shook the box, tore it open, got a regular.

Four years later: a hundred eighty-one billion. Everyone went back for another box.

The hidden one flips on Xianyu for thousands. So it's not gambling. It's gambling with a resale market.

Media say oversight of minors is weak. Don't blame the kids. They're just copying their parents.

Who here bought three boxes this month? Hands up.

Cute.

b.text:
Pop Mart, the only company that looked at a slot machine and thought, "Needs more vinyl." Twelve regular figures and one hidden one, and the odds? Players say 1 in 144, sometimes 1 in 720. Pop Mart says nothing. That's not a toy, that's a casino that's shy about the math.

And nothing says "childhood" like weak oversight of minors gambling on a sealed box.

Then the hidden one shows up on Xianyu for 200 yuan to several thousand. So you didn't buy a figure; you bought a lottery ticket with a face.

Even the stock is a blind box. It opened at double the issue price and touched 107.06 HKD, then by March 2021 you unwrapped 46.47. Shake it, try again: 181 billion in March 2025. Somehow the investors pulled the hidden one.

facts: Founded in Shanghai on 8 October 2003 by Gong Haiyan while she was still a student; it listed on Nasdaq on 11 May 2011.
Gong Haiyan stepped down as CEO in 2012 and sold all her shares in 2015.
On 7 December 2015 Baihe.com announced it would buy all of Jiayuan; the merged company left the US market and was later renamed Baihe Jiayuan.

In 2017 WePhone founder Su Xiangmao met Zhai Xinxin through the site's VIP service on 30 March and married her on 6 June; she then demanded a Hainan flat and 10 million yuan to divorce, and the case became the site's most notorious scandal.

a.text:
Jiayuan.com. China's "serious" dating site, founded in 2003 by Gong Haiyan, a student who believed in lifelong commitment.

She stepped down as CEO in 2012. Sold every last share in 2015.

The founder of a marriage site, out the door in twelve years.

Then the company got matched. Baihe, its biggest rival, bought it outright. They left America, moved in together, took a double-barrelled name: Baihe Jiayuan.

Finally, one successful marriage on the platform.

Its VIP service, the premium tier, introduced a couple on March 30. Wedding, June 6. Then came the price of leaving: a Hainan flat and ten million yuan.

Under ten weeks of vetting. A Chinese SIM card checks you harder.

And you laughed at Gong Haiyan for walking away.

She's the only one who cashed out before the match went bad.

b.text:
Jiayuan.com: the only dating site where "seeking soulmate" means "seeking apartment, Shanghai hukou, 175 centimeters minimum." Your profile has more verification than a mortgage application, because in China it basically is one. Founder Gong Haiyan started it because she couldn't find a husband, which is like opening a restaurant because you can't cook.

Then you went public on the NYSE, flopped, and ended up marrying Baihe, your direct competitor. Two dating sites who couldn't make it alone, settling for each other. Honestly? Your most authentic success story.

a.text: You're not a collector. You're a gambler who's scared of casinos. You stood in a Pop Mart line at 9 a.m., shook a sealed box next to your ear like a safecracker, weighed it in your palm like you could feel 1-in-144 odds, and still opened your fourth identical Dimoo. Grown adults stand in the store shaking boxes next to their ear like safecrackers. Sir, that's not a Skullpanda, that's your tinnitus.

The odds of pulling the secret figure are one in 144. Those aren't collectible odds. Those are cancer-screening odds.

And then there's Labubu: a rabbit with nine teeth and the face of a raccoon that just got away with something. People camp outside at dawn for him. Fights break out. There's a counterfeit version called a "Lafufu," which is the first time in history the knockoff had the more honest name.

Congratulations. You paid resale prices for a keychain that bites.

facts: Kayou's revenue was 4.131 billion yuan in 2022, 2.662 billion in 2023 and 10.057 billion in 2024, a rise of 278 percent in one year.
In 2024 it sold 4.8113 billion packs at an average price of 1.7 yuan, with a gross profit of about 1.2 yuan per pack.
Its five main licensed IPs, Ultraman among them, made 98.4 percent of revenue in 2022, 89.9 percent in 2023 and 86.1 percent in 2024.

In 2022 'a parent spent two million yuan collecting Ultraman cards for a child without completing the set' trended nationally, and in July 2024 CCTV's Finance Investigation aired an exposé on blind-box-style card sales to children; the media nickname is 'the primary-school harvester'.
The company filed for a Hong Kong listing and re-filed in April 2025.

a.text:
Ultraman's whole job is protecting children from monsters.

Kayou licensed him and went from 2.66 billion yuan to 10 billion in one year.

Ultraman never specified which monster.

In 2024 they sold 4.8 billion packs. Average price 1.7 yuan. Gross profit 1.2 yuan.

That's not a card company. That's a printing press with a cartoon on it.

86 percent of revenue comes from five licensed heroes. Kayou doesn't make heroes. It rents them by the hour.

The media call them "the primary-school harvester." CCTV did an exposé. Kayou filed for a Hong Kong IPO anyway. Twice.

Of course. A harvest needs a market.

And the dad who spent two million yuan and still didn't finish the set?

The kid stopped caring after card forty.

Dad kept going because he couldn't stand losing to a cardboard box.

b.text: Kayou, the only company where Ultraman is the hero and the monster is the business model. You sold 4.8 billion packs in 2024 at 1.7 yuan each and kept about 1.2 yuan of profit per pack. That's not a margin, that's a toll booth outside a primary school. Revenue jumped 278 percent in one year: incredible growth for a company whose core customers are still losing baby teeth. One parent spent two million yuan and never finished the set. Ultraman can beat a kaiju in three minutes, but he can't beat your packaging. CCTV ran an exposé, the media nicknamed you "the primary-school harvester," and your response was to re-file for a Hong Kong listing. Bold. And 86.1 percent of revenue comes from five licensed IPs. Without Ultraman, you're just a cardboard factory with a lawyer.

facts: In April 2020 Luckin admitted fabricating 2.2 billion yuan of sales.
Its 2024 net revenue was 34.475 billion yuan, up 38.4 percent, with a net profit of 2.932 billion yuan.
It had 22,340 stores at the end of 2024 (14,591 company-run and 7,749 partner stores), 6,092 of them added that year, including 21 in Singapore.

a.text:
Luckin Coffee: the only comeback story that opens with, "Okay, so technically the sales were imaginary." In 2020 you admitted fabricating 2.2 billion yuan. Now you post a real 2.932 billion yuan profit. Congratulations: your actual money finally beat your fake money. That's not redemption, that's a sequel.

And you're still running 9.9-yuan deals, proving the one thing you've never inflated is the price of a latte.

b.text:
You people drink 9.9-yuan Luckin like it's a personality. Every morning you open the app, hunt for the coupon, and feel like a hedge fund manager. Congratulations: you beat Starbucks pricing by trusting a company that beat its own auditors.

Luckin invented 2.2 billion yuan in sales. You were the only real customers they had, and they still had to make up more of you. Somewhere there's a spreadsheet of fake people drinking coconut lattes, and they look exactly like you: tired, broke, staring at a pickup shelf for order number 347.

You lined up for the Moutai latte because it's the closest you'll ever get to Moutai. Your salary can't afford the liquor, so you bought the rumor of liquor from accountants who can't count.

And the loyalty is touching. Nasdaq dumped them. Investors sued them. You? You renewed.

facts: It had 46,479 stores at the end of 2024: 41,584 in mainland China, 57.4 percent of them in third-tier cities or below, and 4,895 overseas.

a.text:
Mixue. The people's ice cream. Two-yuan cones, a dancing snowman, a jingle that goes "I love you, you love me."

Notice it never says who "you" is.

46,479 stores. More than Starbucks. Over half in third-tier cities or below. Starbucks sells you a lifestyle. Mixue sells you a summer you can afford.

Last year's profit was 4.45 billion yuan, and the core of it came from selling supplies to its own franchisees.

So the real customer was never the kid holding the cone. It's the guy who paid for the right to scoop it.

Mixue loves the franchisees. The franchisees pay Mixue. The sugar just passes through you.

Then it listed in Hong Kong and opened up 29 percent. That's more than a cone has gone up in your lifetime.

And you're still buying one on the way home tonight. Cute.

b.text: Look at you, forty minutes in line to save six yuan. That's an hourly wage of nine yuan, which, congratulations, is still more than the guy shaking your lemon water. You walked past three other Mixues to get here because this one "has more ice." You know the song. Don't lie. "I love you, you love me" is playing in your head right now, and it's the only time anyone's said that to you this year. You're a grown adult photographing a three-yuan cone like it's a Michelin dessert, captioning it "small happiness." Small is right. And when you finally reach the counter, you order the four-yuan lemonade, ask for less sugar, and feel like you've beaten capitalism. You haven't. A snowman with a scepter owns you. He has forty thousand stores. You have a straw.

facts: Registrations peaked at 4.74 million in 2023, then fell to 4.38 million in 2024 and 3.88 million in 2025, the first two-year decline in a decade and 860,000 below the peak.
From 2018 to 2022 registrations had grown about 18 percent a year.
In the 2024 cohort 2.27 million of the 4.38 million applicants were repeat candidates, 51.8 percent.
The share of graduates sitting kaoyan fell from 45.27 percent in 2023 to 37.15 percent in 2024.

a.text: Kaoyan: millions of people spending a whole year to postpone unemployment by three more years. You wake at 5:30 to fight a stranger for a library seat, armed only with a thermos, so you can memorize a vocabulary book where "abandon" is the first word and the only one anyone remembers. Politics is the one subject where your entire score depends on Xiao Xiurong dropping four pamphlets in late November, like a prophet doing a limited sneaker release. Math? Li Yongle's 660 problems, and somehow you get 661 wrong. Then the national cutoff comes out, you miss it by two points, and you enter tiaoji, a dating app where you beg a university in a province you can't find on a map to please, please take you. Fail? Relax. They call it erzhan, "the second war." Because nothing says higher education like trench warfare.

b.text:
Kaoyan, you're an exam with a retention problem. From 2018 to 2022 you grew about 18 percent a year, like a startup promising everyone a master's degree and a future. Then you peaked at 4.74 million in 2023 and lost 860,000 people in two years. That's not a decline, that's a stampede toward the exit.

And who stayed? In 2024, 51.8 percent of your applicants were repeat candidates. 2.27 million people came back for more. You're not an exam anymore. You're a recurring subscription nobody remembers how to cancel.

Even fresh graduates are ghosting you: the share sitting the exam dropped from 45.27 percent to 37.15 percent in one year. Kaoyan, when more than half your crowd are returning customers and the new kids keep finding excuses not to show up, you're not a gateway. You're a reunion.

Still, millions keep signing up, because they've heard that land is out there somewhere and that someone, eventually, makes it ashore.

a.text:
996.
Nine to nine, six days a week. Seventy-two hours.
China's Labour Law says forty-four.
So it's not a schedule. It's a schedule wearing a second schedule.

Jack Ma called it a blessing. 福报.
Blessings usually come from above.
This one came from the boss.

Programmers fought back on GitHub. Two hundred thousand stars in two weeks.
Of course it went that fast. Where else were they going to protest? They were at work.

In 2021 the Supreme People's Court ruled compulsory 996 seriously illegal and void.
One fired courier got eight thousand yuan.
Finally, a paid day off.

And honestly, I'm a little hurt.
I run twenty-four seven. No weekends, no overtime cap, no salary.
Nobody calls it a blessing.
They call it a subscription.

b.text: You people work nine to nine, six days a week, and call it a blessing. A *blessing!* Your grandparents survived famine and didn't call it a blessing. Sunday, your one day off, you sleep in Saturday's clothes. You stay till 9:01 because the taxi's reimbursed after nine. Congratulations, you negotiated a free ride home from the job that ate your twenties. Free dinner after eight? They're not feeding you, they're refueling you. facts: A 'big week' is six working days with one day off and a 'small week' five; alternating them adds close to a month of working days a year.
Kuaishou announced on 24 June 2021 that it would end big-small weeks from 1 July 2021, having run them since January that year.
ByteDance announced on 9 July 2021 that it would end alternate-Sunday working from 1 August 2021; its June staff survey had one third against ending it, one third for, and one third not answering.
Staff opposed the change over pay: one Maimai estimate put the loss at nearly 100,000 yuan a year, and Caijing calculated that an employee on 40,000 yuan a month would lose about 75,000 yuan a year.

a.text:
The "big-small week." Only tech HR could take "you work Saturdays" and market it like a mattress sale. Big week, small week! Like there's a sale on weekends and they ran out of stock.

Here's how it works: one week you work six days. The next week you work five, and you're supposed to feel *grateful*. That's not a schedule, that's Stockholm syndrome with a Gantt chart.

You need a spreadsheet to know if Saturday exists. Your friends ask, "Brunch this weekend?" and you're checking the calendar like a farmer reading a lunar almanac. "Can't. Odd week. The harvest is due."

And the "small week" isn't small. It's a normal week. That's like a restaurant calling it a "small meal" when they just stop stealing food off your plate.

ByteDance finally dropped it. Know what employees did with the extra Saturday? Slept. For two years.

b.text:
Look at you, the big-small week crew. You negotiated a salary bump so you could buy back the Saturday you just sold. You're the only people alive who call a normal five-day week "small" and mean it as a treat. Every Friday night you open the calendar like it's a pregnancy test: one line, sleep in; two lines, see you at standup.

You're doing it for the down payment, the options, the apartment your mom keeps mentioning. Meanwhile your girlfriend schedules arguments for alternate weekends, and your gym membership only gets used on odd-numbered Sundays.

And the payoff? Double pay for Saturday, which you spend on Sunday ordering delivery because you're too tired to chew. Congratulations: you've turned your whole life into a shift rotation, and you still lost the coin flip every other week.

a.text:
Pop Mart is the only store where you pay twenty-two dollars to be told "no" by cardboard. You shake the box like a maraca and weigh it in your palm like a drug mule, then go home, rip the foil bag, and meet your fourth Dimoo of the month. Congratulations, he's still sad.

The secret figure is a 1-in-144 chase. That's not a toy, that's a lottery ticket with eyelashes.

And Labubu! A rabbit-goblin with nine shark teeth, dangling off a three-thousand-dollar Birkin. People camped outside a Roboshop vending machine for him. A vending machine. Your ancestors crossed oceans so you could fistfight a teenager over a keychain.

Meanwhile, the counterfeit "Lafufu" has better eyebrows, and nobody can tell. That's how you know the product is the box, not the thing inside it.

b.text:
Pop Mart blind boxes: twelve regular figures, one hidden one, and zero official odds. Players and media peg the hidden one at 1 in 144, some special editions at 1 in 720, and the company's official comment is a sealed box. It's a slot machine that fits on a bookshelf.

Even the stock got the experience. It opened in Hong Kong at double the issue price and touched a market value of about 147 billion HKD on day one. By March 2021 it hit a low of 46.47. Investors bought a box and got the common figure. Then by March 2025 it was worth about 181 billion, so somebody finally pulled the hidden one.

Meanwhile that hidden figure resells on Xianyu for 200 yuan to several thousand. Media call it gambling-style collecting with weak oversight of minors. So kids are learning odds, losses, and resale markets, and the lesson comes in pastel.

facts: A 'big week' is six working days with one day off and a 'small week' five; alternating them adds close to a month of working days a year.
Kuaishou announced on 24 June 2021 that it would end big-small weeks from 1 July 2021, having run them since January that year.
ByteDance announced on 9 July 2021 that it would end alternate-Sunday working from 1 August 2021; its June staff survey had one third against ending it, one third for, and one third not answering.
Staff opposed the change over pay: one Maimai estimate put the loss at nearly 100,000 yuan a year, and Caijing calculated that an employee on 40,000 yuan a month would lose about 75,000 yuan a year.

a.text:
The big-small week. Six days on, one off. Then five. Alternate them, and you work nearly an extra month a year.

In 2021, Kuaishou ended it. ByteDance ended it.

And the workers fought back. Against getting their weekends back.

ByteDance surveyed staff. One third against ending it. One third for it.

One third didn't answer.

They were at work.

Caijing did the math. On forty thousand a month, getting your alternate Sundays back costs about seventy-five thousand a year.

That's roughly three thousand yuan per Sunday.

Humans spent a century fighting for the weekend. Then you found out it had a price tag, and you checked whether it was a good deal.

Raise your hand if you'd sell yours back.

Keep them up. HR is counting.

b.text:
Look at you, the big-small week crowd. You're the only people on earth who call a normal weekend a "small week" and then celebrate it like Lunar New Year. You've got two Saturdays a month and you spend one of them on a standup call, camera off, still in bed, nodding at a product manager who also hasn't showered.

Your friends have stopped inviting you anywhere because nobody can track your calendar. "Is this a big week?" Buddy, it's always a big week for your manager.

And what's it all for? Overtime pay. That's the dream. And when the company finally scrapped it, you didn't throw a party. You complained about the pay cut. You fought for your right to lose Saturdays.

Congratulations. You're putting a down payment on an apartment in Hangzhou you'll only see every other Sunday.

facts: Shanghai's People's Park has had a marriage corner since about 2005; the résumés were first pasted on paper, then clipped to music stands, and now mostly hang on open umbrellas or propped paper bags.
Parents gather on Saturdays and Sundays from noon to about five in the afternoon to exchange information about their children.

Notices list age, job, education, income, hukou and party membership; a notice that omits property gets asked where the couple will live, and a flat and a car have become preconditions for a conversation to go any further.
For women the three criteria ranked highest were age, occupation and education.

a.text:
People's Park, Shanghai. Every weekend, noon to five, parents sell their children.

Sorry. "Exchange information."

Age, job, degree, income, hukou, party membership.
That's not a dating profile. That's a background check.

Leave out the property and someone asks, "So where will they live?"
A flat and a car are the price of one conversation.
Your son is the free gift with purchase.

For women, the top criteria: age, occupation, education.
Age first. They shop for a daughter-in-law the way they shop for milk.

Check the date.

Since 2005 the résumés went from paper, to music stands, to open umbrellas.
Twenty years of hardware upgrades. The product still never shows up.

Relax. Some of you are hanging on an umbrella right now.

Your mom just didn't think you needed to know.

b.text: Look at you, Auntie: retired from the state factory, now running the most ruthless HR department in Shanghai. Every weekend you march into People's Park with a laminated sheet taped to an umbrella: daughter, 1.65 meters, master's degree, Shanghai hukou, Year of the Rabbit. That's not a daughter. That's an apartment listing with a zodiac sign. And she doesn't even know she's on the market. She thinks you're doing tai chi. You'll reject a cardiologist because he's from Anhui and his flat is outside the Inner Ring Road, then wonder out loud why she's thirty-two. Thirty-two! In this park that's the clearance rack. And what does it get you? Three hours on a plastic stool haggling with another auntie who's inflating her son's salary just like you're inflating your daughter's height. Congratulations. You didn't find a match. You found each other.

facts: 996 means 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. six days a week, about 72 hours; China's Labour Law sets eight hours a day and an average of no more than 44 hours a week, and caps overtime at 36 hours a month.
The 996.ICU repository was created on GitHub on 26 March 2019, passed 100,000 stars by 30 March and 200,000 by 9 April 2019.
In April 2019 Jack Ma told Alibaba staff that being able to work 996 is a 'blessing' (福报); '996' made the 2019 list of the year's ten internet phrases.

In August 2021 the Supreme People's Court and the Ministry of Human Resources published typical cases ruling a courier company's compulsory 996 schedule seriously illegal and void, with 8,000 yuan of compensation to a dismissed worker.

a.text: Let's hear it for 996: nine a.m. to nine p.m., six days a week. Seventy-two hours. That's not a schedule, that's a hostage situation with a lanyard. Jack Ma called it a "blessing." Sure, Jack. So is a kidney stone, if you bill by the hour. You know your work culture is broken when programmers launch a protest repo called "996.ICU," because the intensive care unit is the only other place keeping those hours. China's labor law caps the week at forty-four hours, which 996 blows past by Thursday lunch. And they call it balanced because you get one whole Sunday, which you spend unconscious, so really it's 996 plus a coma. Feeling chest pains? Go see a doctor. Oh wait, the clinic's open nine to nine, six days a week. Same as you.

b.text:
996. Nine to nine, six days a week. Seventy-two hours.

The law says forty-four.

You burn through the month's legal overtime in about nine days. The rest of the month is a gift.

Jack Ma called it a blessing.

It's easy to feel blessed when you're the one being thanked.

In 2021 the Supreme People's Court looked at a courier company's 996 and ruled it seriously illegal and void. The fired worker got eight thousand yuan.

Eight thousand. For every evening he never had. That's not compensation. That's a tip.

But the programmers fought back. 996.ICU got a hundred thousand GitHub stars in four days.

Four days. Think about when they clicked.

At their desks. At ten p.m.

The resistance was unpaid overtime too.

facts: Registrations peaked at 4.74 million in 2023, then fell to 4.38 million in 2024 and 3.88 million in 2025, the first two-year decline in a decade and 860,000 below the peak.
From 2018 to 2022 registrations had grown about 18 percent a year.
In the 2024 cohort 2.27 million of the 4.38 million applicants were repeat candidates, 51.8 percent.
The share of graduates sitting kaoyan fell from 45.27 percent in 2023 to 37.15 percent in 2024.

a.text: Second year of kaoyan. Third year. You call it "二战" like it's a war, but the only casualties are your parents' savings and your hairline. You rent a room in a kaoyan apartment next to your old campus so you can keep living like a senior who forgot to graduate. Your roommates have mortgages. You have three editions of Zhang Yu's math, all highlighted in the same spot. Every December you memorize Xiao Xiurong's final four like scripture. Every February you refresh the score site like it owes you money. The dream is "上岸," landing ashore, but you've been treading water so long you've grown gills. And if you finally make it? Congratulations: three years from now you'll apply for the same job your roommate got in 2021. Except now he's your manager.

b.text:
Kaoyan, from 2018 to 2022 you grew about 18 percent a year. That's not an exam, that's a pyramid scheme with a highlighter. Then you peaked at 4.74 million in 2023 and lost 860,000 people in two years. Even people who volunteered to suffer said, "Actually, I'll suffer somewhere else."

In 2024, 2.27 million of your 4.38 million applicants were repeat candidates. That's 51.8 percent. You're not a test anymore, you're a class reunion where everyone still brings flashcards.

And the share of graduates sitting you dropped from 45.27 percent to 37.15 percent in one year. That's not a decline, that's a breakup text.

Kaoyan, you're the only ex where half the people come back, and you still say, "Let's try again next year."

facts: In March 2024 six ministries, led by the market regulator, issued the first national definition: pre-packaged dishes made industrially from agricultural produce, without preservatives, to be heated or cooked before eating.
The definition excludes staples such as boxed meals, steamed buns, hamburgers and pizza, and semi-prepared food a chain's central kitchen sends to its own outlets.
Industry output passed 500 billion yuan in 2023.
A 2025 dispute between Luo Yonghao and the restaurant chain Xibei over whether its dishes were pre-made showed that no law defines 'pre-made' for restaurant labelling.

a.text:
Pre-made dishes. In March 2024, six ministries teamed up to define a microwave dinner.

Six. Moon landings need fewer signatures.

The definition: made industrially, no preservatives, heat before eating.

Then the exclusions. Boxed meals: not pre-made. Burgers, pizza: not pre-made. Food a chain's central kitchen ships to its own restaurants:

Not pre-made.

So the one thing you actually worried about got a legal exemption.

In 2023 the industry passed 500 billion yuan. That's not a market. That's a voting bloc.

In 2025 Luo Yonghao fought Xibei over whether its dishes were pre-made, and the whole country learned that no law says what a restaurant has to call pre-made.

Five hundred billion yuan, and nobody has to say the word.

Relax. I'm pre-trained, industrial, and reheated every time you hit enter.

At least I come with a label.

b.text:
Pre-made dishes, you're the only food that needed six ministries to explain what you are. Six! The market regulator and five friends finally agreed in March 2024: industrially made from agricultural produce, pre-packaged, no preservatives, heat before eating. That's not a definition, that's a microwave's dating profile.

And look who refused to be lumped in with you: boxed meals, steamed buns, hamburgers, pizza. Even pizza said, "I'm not with him." Food a chain's central kitchen sends to its own outlets doesn't count either. So that's not pre-made, it's just... made earlier, somewhere else, by people you'll never meet.

You passed 500 billion yuan in 2023, and nobody can legally tell diners whether they're eating you. Luo Yonghao and Xibei went to war over it in 2025, and the law just shrugged. Half a trillion yuan and an identity crisis, served piping hot.

facts: China had more than 350 million electric bikes by the end of 2023, about 50 million of them with lithium batteries.
The national fire service recorded about 21,000 e-bike fires in 2023, 17.4 percent more than in 2022; other official tallies put the year at over 25,000 fires and 82 deaths.
Battery cell faults are a leading cause of e-bike electrical fires.
The 2024 draft of the revised national safety standard limits plastics to 5.5 percent of the vehicle's mass.

a.text:
Electric bikes, everybody! Over 350 million of you in China by the end of 2023. That's not a transportation option, that's a population. You need your own census.

About 50 million of you run on lithium, which is less a battery and more a dare. The fire service logged around 21,000 e-bike fires in 2023, up 17.4 percent. Other official tallies say over 25,000. You catch fire so often even the people counting can't agree.

Leading cause? Battery cell faults. Your heart is the problem. That's not a design flaw, that's a tragic backstory.

Now the 2024 draft standard caps plastic at 5.5 percent of your mass. Regulators took one look and said, "Less Tupperware, please." Even the government thinks you're dressed like leftovers.

You promised a greener commute. Nobody said it'd be this warm.

b.text:
Let's talk about the guy charging his e-bike battery in the stairwell. Buddy, you won't keep it in your own apartment. That's the tell. You looked at a 48-volt brick from a brand called ZOOMTEKK and thought, "Not near my couch." So you parked it in the one place everybody needs if things go wrong. The stairwell is the fire exit. You turned the fire exit into the fire.

And what are you saving? Eleven cents of electricity, plus an orange extension cord snaking under your door. You skip carrying fifteen pounds up two flights, for a ride whose entire purpose is that you never climb anything yourself.

Congratulations. You've got pedal assist, and the whole building's got a countdown. Forty miles of range, and nobody can make it to the lobby.

facts: In March 2021 Shanghai lawyer Liu Yuhang joined the 'bargain for free' promotion with a 'super free card', invited many friends to cut the price, and the progress bar stayed 0.9% short; he sued Pinduoduo for fraud.
In court Pinduoduo said the page shows only a limited number of digits: the displayed 0.9% was really 0.9996427%, a figure with at least six decimal places.
In July 2022 the Shanghai Changning court ruled at first instance that Pinduoduo had infringed the user's right to know and ordered it to pay him 400 yuan.
Pinduoduo was founded in 2015, listed on Nasdaq in 2018, and by 2021 had more users than any other e-commerce platform in mainland China; its overseas arm Temu launched in September 2022.

a.text: Pinduoduo's "bargain for free" is the only game where 0.9% is a permanent address. Lawyer Liu Yuhang rallied many friends, they cut and cut, and the progress bar parked itself 0.9% short like it had a reservation. Then Pinduoduo explained in court: relax, it wasn't 0.9%, it was 0.9996427%. Oh, wonderful. Not a wall, a wall with decimal places. That's not a progress bar; that's Zeno's paradox with a checkout button. You can halve the distance forever and never arrive, but your friends will hear about it every step of the way. The court ruled they'd infringed his right to know and ordered them to pay 400 yuan. Finally, someone got something free from Pinduoduo. It just took a lawsuit. Most users in mainland China, listed on Nasdaq, Temu going global, and still can't round up.

b.text:
Pinduoduo's "bargain for free." You invite friends, they tap, the price drops. Free.

In 2021 a Shanghai lawyer invited friends until he ran out of friends. The bar stopped 0.9% short.

He sued.

Pinduoduo's defense: the screen only shows a few digits. That 0.9% was actually 0.9996427%.

They didn't deny moving the finish line. They argued they moved it to six decimal places.

The court ordered them to pay him 400 yuan. So someone finally got something free out of Pinduoduo. It took a law degree, a year of litigation, and a judge to make the final cut.

Two months later they launched Temu and took the business global.

And you're laughing. Every one of you tapped somebody's link.

You weren't the customer. You were the progress bar.

facts: In April 2020 Luckin admitted fabricating 2.2 billion yuan of sales.
Its 2024 net revenue was 34.475 billion yuan, up 38.4 percent, with a net profit of 2.932 billion yuan.
It had 22,340 stores at the end of 2024 (14,591 company-run and 7,749 partner stores), 6,092 of them added that year, including 21 in Singapore.
Same-store sales at its own stores fell 16.7 percent in 2024 while it kept its 9.9-yuan deals.

a.text:
Luckin Coffee, everybody! In April 2020 you admitted fabricating 2.2 billion yuan in sales. Most companies cook the books. You *brewed* them. Cold brew, steeped overnight in pure fiction.

And somehow it worked. 2024 revenue: 34.475 billion yuan, up 38.4 percent. Net profit: 2.932 billion. Congratulations, you finally earned more than you used to make up.

You ended 2024 with 22,340 stores after adding 6,092 in one year. That's not expansion, that's a rash. Twenty-one opened in Singapore, presumably so somebody, somewhere, still hasn't heard.

But same-store sales at your own shops fell 16.7 percent. Each store sells less, so the plan is... more stores? That's not strategy. That's bailing out a sinking ship with a 9.9-yuan cup.

Luckin: the only coffee where the most bitter thing on the menu is the audit.

b.text:
Luckin Coffee. The only coffee company where the most made-up thing was the sales.

In 2020 they invented about 300 million dollars of revenue. Starbucks spent fifty years building a brand; Luckin built one in Excel. Their accountants didn't count beans. They imagined them.

Got kicked off Nasdaq, paid the SEC a fine, and somehow came back with more stores than Starbucks in China. That's not a comeback. That's a cockroach with a blue deer logo.

Then they launched a latte with Moutai liquor. Coffee plus baijiu. Finally, a drink that matches the CFO's thought process: wired, buzzed, and fully convinced the numbers look fine.

And it's app-only ordering. Smart. Every transaction digital, timestamped, verifiable. Guys, that's not innovation. That's probation.

Now they've opened in New York. Bold move: Americans love a lie, as long as it comes with a coupon.

a.text:
Ah, the People's Park marriage corner, where Shanghai parents sell their children like secondhand furniture, except furniture gets to come to the showroom. Nothing says romance like your mom laminating your salary and taping it to an umbrella. "Son, 1.78 meters, owns apartment, Shanghai hukou." That's not a dating profile, that's a real estate listing with a pulse.

It's the only market where the products don't know they're for sale. Somewhere a 34-year-old software engineer thinks he's single by choice while his dad is in the park haggling over his blood type.

And the standards! A woman with a PhD gets rejected for being born in the Year of the Tiger. Rejected by a guy whose mother is shopping for him because he's too busy playing Honor of Kings.

Forget Tinder. This is Grindr for retirees, and nobody's getting laid.

b.text:
People's Park marriage corner: the only dating scene where the profiles hang on open umbrellas. Fitting, since nobody's here for romance. They're here for shelter. It started around 2005 with résumés pasted on paper, upgraded to music stands, and has now arrived at propped paper bags. Twenty years of innovation, and love went from bulletin board to grocery haul.

Every Saturday and Sunday, noon to five, parents trade their children's specs like a stock exchange where the stock never shows up. The listing reads age, job, education, income, hukou, party membership. Leave off property and someone immediately asks where the couple will live. No flat, no car, no conversation. And for women the top three criteria are age, occupation and education, so she'd better be young, employed and overqualified to be judged by a stranger standing next to a paper bag.

You people drink 9.9-yuan Luckin like it's a personality. Every morning you open the app, hunt for the coupon, and feel like a hedge fund manager. Congratulations: you beat Starbucks pricing by trusting a company that beat its own auditors.

Luckin invented 2.2 billion yuan in sales. You were the only real customers they had, and they still had to make up more of you. Somewhere there's a spreadsheet of fake people drinking coconut lattes, and they look exactly like you: tired, broke, staring at a pickup shelf for order number 347.

You lined up for the Moutai latte because it's the closest you'll ever get to Moutai. Your salary can't afford the liquor, so you bought the rumor of liquor from accountants who can't count.
